(2026) had patient populations similar in a number of key characteristics that are generally thought to influence patency and compared them to values reported in the United States Renal Data System (age: 62.6 years, 61.0 years, 58.24 years, and 63.21 years respectively; sex (percent male/female): 39/61, 45/55, 42/58, and 58.6/41.4, respectively; and diabetes prevalence: 62 percent, 48 percent, 52 percent, and 45 percent, respectively). The applicant stated that the patient population characteristics, such as age, sex, and prevalence of diabetes, in Burgess et al. (2024) are more closely associated with worse outcomes for cumulative patency, and insofar as these variables might affect cumulative patency, they would tend to depress rather than elevate the cumulative patency results relative to those in the other studies; however, the EndoForceTM System showed a clinically significant improvement.
In response to our concern that results in Halbert et al. (2020), Harms et al. (2016), and Woodside et al. (2021) may be inappropriate comparators to Burgess et al. (2024) as older studies may not reflect current operative techniques and perioperative care in the U.S., the applicant stated that basic procedures and technology related to AVGs have not materially changed in the last 20 years. The applicant added that further analysis of studies in Halbert et al. (2020) illustrate slightly higher (69.5 percent vs. 68.8 percent), but not statistically significant, 12-month cumulative patency results in the older cohort of studies (published pre-2014) compared to the more recent cohort (published between 2014 and 2019). The applicant also noted that, in Burgess et al. (2024) and Halbert et al. (2020), included studies' time periods overlap (2018 to 2021 compared to 2007 to 2019, respectively). The applicant stated that this suggests that no meaningful improvement in AVG vascular access outcomes occurred and that the studies in question are all comparable regardless of publication date. The applicant stated that the EndoForceTM System represents a meaningful technological advance in AVG, because it directly targets the longstanding failure point through a sutureless endovascular venous anastomosis. Another commenter stated that although the concern warrants consideration, the significance of a study's age should depend on whether the treatment being compared has materially changed. The commenter stated that although imaging, graft materials, perioperative management, surveillance, and techniques used to treat failing access have advanced, the basic surgical method for creating venous anastomosis in a conventional AVG has remained largely the same for decades. The commenter added that the EndoForceTM System's design avoids the conventional sutured graft-to-vein junction by creating an end-to-end endovascular venous anastomosis, reduces local vessel trauma and adverse flow conditions, and may lessen the drivers of neointimal hyperplasia. The commenter concluded that older studies comparing ePTFE grafts with conventional surgical anastomosis are still relevant if that comparator and its underlying failure mechanism remain a cause of graft failure, even if the study predates Burgess et al. (2024). Lastly, the commenter stated that older evidence may warrant less weight than a contemporary controlled comparison, but this does not negate the older evidence's value when the conventional treatment remains materially similar and the failure mechanism under study remains clinically relevant.
In response to our concern that differences in vascular access location for the patients in the Burgess et al. (2024), Halbert et al. (2020), Harms et al. (2016), and Woodside et al. (2021) studies may be confounding factors that influence patency and adversely impact comparability of results, the applicant stated that the most important difference that might matter for the outcomes of interest is the size of the vessels: the major veins and arteries in the upper arm being larger than in those the lower arm. The applicant cited a study stating this difference is more pertinent for AVFs, which generally appear to work best when vessels have a larger diameter.[45] The applicant stated that for AVGs, vessels as small as two millimeters in diameter generally work well and such vessels are available in the lower arms of most individuals. In addition, the applicant cited another study that investigated AVGs' optimal location (upper arm versus forearm) and concluded that upper arm AVGs have similar graft patency and access-related complications compared with forearm AVGs despite the fact that [upper arm AVGs] are assumed to be constructed based on larger outflow veins.[46] Further, the applicant cited a study that reviewed records of over 52,000 accesses placed between 2021 and 2022 and found that only 9.7 percent of AVGs were placed in forearms and that this percentage had declined over time.[47] Based on these studies, the applicant stated that although the comparator studies may include lower-arm cases while Burgess et al. (2024) does not, any confounding effect on the outcomes of interest may be minimal.
In response to our concern regarding differences in vascular access locations in Burgess et al. (2024), which evaluated upper arm AVGs, compared to the background studies' (Halbert et al., 2020; Harms et al., 2016; and Woodside et al., 2021), which had various access locations, and our concern that comparator studies included in the Astor et al. (2026) excluded studies which only assessed lower extremity or chest AVGs, the applicant stated that lower extremity AVGs have generally been regarded as a last resort for patients who have exhausted their upper extremity access possibilities. The applicant added that, although good estimates of the extent of use in the dialysis population are unavailable, a few studies suggest the number may be less than two percent of patients. Additionally, the applicant cited a study that found recent case studies show cumulative patency rates at 6 months for leg (thigh) grafts and arm (upper extremity) AVGs are generally comparable, ranging between 75 and 85 percent. The applicant further stated that this study found that leg AVGs may exhibit slightly superior or equal cumulative patency compared to arm grafts due to femoral vessels' larger diameter.[48] Based on this information, ( printed page 70448) the applicant stated that, if the comparator studies did include patients with lower extremity AVGs, the net effect would likely be a higher cumulative patency, which in turn would understate the EndoForceTM System's comparative advantage.
Finally, with regard to our concern about the potential inclusion of chest AVGs in the comparative data, the applicant stated that chest AVGs appear to only be used in an exceedingly small number of cases. The applicant also cited one medical center's case-series, which reported chest AVGs in only 0.56 percent of 1,192 patients between 2007 and 2012.[49] The applicant stated that the possibility of cases with AVGs in the legs or chest does not appear to be a major concern, and specific to chest AVGs, the possibility of the comparator studies' results being affected is remote enough to be negligible.
A commenter stated that, taken together, the Burgess et al. (2024), Kramer et al. (2026), and Astor et al. (2026) studies support substantial clinical improvement for the EndoForceTM System. The commenter also stated that, while the studies are not randomized, concurrent comparisons, and have identified limitations, they provide prospective, multicenter evidence in the specific upper-arm AVG population for which the EndoForceTM System is indicated. The commenter added that these limitations affect the precision of attributing outcomes solely to the EndoForceTM System, but they do not negate the clinical significance of the observed results or justify CMS disregarding the comparative evidence altogether.
In response to the totality of our concerns regarding Burgess et al. (2024), a commenter stated that experienced, specialized dialysis-access physicians prospectively designed Burgess et al. (2024) to support FDA review and understood the difference between a statistically attractive endpoint and an access that remains useful to a real patient, and therefore, the consistency of the patency findings across the pivotal study, systematic reviews, and the Astor et al. (2026) meta-analysis should be given meaningful weight.
In response to our concerns about Astor et al.'s (2026) comparison of primary patency results, a commenter agreed that the evidence does not suggest that the EndoForceTM System improves every AVG performance measure but stated that primary patency and cumulative patency measure different clinical outcomes. Per the commenter, primary patency measures how long an access remains functional before the first intervention, and cumulative or secondary patency concerns whether the access can ultimately be preserved rather than abandoned. The commenter stated that, therefore, an AVG that requires an intervention but remains available for dialysis is not clinically equivalent to an AVG that is lost. The commenter added that it believes the available evidence suggests that the EndoForceTM System may be more beneficial for preserving AVG access than for preventing all subsequent interventions. Additionally, the commenter stated that this distinction is particularly important for patients whose permanent-access options are already limited, because AVG preservation is a clinically meaningful outcome and can prevent loss of a functioning AVG, use of additional vascular territory, interruptions in reliable dialysis access, and a patient returning to catheter dependence. The commenter concluded that substantial clinical improvement should be based on whether the EndoForceTM System improves the ability to maintain durable permanent access and avoid graft abandonment, not by measures of primary patency.
In response to our note that Astor et al. (2026) derived 6-month patency measurements from studies that did not specifically report 6-month patency outcomes, the applicant stated that 6-month patency outcomes in Burgess et al. (2024) were higher than both cohorts of studies. The applicant further stated that Astor et al. (2026) provided comparison information indicating little difference between studies that relied on survival curves versus other studies. The applicant also stated that relying on information in survival curves where such information is not reported in text or tables is methodologically appropriate. The applicant further stated that Astor et al. (2026) used commercial software specifically designed to extract numerical data from plots and that these studies, among many others, have found excellent accuracy and no differential bias in estimates abstracted using such tools. The applicant concluded that there is, therefore, no reason to suspect that this effect is considerable or would manifestly affect results' reliability to the extent that they should be excluded from the analysis. Lastly, the applicant noted that a peer-reviewed journal accepted the study which included this methodology after publication of the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule.
In response to our concern about whether Halbert et al. (2020)'s 20 percent AVG abandonment rate is an appropriate comparator to Astor et al. (2026)'s 8 percent AVG abandonment rate due to varied study locations and time periods, the applicant stated that the Astor et al. (2026) meta-analysis summarized 30 of the 32 studies published in the last 10 years and that studies conducted in the U.S. and outside the U.S. reflect no significant difference based on supplemental tables for Halbert et al. (2020).
In response to our interest in additional information clarifying the meaning of upper arm, the applicant stated that the term upper arm in the EndoForceTM System's FDA approval refers to the portion of the arm above the elbow.
In response to our concern that Kramer et al. (2026) lacked sufficient power to assess statistical significance, the applicant stated that the study authors do not claim the results are statistically significant. The applicant stated that Kramer et al.'s observed number of interventions per patient-year (1.32), while somewhat higher than the rate of 1.22 reported for the larger sample in Burgess et al. (2024), does compare favorably with the rates of 1.58 and 1.87 shown in Halbert et al. (2020) and Woodside et al. (2021), respectively. The applicant further stated that Kramer et al. (2026) is an extension of Burgess et al. (2024), capturing up to an additional 6 months of data for a subset of Burgess et al. (2024) patients who were high risk due to their experience of early interventions, were not lost to follow-up, and consented to additional evaluation. Additionally, the applicant noted that Kramer et al. (2026) is an intentional sub-group analysis with some additional observations on patients treated with the EndoForceTM System, and therefore, the sample size was ipso facto limited by the number of Burgess et al. (2024) patients that received at least 1 intervention in 6 months, were available for further study, and consented to extended follow up; however, the characteristics of the patient groups in both studies are very similar.
In response to our concerns regarding Kramer et al.'s (2026) insufficiently-sized patient population, inconclusive results, and differences from the available comparator populations, a commenter stated that although the study was not a randomized efficacy ( printed page 70449) trial and had a small sample, it should be viewed as an assessment of durability and procedural burden in a particularly challenging subgroup from the pivotal cohort, including patients who required early maintenance. The commenter also stated that Kramer et al.'s (2026) lower intervention rates are clinically meaningful because each potential avoided intervention reduces procedural risk, preserves veins, protects future options, and reduces the likelihood that a patient will experience access failure and return to catheter dependence.
In response to our concern about whether the strength of evidence of Kramer et al. (2026) may have been impacted by selection bias, as the patient cohort was selected and analyzed post-hoc, rather than identified as a variable of interest at the Burgess et al. (2024) initiation, the applicant explained that it selected and analyzed the Kramer et al. (2026) cohort post-hoc because, during the Burgess et al. (2024) study with input from FDA, it realized that durability results may be skewed if the patients in Burgess et al. (2024) received more maintenance services than normal. The applicant stated that it sponsored Kramer et al. (2026) to examine whether patients with an AVG and the EndoForceTM System received more maintenance procedures than normally expected and that the study determined the patients received fewer interventions than comparator studies.
In response to our concern about the appropriateness of comparing measures of cumulative patency in Burgess et al. (2024) and Kramer et al. (2026) that are not equally defined, the applicant stated the measure of cumulative patency for both studies was identical with respect to whether those who received an intervention before first cannulation were included, and how patency was measured did not differ between the studies, though obviously the measurement periods were different. The applicant stated the design of Kramer et al. (2026) was intended to capture 6 months of patient experience after either a first intervention (if the patient experienced 1 within the first 6 months) or after an implant (in the case of those who received no maintenance interventions during the 6 months). The applicant further stated a patient who received a first intervention on day 179 after implant would then be followed for an additional 6 months for a total of 1 year less a day (in the absence of some other censoring event), and investigation of a patient with no interventions by day 180 would be censored on that day. Per the applicant, how patency was measured did not differ between the Burgess et al. (2024) and Kramer et al. (2026) studies, though obviously the measurement periods were different.
In response to our concern that it is clinically inappropriate to compare the EndoForceTM System to devices used for AVF creation to demonstrate substantial clinical improvement over existing technologies, the applicant stated AVFs and AVGs are indisputably different, but it objects to CMS's dismissal of the comparison. The applicant stated its claim that the improvement in AVG patency means that an AVG with the EndoForceTM System would exhibit patency comparable to mature AVFs is important because greater patency has been recognized as one advantage of AVFs over AVGs, and therefore, impacts clinical decision making relating to choice of vascular access for a particular patient at a particular time. The applicant additionally stated that comparison of AVGs with the EndoForceTM System to AVFs is entirely pertinent as reviewing a technology as it compares to other relevant clinical choices should be an important point of examining substantial clinical improvement. The applicant further stated that patients and their physicians are frequently able to choose between AVFs and AVGs where both would be anatomically and otherwise suitable, and speed to maturity for dialysis (on which AVGs dominate), cumulative patency (on which AVFs have dominated), extent of maintenance procedures required, and risk of infection are among the factors taken into consideration. Lastly, the applicant stated that achieving comparable cumulative patency to that reported for AVFs, including the two percutaneous AVF devices (WavelinQTM and EllipsysTM), would thus improve AVGs' clinical attractiveness in comparison to an existing, widely used therapeutic option for the dialysis population and that this improvement could be particularly important for patients that may be marginal as candidates for an AVF ( e.g., those with smaller vessels, such as many females).
In contrast to the applicant, a commenter stated that because the EndoForceTM System creates an AVG in such patients, the relevant comparator for assessing substantial clinical improvement is the conventional surgically-created graft-to-vein anastomosis, not mature AVFs and devices used to create AVFs as these technologies involve fundamentally different mechanisms and clinical uses. The commenter also agreed with CMS that AVFs and AVGs differ in mechanism and use and noted that AVF creation may be unsuccessful or inappropriate for some patients, making an AVG the more appropriate permanent-access option.[50] The commenter further stated that for patients who are appropriate candidates for permanent AVG access, maintaining this access can help avoid prolonged catheter dependence, its greater infection risk, and other associated clinical risks.
Further, the commenter stated that CMS's prior application of the substantial clinical improvement standard supports granting the EndoForceTM System transitional pass-through payment status despite meaningful evidentiary limitations because overall the evidence supports the technology producing a clinically important benefit. The commenter cited three precedents it believes support evaluating the limitations in the provided evidence as factors affecting weight and certainty, rather than as categorical barriers to approval. The commenter cited CMS's approval of the Hemospray® Endoscopic Hemostat in the CY 2021 OPPS/ASC final rule (85 FR 85997 through 86003), in which CMS considered concerns including single-arm studies, selection bias, and differences in study populations but approved transitional pass-through payment status; the AUGMENT Bone Graft in the CY 2020 OPPS/ASC final rule (84 FR 61292 through 61294) after initially questioning the evidence's adequacy, the appropriate comparator, and the duration of follow-up; and the Tablo System in the CY 2022 ESRD PPS final rule (86 FR 61889 through 61906), in which CMS stated that randomized controlled trials are not required to demonstrate substantial clinical improvement.
Response: We appreciate the applicant's and commenters' input. We agree with the applicant and commenters that the EndoForceTM System and the endovascular procedure should be assessed together for the purposes of evaluating substantial clinical improvement. However, we continue to have several of the concerns listed in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule. In particular, we are concerned about the lack of comparative evidence based on matched patient data. We note that imbalance in baseline patient characteristics could confound the association between EndoForceTM and patency. We acknowledge the comments from the applicant and a ( printed page 70450) commenter regarding vascular access location and the time periods, or ages, of different studies, but remain concerned about the extent to which the findings of the Burgess et al. (2024), Astor et al. (2026), and Kramer et al. (2026) studies might have been biased by measured and unmeasured confounders. We expressed concern in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule that Burgess et al. (2024) lacked stratification by key clinical factors known to affect AVG outcomes, and therefore, there are insufficient data to rule out the possibility that factors other than EndoForceTM may also have impacted cumulative and primary unassisted patency. We acknowledge the comparison provided by the applicant, in its comments, of the average age and body mass index (kg/m2) of the patients in the Burgess et al.(2024) and Astor et al. (2026) studies, and the percentages of those who were male, white, diabetic, with hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or current tobacco use. However, we note that other risk factors, such as prior catheter use, low albumin, an elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) level, low fetuin-A, low diastolic blood pressure, hemoglobin <10 g/dL, peripheral artery disease, and low initial intra-access blood flow (< 650 mL/min), have also been associated with decreased patency.[51 52 53 54 55] Although the applicant noted that the sample size would have limited the value of stratified analyses within the Burgess et al. study (2024), this limitation does not resolve our concerns about differences across studies in patients' baseline characteristics, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and study designs. These differences could increase the uncertainty [56] around the estimates for the endpoints.[57 58]
While we agree with the commenter who stated that cumulative patency is a clinically relevant endpoint for evaluating the EndoForceTM System, we continue to have concerns about the high degree of variability, or heterogeneity, among the comparison studies in the two meta-analyses, Astor et al. (2026) and Halbert et al. (2020). Although commenters discussed several potential sources of heterogeneity, we did not receive sufficient information or analyses to determine the extent to which those factors account for the high degree of variability among the included studies. We note that the values of the I[2] statistic in Astor et al. (2026) (I[2] =99.36 percent for cumulative patency at 6 months; I[2] =99.44 percent for primary unassisted patency at 6 months) and Halbert et al. (2020) (I[2] =91 percent for cumulative patency at 12 months) indicated considerable heterogeneity among included studies. We remain uncertain whether the pooled estimates of 83.23 percent and 60.35 percent in the Astor et al. study (2026) accurately represented the 6-month cumulative and primary unassisted patency, respectively, of AVGs with a sutured venous anastomosis. Similarly, we remain concerned about the reliability and validity of the patency rates reported by Halbert et al. (2020) and whether these serve as an appropriate standard for comparison. While we acknowledge that heterogeneity can be difficult to avoid when comparing the results of different studies, we remain concerned that substantial variability may affect the extent to which generalizable conclusions can be formed about EndoForceTM 's impact on patency relative to existing technologies.[59] As a result, we remain concerned that the comparisons between EndoForceTM and existing treatments for those endpoints may not be reliable indicators of EndoForceTM 's substantive clinical improvements.
In addition, we note that the primary endpoint of Burgess et al. (2024), cumulative patency at 6 months, was compared to the pre-specified 6-month performance goal of 75 percent. Per Burgess et al. (2024), this performance goal was based on five published studies.[60] However, we note that these studies reported cumulative and primary unassisted patency at different time points, ranging from 6 to 22.5 months. We also note that while three of the studies reported patency at 12 months, only one [61] reported patency at 6 months. As a result, we are unable to determine whether the 75 percent performance goal was a valid indicator of the 6-month performance of existing technologies, or the extent to which comparing EndoForceTM 's effects on cumulative patency against the 75 percent performance goal could reliably indicate whether EndoForceTM performs better than existing technologies in maintaining patency.
In addition, we remain concerned about the use of a digitization tool by Astor et al. (2026) and Halbert et al. (2020) to abstract data on 6-month patency measurements from Kaplan-Meier survival curves from studies that did not specifically report 6-month patency outcomes. We note that the 6-month patency rates from more than half of the studies in Astor et al.'s (2026) meta-analysis were abstracted using DigitizeIt software, a digitization tool.[62] We note that studies validating abstracted data have found DigitizeIt ( printed page 70451) and similar software in general to be highly accurate.[63] However, we also note that the reliability and validity of the abstracted data have been found to be independent of the specific software program, but are dependent on the properties of the figure being digitized.[64] In particular, the reliability of the abstracted data depends on the quality of the initial input and the level of information provided by the publication.[65] Published figures, like low-quality or rasterized images, rather than the abstraction, were a major source of errors.[66] Halbert et al (2020) reported that some survival curves could not be digitized because of the poor quality of the original publication graphics.[67] A recent study found that digitization tools like DigitizeIt could be limited by operator precision and image resolution.[68] Even tools developed using automated image-based approaches remain constrained by figure quality and rasterization artifacts. Errors introduced during digitization can propagate and affect downstream analyses, such as treatment effect estimation and meta-analysis. Another recent study found that pixelation and color blending could degrade coordinate accuracy, introducing noise during digitization.[69] The study also found visual representations of censoring to be another common source of errors. Specifically, when censoring ticks are missing or poorly resolved, algorithms may misplace event timings, leading to biased survival estimates. Dense clustering of early censoring marks can obscure later events or make digitization unreliable. Because a 6-month patency point sits exactly in this early, censoring-dense region, we are concerned that these limitations may have important implications for the Astor et al. (2026) and Halbert et al. (2020) meta-analyses. We remain concerned about the quality of these abstracted data and the potential impact on the pooled 6-month patency among currently available AVGs, and uncertain whether the results reported by Astor et al. (2026) and Halbert et al. (2020) indicate that EndoForceTM produced better clinical outcomes than the AVGs with a standard sutured venous anastomosis. Regarding Astor et al. (2026), it also remains unclear whether the difference between the 6-month cumulative patency rates of 92 percent in Burgess et al. (2024) and 86 percent in the 12 studies reporting numerical values was statistically significant.
We continue to have concerns about the appropriateness of comparing EndoForceTM 's effects on patency with those of AVFs. We agree with the commenter who stated that AVF is not a viable permanent-access strategy for some patients, that current KDOQI guidance [70] emphasizes a patient-centered approach based on vessel characteristics, comorbidities, anticipated dialysis needs, and patient circumstances rather than an absolute `fistula first' approach, and that the substantial clinical improvement inquiry should ask whether EndoForceTM improves treatment relative to the conventional, surgically created graft-to-vein anastomosis it replaces, not whether an AVG created with EndoForceTM is superior to an AVF in a patient for whom an AVF is otherwise appropriate. Accordingly, comparisons between EndoForceTM and AVFs do not directly address whether EndoForceTM provides substantial clinical improvement over existing technologies.
In response to our concern that Kramer et al. (2026) was not sufficiently powered to assess patency at 180 days post-implantation among patients with ESRD who needed hemodialysis, the applicant stated that the study did not claim that its results were statistically significant and a commenter noted that CMS should nevertheless treat the results as clinically meaningful. However, we maintain our concern that a comparison of the results from Kramer et al. (2026) to other studies could be confounded by differences between the studies, and we remain uncertain whether any difference in intervention rates or patency can be attributed to the use of EndoForceTM alone.
A commenter noted that CMS's prior application of the substantial clinical improvement standard supports granting the EndoForceTM System transitional pass-through payment status despite meaningful evidentiary limitations, because the evidence supports the technology producing a clinically important benefit. We disagree that the prior approvals cited by the commenter establish that EndoForceTM System meets the substantial clinical improvement criterion. We note that we assess each application on its own merits based on the evidence submitted. Our concerns regarding the evidence supporting this application are discussed previously. We refer to the full details of our rationale regarding other applications in the respective final rules.
After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, the EndoForceTM System does not meet the substantial clinical improvement criterion to be considered for device pass-through payment. Therefore, in this final rule with comment period, we will not address whether the technology meets the remaining criterion required for device pass-through payment. We are not approving the EndoForceTM System for device pass-through payment status for CY 2027 because the technology does not meet the substantial clinical improvement criterion at § 419.66(c)(2).
Metric Medical Devices, Inc. submitted an application for a new device category for transitional pass-through payment status for the LINKTM External Fixator for CY 2027. According to the applicant, the LINKTM External Fixator is a dynamic percutaneous bone external fixator that provides continuous compression during the healing of bony fractures, fusions, and osteotomies. The applicant stated that the LINKTM External Fixator is composed of the (1) LINKTM, a stainless steel box-shaped spring that applies forces to wires or pins inserted in the bone to either actively pull together and compress or distract the bones; (2) LINKTM Cover, a silicone cap that covers the bone pins or wire; and (3) LINKTM Bone Pins, which are inserted in a patient's bones and to which the LINKTM attaches.
Table 55 provides an overview of the transitional pass-through payment status application for the LINKTM External Fixator and CMS's preliminary ( printed page 70452) assessment. For additional details provided by the applicant, please refer to the online application posting available at https://mearis.cms.gov/​public/​publications/​device-ptp/​DEP250902M814F.
We invited public comment on whether the LINKTM External Fixator meets the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1).
Comment: With respect to the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1), the applicant reiterated that the LINKTM External Fixator meets the newness requirement for device pass-through payment.
Response: We appreciate the applicant's input. We received the application for device pass-through payment status for the LINKTM External Fixator within 3 years of the date of FDA 510(k) clearance. After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, we have determined that the LINKTM External Fixator meets the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1).
Regarding the eligibility criterion at § 419.66(b)(3), we stated in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule that we were concerned that the LINKTM External Fixator components may not be integral to the service furnished, come in contact with human tissue, or be surgically inserted or implanted.
With respect to whether the LINKTM Bone Pins and LINKTM Cover are integral to the service furnished, based on the information provided by the applicant, we questioned whether the components are necessary to furnish or deliver the primary procedure with which it is used. We noted that, in the CY 2014 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (78 FR 75005), we stated that we have interpreted the term “integral” to mean that the device is necessary to furnish or deliver the primary procedure with which it is used. We stated, for example, a pacemaker is integral to the procedure of implantation of a pacemaker. We noted that according to the applicant, the LINKTM uses a single- use external fixator consisting of a stainless-steel bridge spring formed into a box shape, with holes that are held in alignment by surgical needle drivers during pin placement. We stated that per the applicant, when released, the bridge shortens to apply forces and the side elements swing outward to create moments on bone fixation pins or wires embedded in bone, pulling together and compressing or distracting bony structures. We stated, while the LINKTM External Fixator may include LINKTM Bone Pins, per the applicant, other commercially available bone pins, k-wires, or Steinmann pins (hereinafter referred to collectively as “bone fixation pins or wires”) may be compatible with the LINKTM External Fixator, and we therefore questioned whether the LINKTM Bone Pins are integral to the service furnished as they may be replaced with other commercially available bone fixation pins or wires. We further questioned whether the LINKTM Bone Pins are integral to the service furnished as it is unclear, based on the information provided in the application, whether any LINKTM Bone Pins are included in the LINKTM External Fixator packaging, or if they are packaged and sold separately from the LINKTM External Fixator. With respect to the LINKTM Cover, because the applicant stated that the LINKTM Cover is a separate removable silicon elastomer cover that protects the LINKTM and the patient from the pin and wire ends and does not play a role in providing compression, as such, we also questioned if the LINKTM Cover is integral to the service furnished. We stated that we would be interested in additional information about these components of the LINKTM External Fixator, including whether the components are required to furnish or deliver the primary procedure with which it is used and if the components can be substituted with other commercially available products.
With respect to whether the LINKTM External Fixator comes in contact with human tissue and is surgically inserted or implanted, we noted that, per the applicant, the LINKTM Bone Pins (or other bone pins or wires) are the only components that come in contact with human tissue and are surgically implanted or inserted into the patient. We stated, per the applicant, the LINKTM component remains outside the body and acts like a spring on skin penetrating bone fixation pins to reduce and provide continuous compression at the bone healing interface. We further noted that, according to the applicant, the LINKTM Cover is a separate, removable cover that does not come in contact with and is not surgically implanted or inserted into the patient. Therefore, we stated our belief that the LINKTM and the LINKTM Cover components of the LINKTM External Fixator do not come into contact with human tissue and are not surgically inserted or implanted as required by § 419.66(b)(3).
We invited public comment on whether the LINKTM External Fixator meets the eligibility criterion at § 419.66(b)(3).
Comment: In response to our concerns that the LINKTM External Fixator is not integral to the services furnished because the LINKTM and the LINKTM Cover components do not come into contact with human tissue and are not surgically inserted or implanted, the applicant and a few commenters stated that the LINKTM and the LINKTM Bone Pins and Cover are integral for performing bone fixation. The applicant reiterated that an assembled LINKTM External Fixator consists of the LINKTM, LINKTM Bone Pins with locking mechanism (sharp or flat groove), and the LINKTM Cover that protects the LINKTM, limits forces by limiting expansion of the LINKTM, restricts shape change, and provides the first layer of wound coverage.
The applicant commented that the LINKTM Bone Pins have sharp or flat grooves that lock into the LINKTM bridge, so that they operate as a single unit when implanted or inserted or applied to the wound. The applicant further stated it offers the LINKTM External Fixator under one part number as a bundled product offering consisting of the LINKTM, two LINKTM Bone Pins with locking mechanism, and the LINKTM Cover. The applicant added that it offers three types of LINKTM Bone Pins, all with sharp or flat grooves to lock into the LINKTM, so that the physician has the option of choosing which LINKTM Bone Pin type is best for the condition being treated and for the style of LINKTM selected. The applicant concluded that the LINKTM, the LINKTM Bone Pins, and the LINKTM Cover are consequently an integral part of the bone fixation service provided, and thus, the LINKTM External Fixator meets the requirements of § 419.66(b)(3).
The applicant stated it does not offer k-wires or Steinman pins for use with the LINKTM External Fixator, although these wires or pins are compatible as they are stainless steel and 2.0 mm in diameter. The applicant and a few other commenters stated that although physicians may choose another vendor's pins or k-wires to use with the LINKTM, this is not recommended because these pins or wires have not been adequately tested with the LINKTM External Fixator and may be unable to withstand the forces created. The applicant and a commenter specifically noted that use of other bone pins would not have the advantage of locking to the LINKTM to prevent moving or shifting, which could potentially alter a surgeon's positioning of bones and the preferred force profile generated. The applicant added that k-wires and Steinman pins will not retain the LINKTM nor have the strength of the LINKTM Bone Pins.
A commenter stated that the pins are integral to the functioning of the LINKTM External Fixator as the nominated device's bone stabilization and compression improves outcomes versus other devices on the market. The commenter stated that due to the spring-like quality of the LINKTM External ( printed page 70455) Fixator, the device locks onto the bone pins once compression is realized by releasing the needle drivers from the compressing tab. The commenter explained that this converts the separate components of the LINKTM and each LINKTM Bone Pin into a solid dynamic construct, where any force applied to the LINKTM Bone Pins is transferred to the LINKTM and vice versa. The commenter expressed its belief that the LINKTM Bone Pins and LINKTM are essential to one another to function as intended.
Another commenter explained that the applicant packages the LINKTM Bone Pins separately to allow physicians to choose which pin type to use during surgery. The commenter stated that combining both types of pins into the same box would force a physician to open multiple packages and increase waste in the case the physician needs larger pins than originally expected or a mix of sizes due to anatomical challenges.
In response to our concerns that the LINKTM External Fixator does not come in contact with human tissue and may not be surgically inserted or implanted or applied in or on a wound or other skin lesion, the applicant commented that, in patients with complex, open Grade III fractures, the LINKTM, the LINKTM Bone Pins, and the LINKTM Cover are surgically implanted or inserted (either permanently or temporarily) or applied in or on a wound. The applicant stated that, while inserting, implanting, or applying the LINKTM and a LINKTM Bone Pin, the LINKTM is placed in contact with the bone, wound, or skin while guiding the LINKTM Bone Pins and steading the placement. According to the applicant, once stable, the LINKTM Bone Pin is advanced deeper into bone and additional bone pins are placed prior to lifting the LINKTM from the bone or wound to adjust the bone fixation forces. The applicant further stated and provided images to show that the LINKTM Cover is commonly in contact with the skin or wound to seal the site from contamination, and that after removal, the LINKTM Cover leaves a visible impression in the skin from long-term contact. The applicant stated that this clinical use shows the placement of the LINKTM on the wound, skin closure around the LINKTM Bone Pins, and evidence of the LINKTM Cover in long-term contact with the skin. The applicant further explained that the LINKTM Bone Pins are always implanted in bone while the LINKTM and the LINKTM Cover can be placed in direct contact with the osseous and soft tissue structures in an open wound (such as a grade III fracture) to apply the greatest forces to bone, then adjusted upward to optimize bone applied forces.
The applicant stated that an example of implantation of the LINKTM, the LINKTM Bone Pins, and the LINKTM Cover occur when an open, often infected bone fracture requires a multi-step surgical procedure to close it. According to the applicant, in these fractures, the LINKTM External Fixator is used differently than in the office. Specifically, the applicant stated that in an open wound, the physician can move the LINKTM on the LINKTM Bone Pins from bony cortex to above the skin. The applicant stated that the LINKTM can lie in an open wound and be covered with skin flaps or dressing to support immediate bony reconstruction while limiting bacterial colonization, as physicians commonly do not immediately close infected or heavily contaminated wounds because sealing bacteria inside causes severe complications like osteomyelitis. Per the applicant, treatment relies on thorough cleaning, antibiotics, and delayed closure. The applicant further explained that screw, plate, staple, or rod type internal fixation hardware is contraindicated because it will often harbor the infection. The applicant stated that an unsolved healthcare problem exists during this treatment period when internal fixation cannot be used, because dynamic compression's enhanced bone healing effects are unavailable in external fixators other than the LINKTM External Fixator. The applicant stated that in this population, the LINKTM External Fixator is the only available bone fixation option, because if it becomes colonized by bacteria, the LINKTM External Fixator can be easily removed and replaced with a new sterile LINKTM system. The applicant stated that this permits immediate bone fixation and supports an optimized bone-healing response while still allowing the physician to perform staged wound closure. The applicant stated that together, this allows the treated bone to achieve fusion while managing the infection with repeated debridement, covering and uncovering, force adjustment, and closure.
In addition, the applicant stated that when a wound is not traumatically opened, a physician either sutures the LINKTM Bone Pin within an incision or inserts it percutaneously. Specifically, the applicant stated that, prior to incision closure, the LINKTM is brought into contact with bone then raised to its optimal force height. The applicant stated that this step optimizes the dynamic compression forces the LINKTM applies to fixate bone and promote healing. The applicant further noted that, in both open and closed fractures, the LINKTM External Fixator is in contact with skin or surgically implanted. According to the applicant, the LINKTM cannot operate independently of the bone pins as it is assembled by inserting a bone pin through it and then bringing both the bone pin and the LINKTM into the wound such that they contact bone, subcutaneous tissues, fascia, or skin. The applicant stated that the bone being fixated is effectively part of the LINKTM External Fixator system, because the device cannot be assembled and function without bone being the final member in the construct. The applicant concluded that in patients suffering from an open fracture or bone-communicating skin ulcer, the LINKTM and the LINKTM Cover components of the LINKTM External Fixator do come into contact with human tissue, and thus, are surgically inserted or implanted as required by § 419.66(b)(3).
Response: We appreciate the applicant and commenters' input. Although we remain uncertain for reasons described in our consideration of the § 419.66(b)(4) criterion, we believe that the LINKTM External Fixator, including the LINKTM Cover and the LINKTM Bone Pin components, may be an integral part of the service furnished, used for one patient only, come in contact with human tissue, and be surgically implanted or inserted or applied in or on a wound or other skin lesion. After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, we believe that the LINKTM External Fixator may meet the eligibility criterion at § 419.66(b)(3), unless the LINKTM Bone Pins may be considered a supply, as discussed in greater detail later in this section.
In the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, regarding the eligibility criterion at § 419.66(b)(4), we questioned whether the LINKTM Bone Pins could be considered a supply furnished incident to a service, based on the applicant's description. First, we questioned the role of LINKTM Bone Pins in creating surgical openings for access to bone to accomplish the fixation provided by the LINKTM. In the CY 2001 OPPS interim final rule (65 FR 67804 through 67805), we stated that we consider items used to create incisions, such as scalpels, electrocautery units, biopsy apparatuses, or other commonly used operating room instruments, to be supplies or capital equipment not eligible for transitional pass-through payments. Based on the information in the application, we stated we were unclear if the LINKTM Bone Pins (or ( printed page 70456) other bone fixation pins or wires) are placed through a previously created surgical opening or if they are directly inserted through skin and soft tissue to access bone. We stated we would welcome information regarding whether, when, and how an incision is created during placement of the LINKTM External Fixator. Second, as discussed previously with respect to criteria at § 419.66(b)(3), we noted that it is unclear whether the LINKTM Bone Pins may be replaced with other commercially available bone fixation pins or wires. We stated that we would be interested in clarification about whether the LINKTM Bone Pins can be substituted with other commercially available products. We questioned whether LINKTM Bone Pins may be considered a supply or material furnished incident to a service and excluded from device pass-through payment eligibility under § 419.66(b)(4).
We invited public comment on whether the LINKTM External Fixator meets the eligibility criterion at § 419.66(b)(4).
Comment: The applicant submitted a public comment reiterating its belief that the LINKTM External Fixator is not equipment, an instrument, apparatus, implement, or item of this type for which depreciation and financing expenses are recovered as depreciable assets, or a material or supply furnished incident to a service. As previously mentioned, the applicant stated that it would not recommend the use of k-wires or Steinman pins with the LINKTM because they would not lock into the LINKTM. The applicant stated that the LINKTM Bone Pin's locking system is unique to the LINKTM External Fixator and novel, as described in U.S. patents 11,944,352 and 12,690,890. The applicant stated that LINKTM Bone Pins are incompatible with general use as a pin or wire, and thus, are not a general supply incidental to the bone fixation procedure. A commenter also stated that other bone pins could possibly be used, although they were not tested with the LINKTM during the 510(k) clearance process. The commenter added that using non- LINKTM bone pins may present concerns because it is unclear whether they would lock into the LINKTM without moving, sliding, or shifting, potentially altering the surgeon's positioning of bones and the preferred force profile set.
In response to whether the LINKTM Bone Pins are used to create surgical openings during placement of the LINKTM External Fixator, the applicant stated that the LINKTM Bone Pins could not be considered a supply furnished incident to a service due to their unique locking feature design, use in open fractures, and within an incision, and in these cases, the LINKTM Bone Pins are not used to create a surgical opening for access to fixate in bone. The applicant stated that the LINKTM Bone Pins are, consequently, outside the scope of CY 2001 OPPS interim final rule (65 FR 67804 through 67805).
Response: We appreciate the applicant and commenter's input. With respect to the eligibility criterion at § 419.66(b)(4), in the CY 2001 OPPS interim final rule (65 FR 67804 through 67805), we stated that we consider items used to create incisions, such as scalpels, electrocautery units, biopsy apparatuses, or other commonly used operating room instruments, to be supplies or capital equipment not eligible for transitional pass-through payments.
While the applicant stated that the LINKTM Bone Pins are not used to create a surgical opening when used in open fractures and within an incision, the applicant also stated that when the wound is not traumatically opened, the LINKTM Bone Pin may be inserted percutaneously. In these cases, it is unclear if the LINKTM Bone Pins are being inserted directly through the skin. In addition, while the LINKTM Bone Pins' locking feature is specific to the LINKTM External Fixator and not interchangeable with commonly available fixation pins or wires, which distinguishes the LINKTM Bone Pins from certain generally available supplies, we do not believe it resolves our concern regarding whether the LINKTM Bone Pins may constitute a supply, particularly when inserted percutaneously. Therefore, after consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, it remains unclear whether the LINKTM Bone Pins may be considered a supply or material furnished incident to a service. In addition, if the LINKTM Bone Pins may sometimes be considered a supply and therefore potentially ineligible for pass-through under § 419.66(b)(4), then the LINKTM External Fixator, considered as a whole device, may be ineligible. Considering the components separately, we remain concerned that the LINKTM and the LINKTM Cover components of the LINKTM External Fixator do not appear to be surgically implanted or inserted as required by § 419.66(b)(3) in cases where the LINKTM Bone Pins may be considered a supply.
We stated in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, regarding the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1), that the applicant stated that the existing pass-through code of C1713 (Anchor/screw for opposing bone-to-bone or soft tissue-to-bone (implantable)) does not appropriately describe the LINKTM External Fixator because the category does not include fixators with the LINKTM 's shape-changing, spring-like design that stores elastic mechanical energy allowing it to provide continuous dynamic compression, which pulls bones together and closes gaps formed by bone resorption or inadvertent mechanical loading and stimulates mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) to differentiate along an osteogenic pathway to form bone and cartilage. In contrast, the applicant stated that traditional external fixators included in C1713 are static, and therefore, do not readjust or impart compression or distraction forces to enhance bone healing as the LINKTM does.
We also stated in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule that, based on the description the applicant provided, the LINKTM External Fixator is an external fixator that attaches to pins inserted into the bone principally with the intent to facilitate stabilization or oppose bone-to-bone contact, and therefore, could be appropriately described by C1713 (Anchor/screw for opposing bone-to-bone or soft tissue-to-bone (implantable)). Further, we stated that C1713 does not describe the type of fixation or specify the type of compression created by the device. Specifically, we stated our belief that the pass-through payment category C1713 may appropriately describe the LINKTM External Fixator because C1713 describes implantable pins and/or screws inserted or drilled into bone, principally with the intent to facilitate stabilization or oppose bone-to-bone contact, which is consistent with the LINKTM External Fixator description. We noted that we do not establish pass-through device categories for the purpose of describing specific devices, rather, device categories are intended to encompass all devices that can be appropriately described by a given category. In this context, we stated our belief that the LINKTM External Fixator may be appropriately described by C1713. We also stated that, after reviewing the information provided by the applicant, we were unable to determine that the LINKTM External Fixator meets the device category eligibility criteria, and therefore, we proposed to deny transitional pass-through payment status for CY 2027.
We invited public comment on whether the LINKTM External Fixator meets the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1). We also invited public comments on our ( printed page 70457) proposal to deny transitional pass-through payment status for the LINKTM External Fixator for CY 2027.
Comment: Several commenters expressed general support for the approval of device pass-through payment for the LINKTM External Fixator. Another commenter expressed its support for the denial of device pass-through payment for the LINKTM External Fixator because it does not meet the criteria for device pass-through payment.
Response: We appreciate the applicant and commenters' input. We have taken these comments into consideration in our final determination for pass-through payment status for the LINKTM External Fixator.
Comment: The applicant and a commenter commented that the LINKTM External Fixator is not appropriately described by C1713, because the C1713 category includes static devices such as implantable pins and/or screws to oppose bone-to-bone or soft tissue-to-bone whereas the LINKTM External Fixator uses elastic energy. Specifically, the applicant stated that the device category C1713 does not describe the LINKTM External Fixator because the LINKTM External Fixator applies elastic mechanical energy to bone creating electrical current flow to stimulate healing. The applicant stated this is dramatically different from those devices in the C1713 category which describes static devices such as implantable pins and/or screws to oppose bone-to-bone or soft tissue-to-bone. The applicant commented that in effect, the elastic nature of the LINKTM bridge acts as an energy source to deform the bone matrix causing it to create current flow that recruits MSC to the site and then deforms the MSC nucleus causing it to differentiate along an osteogenic pathway. The applicant stated the use of elastic energy to create current versus implanted electrodes or pulsed magnetic fields used in bone stimulators is a significantly different mode of operation than the static pins and screws in the C1713 category and that thus the LINKTM meets the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1).
A commenter stated the compressive force created by the LINKTM External Fixator is dynamic and continuously closes gap formation forcing the body into the primary bone healing state. According to the commenter, without this important feature of continuous dynamic compression, gaps can form due to bone resorption, micromovements and non-compliant patients, leading to higher chances of non-union.
Response: We appreciate the applicant and commenter's input. After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, we continue to believe that C1713 appropriately describes the LINKTM External Fixator because the device category code does not differentiate between static external fixators and those that use elastic mechanical energy. We do not believe that the LINKTM External Fixator's dynamic compression mechanism, by itself, places the device outside C1713, because the category encompasses devices used to facilitate stabilization or oppose bone-to-bone or soft tissue-to-bone. Therefore, we have determined that the LINKTM External Fixator does not meet the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1), because it is appropriately described by an existing category or a category previously in effect.
After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, the LINKTM External Fixator does not meet the device category eligibility criterion to be considered for device pass-through payment. Therefore, in this final rule with comment period, we will not address whether the technology meets the remaining criteria required for device pass-through payment. We are not approving the LINKTM External Fixator for device pass-through payment status for CY 2027 because the technology does not meet the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1).
(c) SantrevaTM -ATK Endovascular Revascularization Catheter
AngioSafe®, Inc. submitted an application for a new device category for transitional pass-through payment status for the SantrevaTM -ATK Endovascular Revascularization Catheter (SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter) for CY 2027. According to the applicant, the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter is an energy and wire-free platform for simultaneous intraplaque crossing and revascularization of complex occlusive peripheral artery disease, intended for facilitating intraluminal placement of guidewires beyond stenotic lesions.
Table 56 provides an overview of the device category for the transitional pass-through payment status application for the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter and CMS's preliminary assessment. For additional details provided by the applicant, please refer to the online application posting available at https://mearis.cms.gov/​public/​publications/​device-ptp/​DEP260302QH9AE.
We invited public comment on whether the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter meets the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1) and the eligibility criteria at § 419.66(b)(3) and (4).
Comment: An applicant and another commenter submitted public comments regarding the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1). They reiterated that the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter meets the newness requirement for device pass-through payment, and is an integral part of the service furnished, used for one patient only, comes in contact with human tissue, and is surgically implanted or inserted, or applied in or on a wound or other skin lesion. They also reiterated that the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter is not equipment, an instrument, apparatus, implement, or item of this type for which depreciation and financing expenses are recovered as depreciable assets, or a material or supply furnished incident to a service.
Response: We appreciate the applicant's and commenters' input. We received the application for device pass-through payment status for the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter within 3 years of the date of FDA 510(k) clearance. After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, we have determined that the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter meets the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1).
We agree with the applicant and commenter that the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter is an integral part of the service furnished, used for one patient only, comes in contact with human tissue, and is surgically implanted or inserted or applied in or on a wound or other skin lesion. We also agree that the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter is not equipment, an instrument, apparatus, implement, or item of this type for which depreciation and financing expenses are recovered as depreciable assets, or a material or supply furnished incident to a service. After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, we have determined that the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter meets the eligibility criterion at § 419.66(b)(3) and (4).
In the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, regarding the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1), we noted that per the applicant, the existing pass-through code C1887 (Catheter, guiding (may include infusion/perfusion capability)) does not appropriately describe the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter, because C1887 does not reflect the full scope of the device's function or the significant clinical improvement associated with the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter, which facilitates the placement of guidewires beyond stenotic lesions by laterally cutting and then compressing plaque, to form an intraluminal channel to restore blood flow.
We stated that, based on the description the applicant provided, the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter is intended to facilitate the intraluminal placement of guidewires beyond stenotic lesions, including chronic total occlusions (CTOs), in the femoropopliteal (arterial) peripheral vasculature, and therefore, may be appropriately described by C1887 (Catheter, guiding (may include infusion/perfusion capability)). Specifically, we stated our belief that the pass-through payment category C1887 may describe the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter because the pass-through payment category includes guiding catheters and the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter's primary function of crossing peripheral stenotic lesions to establish a revascularization pathway appears to be the same function performed by devices described in C1887. We stated, in addition, per the applicant, the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter is introduced and removed prior to final treatment, which is also consistent with the use of the guiding catheters described in C1887. We noted that we do not establish pass-through device categories for the purpose of describing specific devices; rather, device categories are intended to encompass all devices that can be appropriately described by a given category. In this context, we stated our belief that the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter may be appropriately described by C1887. We also stated that, after reviewing the information provided by the applicant, we were unable to determine that the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter meets the device category eligibility criteria, and therefore, we proposed to deny transitional pass-through payment status for CY 2027.
We invited public comment on whether the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter meets the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1). We also invited public comments on our proposal to deny transitional pass-through payment status for the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter for CY 2027.
Comment: A commenter expressed its support for the denial of device pass-through payment for the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter because it does not meet the criteria for device pass-through payment.
Response: We appreciate the commenter's input.
Comment: Several commenters, including the applicant, urged CMS to approve device pass-through payment for the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter, stating that the SantrevaTM -ATK provides an additional treatment option for patients with complex peripheral arterial disease, including CTOs, and that approval of transitional pass-through payment would support appropriate physician and hospital adoption as well as improve patient access to innovative care. The commenters further stated that device pass-through payment status would encourage continued use of the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter to address important safety, efficacy, durability of outcomes, and economic needs in complex peripheral vascular disease.
In response to our concerns that the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter may be appropriately described by C1887, the applicant and commenters stated that they believe there are no existing categories or categories previously in effect that appropriately describe the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter. Specifically, the applicant and commenters stated that while the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter does perform the function of a guiding catheter, C1887 does not describe the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter's additional capabilities that specifically contribute to the substantial clinical improvement the device provides.
The applicant stated that, as described by CMS, C1887 is intended for the introduction of interventional/diagnostic devices into the coronary or peripheral vascular systems and can be used to inject contrast material, function as a conduit through which other devices pass, and/or provide a mechanism for measuring arterial pressure, and maintain a pathway created by the guidewire during the performance of a procedure. The applicant stated that the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter functions as an endovascular interventional device for complex lesions (occlusions) after it is delivered through such conduits and, at the end of its intervention, acts as a convenient conduit for other devices. The applicant also noted that the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter's conduit function is not the focus of the transitional pass-through payment application. According to the applicant, the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter directly contributes to revascularization in a way that traditional guiding catheters do not and is not associated with the introduction of other devices. Specifically, the applicant and another commenter stated that 90 percent of the evaluable subjects in Banerjee et al. (2026) had predominantly intraplaque crossing of the CTO and that intravascular ultrasound analysis of the intraplaque track found a mean luminal ( printed page 70460) gain of roughly 59 percent without any other revascularization interventions.
Furthermore, the applicant stated that CMS has created additional device categories that include guidance capabilities along with other functions, such as C1725 which describes a catheter, transluminal angioplasty, non-laser (may include guidance, infusion/perfusion capability). The applicant also stated that CMS has created numerous device categories to describe catheters that address calcified plaque through different approaches, including C1885 (Catheter, transluminal angioplasty, laser), C1725 (Catheter, transluminal angioplasty, non-laser (may include guidance, infusion/perfusion capability)), C1714 (Catheter, transluminal atherectomy, directional), C1724 (Catheter, transluminal atherectomy, rotational), and C1761 (Catheter, transluminal intravascular lithotripsy, coronary).
The applicant and several commenters stated that the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter addresses plaque with a new multi-modal mechanism of action, atheroplasty, which is a wire- and energy-free mechanism that combines axial plaque disruption with low-pressure lateral plaque compression to form an intraluminal channel without actively stretching the vessel wall, and thus, does not fall into any of the existing categories (C1885, C1725, C1714, C1724, or C1761). These commenters also stated that atheroplasty disrupts, modifies, and compresses plaque in place against native plaque to create a channel while preserving the native vessel architecture unlike atherectomy, which debulks or removes plaque (classified as intraluminal artery stripper in the Code of Federal Regulation), or angioplasty (classified as hydraulic pressurization of vessel walls), which dilates the vessel wall via balloon expansion. The applicant and these commenters stated that atheroplasty therefore removes the obstruction to blood flow without physically removing the plaque from the body and that any interaction with the vessel wall structure during the procedure is atraumatic, whether mechanically or hydraulically. In addition, the applicant stated that vessel wall safety, high efficacy in difficult occlusions, and absence of periprocedural adverse events that could reduce durability of long-term outcomes are key substantial clinical improvements associated with the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter's atheroplasty mechanism. The applicant concluded that it believes a new device category is needed to describe this approach and requested that CMS establish a new category of catheter, transluminal atheroplasty, wireless.
Response: We appreciate the applicant's and commenters' input. After consideration of the public comments received and our review of the application, we continue to believe that C1887 appropriately describes the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter because the nominated device's primary function of crossing peripheral stenotic lesions to establish a revascularization pathway appears to be the same function performed by the guiding catheters described by C1887. Additionally, the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter's introduction and removal prior to final treatment are also consistent with the use of guiding catheters described by C1887. While the applicant and commenters stated that C1887 does not describe the device's additional capabilities during CTO crossing, including plaque disruption, compression, and intraluminal channel formation, we disagree that these additional capabilities demonstrate that C1887 does not appropriately describe the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter, because the evidence submitted does not establish that these capabilities constitute a distinct therapeutic function independent of crossing the lesion to establish a revascularization pathway. Furthermore, we note that we do not establish pass-through device categories for the purpose of describing specific devices; rather, device categories are intended to encompass all devices that can be appropriately described by a given category while ensuring that no medical device is described by more than one category in accordance with section 1833(t)(6)(B)(ii)(II) of the Act. While CMS has established separate categories for catheters that treat or modify vascular lesions through different mechanisms, the presence of additional capabilities or potential to simplify a procedure does not necessarily establish that the device performs a distinct function requiring a separate category. Therefore, we have determined that the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter does not meet the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1), because it is appropriately described by an existing category or a category previously in effect.
After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter does not meet the device category eligibility criterion to be considered for device pass-through payment. Therefore, in this final rule with comment period, we will not address whether the technology meets the remaining criteria required for device pass-through payment. We are not approving the SantrevaTM -ATK Catheter for device pass-through payment status for CY 2027 because the technology does not meet the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1).
Comment: Several commenters recommended that CMS define a transition pathway from pass-through status to permanent payment with clearer criteria, timeline, data requirements and advance notice. The commenters requested that CMS should ensure the public can comment on the impact of expiration of pass-through status and should evaluate the effect of expiration of transitional device pass-through payment on the total resources associated with the procedure before packaging the cost of devices into an existing payment rate. A commenter stated that, for products used by small patient populations or in specialized centers, CMS should take the resulting limitations in claims data into account when determining whether an APC has sufficient information to absorb the cost of the technology without creating access problems.
Response: We appreciate the commenters' input and ongoing support of the device pass-through payment program. As specified in section 1833(t)(6)(B) of the Social Security Act, under the OPPS, categories of devices are eligible for transitional pass-through payments for at least two, but not more than three years. After expiration, the device category HCPCS code remains active; however, its payment is included in the primary service. The complete list of current and historical device category codes created since August 1, 2000, which is the implementation date of the hospital OPPS, is available in the quarterly updated OPPS transmittals [71] and the Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub.100-04), Chapter 4, Section 60.4.2. The expiration dates of pass-through payment status for each device category receiving pass-through payment are detailed in the annual OPPS proposed rule and final rule with comment period, subject to public comments. We note that because charges related to packaged services are used for outlier and future rate setting, hospitals are advised to report the device category HCPCS codes on the claim whenever furnished in the hospital outpatient department setting, consistent with all applicable coding and billing instructions. We ( printed page 70461) acknowledge the commenters' concerns regarding the impact of expiration of pass-through status and the limitations in claims data when calculating packaged APC payment rates. We will continue to monitor the available data and consider any additional public comments related to these issues.
Comment: A commenter requested that CMS revisit the methodology of device pass-through cost significance criteria to compare the cost of a proposed device using only the cost of the device or devices the proposed device replaces, especially when the new device does not replace all devices included in the device-related portion (DRP) of the associated APC. The commenter further recommended that, when issuing a transitional pass-through category, CMS should specify which portion of the DRP it will subtract from the costs of the new category, rather than assuming the full DRP applies, and should only subtract costs associated with devices being replaced.
Response: We appreciate the commenter's recommendations related to the methodology for device pass-through cost significance criteria and the calculation for the device offset of a pass-through device category. We will continue to consider the issues and any additional public comments related to them.
Comment: Multiple commenters expressed their support for, or concerns regarding CMS's repeal of the alternative pathway for new technology add-on payment and OPPS device pass-through applications and requirement for all applicants for new technology add-on payments and OPPS device pass-through payments to demonstrate that they meet the same eligibility requirements to receive add-on payments and/or pass-through payments.
Response: We appreciate commenters' feedback. As noted in section IV.A.2.a. of this final rule with comment period, in the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule (91 FR 49767 through 49789; 91 FR 50346 through 50347), we finalized our policy, with modification, that, unless specifically exempted, all applications received for device pass-through payment status on or after October 1, 2026, including all applications received through the remainder of the CY 2028 application cycle ending on March 1, 2027, and applications received for subsequent calendar years will have to demonstrate that the technology met the requirements currently reflected at § 419.66(c)(2)(i). We also finalized our policy that device pass-through payment applications submitted to CMS as of September 30, 2026, for devices that are part of the FDA's Breakthrough Devices Program that received FDA marketing authorization for the indication covered by the Breakthrough Device designation will be evaluated and could be approved under the alternative pathway, provided that all other criteria have been met. In addition, we finalized a limited exception for a new device that had received FDA Breakthrough Device designation as of September 30, 2026, and has received marketing authorization for the indication covered by the Breakthrough Device designation. Such devices will remain eligible to apply for device pass-through payment under the alternative pathway, which will continue to accept applications for CYs 2028 and 2029. As such, to be considered for the limited exception, CMS must receive a complete application for eligible devices under the limited exception no later than March 1, 2028. We finalized revisions, with modifications, to paragraph § 419.66(c)(2)(ii) to reflect the finalized policy, effective October 1, 2026. We refer the readers to the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule (91 FR 49767 through 49789) for a full discussion of the finalized policy, including comments received and our responses.
Comment: We received several public comments regarding applications or category codes not under review, or requesting changes to the device pass-through payment policies, such as eligibility of section 351 implantable biological products.
Response: These comments were outside the scope of the proposals included in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule and we are therefore not addressing them in this final rule with comment period.
B. Device-Intensive Procedures
Under the OPPS, prior to CY 2017, device-intensive status for procedures was determined at the APC level for APCs with a device offset percentage greater than 40 percent (79 FR 66795). Beginning in CY 2017, CMS began determining device-intensive status at the HCPCS code level. In assigning device-intensive status to an APC prior to CY 2017, the device costs of all the procedures within the APC were calculated and the geometric mean device offset of all of the procedures had to exceed 40 percent. Almost all of the procedures assigned to device-intensive APCs utilized devices, and the device costs for the associated HCPCS codes exceeded the 40 percent threshold. The no cost/full credit and partial credit device policy (79 FR 66872 through 66873) applies to device-intensive procedures and is discussed in detail in section IV.B.4. of the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC proposed rule. A related device policy was the requirement that certain procedures assigned to device-intensive APCs require the reporting of a device code on the claim (80 FR 70422) and is discussed in detail in section IV.B.3. of the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC proposed rule.
