Cir. 2025) (finding similar statutory rulemaking authority supported conclusion that Congress delegated significant discretion to agency), and in the context of a statute (section 1833(t) of the Act) that repeatedly delegates significant discretionary authority to the Secretary to design the manner in which OPPS payments will be calculated.
As we noted in the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (83 FR 58818) and in our decision to complete the two-year phase of this policy in the CY 2020 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (84 FR 61366), “[a] large source of growth in spending on services furnished in hospital outpatient departments (HOPDs) appears to be the result of the shift of services from (lower cost) physician offices to (higher cost) HOPDs.” We continue to believe that these shifts in the sites of service are unnecessary if the beneficiary can safely receive the same services in a lower-cost setting but instead receives care in a higher-cost setting due to payment incentives. We continue to believe that the difference in payment is leading to unnecessary increases in the volume of covered outpatient department services, and we remain concerned that this shift in care setting increases beneficiary cost-sharing liability because Medicare payment rates for the same or similar services are generally higher in hospital outpatient departments than in freestanding physician offices. We continue to believe that our method addresses the concerns described in the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (83 FR 59005).
As we stated in the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (83 FR 59013), we believe implementing a volume control method in a budget neutral manner would not appropriately reduce the overall unnecessary volume of covered OPD services and instead would simply shift services within the OPPS system because of payment rather than medical necessity. We also outlined in the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (83 FR 59013) that while section 1833(t)(9)(B) of the Act requires that certain changes made under the OPPS be made in a budget neutral manner, this section does not apply to the volume control method under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act.
Here, as in AHA v. Azar, we have identified an unnecessary increase in volume in a set of OPPS payment codes based on payment differentials between the OPPS and the PFS. As in AHA v. Azar, CMS has tailored a methodology to eliminate that unnecessary volume increase by eliminating its cause. And as the D.C. Circuit already found in AHA v. Azar, that falls comfortably within the agency's delegated authority under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act.
The D.C. Circuit's decision in Bridgeport Hospital does not undermine the precedential value of the D.C. Circuit's earlier decision in AHA v. Azar. See LaShawn A. v. Barry, 87 F.3d 1389, 1395 (D.C. Cir. 1996) (en banc) (explaining that when a prior panel in the same circuit has decided an issue, the law-of-the-circuit doctrine precludes reconsideration of that decision). Moreover, Bridgeport Hospital addressed a completely different payment policy promulgated under a completely different statute. The Bridgeport panel concluded that a particular wage-index policy applied under the Inpatient Prospective Payment System (IPPS) exceeded the Secretary's authority under sections 1886(d)(3)(E) and 1886(d)(5)(I)(i) of the Act. See 108 F.4th at 887-91. In doing so, the Bridgeport panel focused on the specificity and length of section 1886(d)'s wage-index provision and section 1886(d) as a whole, concluding that it did not give the Secretary discretion to change the wage-index values produced within the statutory formula. See id. at 889 n.3 (observing that the IPPS “section on inpatient reimbursement formulas” is “longer than many books”).
Here, in contrast, section 1833(t)(2) of the Act (entitled “System requirements”) expressly gives the Secretary significant discretion by ( printed page 70594) instructing in subparagraph (F) that “the Secretary shall develop a method for controlling unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services.” The statute does this in the context of a statutory payment scheme (OPPS) where Congress has delegated to the Secretary significant discretion to design the particulars of that payment system. For example, in contrast to the IPPS statute's wage-index language in section 1886(d)(3)(E) of the Act, section 1833(t)(2)(D) of the Act delegates to the Secretary authority to “determine a wage adjustment factor [for OPPS] to adjust the portion of payment and coinsurance attributable to labor-related costs for relative differences in labor and labor-related costs across geographic regions in a budget neutral manner” in the context of a statute that expressly precludes judicial review of such determinations—and numerous others related to OPPS, including the Secretary's development of volume control methods under section 1833(t)(2)(F)—in section 1833(t)(12) of the Act.
Finally, as we stated in the FY 2026 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule (90 FR36853), we respectfully disagree with the D.C. Circuit's decision in Bridgeport.
Comment: Commenters stated that the D.C. Circuit in AHA v. Azar failed to account for section 603 of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 (BBA of 2015), which enacted section 1833(t)(21) of the Act. Commenters stated that the BBA of 2015 created two categories of provider-based departments (PBDs): (1) those established before November 2, 2015, and (2) those established after that date. For those PBDs in existence prior to November 2, 2015, commenters stated that the Congress required CMS to continue paying off-campus PBDs, referred to in the statute as excepted off-campus PBDs, under the OPPS; however, for post-November 2, 2015 PBDs, the Congress required CMS to pay PBDs under another applicable Part B payment system. Commenters believed that the Congress reinforced this policy choice by providing that certain “mid-build” PBDs should receive the same payment treatment as existing, pre-November 2, 2015 off-campus PBDs in section 1833(t)(21)(B)(v) of the Act.
Some commenters noted that section 603 of the BBA of 2015 represents Congress' thoughtful consideration of recommendations to eliminate differences in payment between hospital outpatient departments and freestanding physicians' offices in certain circumstances, and that CMS's proposal undermines the balance struck by Congress. Commenters stated that the agency cannot rely solely on AHA v. Azar and must instead address why the text and history of section 603 of the BBA of 2015 do not foreclose the agency's authority to apply the proposed volume control method to imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs.
Response: As we stated in the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (83 FR 59008), we continue to believe the changes required by section 603 of the BBA of 2015 made in section 1833(t) of the Act had the effect of addressing some of the concerns related to shifts in settings of care and overutilization of services in the hospital outpatient setting for new off-campus PBDs that began billing Medicare for OPPS services after November 1, 2015. In enacting section 603 of the BBA of 2015, Congress addressed the specific circumstances that lead to the proliferation of new off-campus provider-based departments. As we stated in the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (81 FR 79711), with section 603 of the BBA of 2015, we believe Congress may have been trying to address the incentive for hospitals to purchase physician's offices and convert them to OPDs without changing their location or patient population. In this final rule with comment period, we are addressing new and separate circumstances: the over utilization of imaging without contrast services in the OPPS.
We disagree with commenters that by enacting legislation that does not reference section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act, Congress meant to circumscribe our authority under that preexisting statutory provision. As the D.C. Circuit explained when rejecting the same claim in AHA v. Azar: “Nothing in the text of section 603 [of the BBA of 2015] indicates that preexisting off-campus PBDs are forever exempt from adjustments to their reimbursement. Rather, the text of the law exempts those providers from the change mandated by section 603 itself, leaving the exempted providers subject to all the provisions of the OPPS statute, including subparagraph (2)(F).” 964 F.3d at 1246.
Additionally, as the D.C. Circuit there explained, even assuming that section 603 of the BBA of 2015 could be read to judge increases in volume at preexisting off-campus PBDs are not “unnecessary” under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act, that judgment would extend only to 2015 and “would not mean that Congress considered acceptable the continued volume increases later taking place” in other years. Id.
Finally, the commenters are also wrong that Loper Bright undermines the D.C. Circuit's analysis of section 603 of the BBA of 2015 in AHA v. Azar. Nothing in the appellate court's analysis of section 603 of the BBA of 2015 suggests that the court found the provision ambiguous or incorrectly deferred to the agency's interpretation of it. See id. And contrary to the commenters' suggestion, the court fully considered any impact of section 603 of the BBA of 2015 on the agency's authority under the OPPS statute, even if it characterized the section 603 argument as an “alternative” argument made by the plaintiffs in that case.
Comment: Commenters reiterated their objections from prior rulemaking that the proposed payment reductions constitute “adjustments” that are subject to the budget neutrality requirements set forth in section 1833(t)(9)(B) of the Act and urged CMS to implement any volume control method in a budget neutral manner.
Commenters stated that section 1833(t)(9)(A) of the Act refers to the groups, relative payment weights, wage adjustments, and “other adjustments described in paragraph (2),” and therefore encompasses a payment reduction implemented under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act. Commenters stated that characterizing the policy as a “method” rather than an “adjustment” does not change the fact that the policy reduces payment rates for particular OPD services.
Some commenters also disagreed with CMS's interpretation of section 1833(t)(9)(C) of the Act. Commenters stated that this provision provides a specific mechanism for responding to volume that exceeds amounts established through methodologies under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act—an adjustment to the update to the conversion factor in a subsequent year—and does not authorize CMS to implement service-specific payment reductions in a non-budget neutral manner.
Response: As we stated in the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (83 FR 59009), we believe that while section 1833(t)(9)(B) of the Act does require that many changes made under the OPPS be made in a budget neutral manner, this provision does not apply to the volume control method under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act as outlined through our proposals in CY 2019, CY 2026, and CY 2027 rulemakings. As we noted in the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (83 FR 37138 through 37143), unlike the wage adjustment under section 1833(t)(2)(D) of the Act and the outlier, transitional pass-through, and equitable adjustments ( printed page 70595) under section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act, section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act refers to a “method” for controlling unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services, not an adjustment. Likewise, sections 1833(t)(2)(D) and (E) of the Act also explicitly require the adjustments authorized by those paragraphs to be budget neutral, while the volume control method authority at section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act does not include such a requirement. Therefore, we continue to believe that the volume control method proposed under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act is not one of the adjustments under section 1833(t)(2) of the Act that is referenced under section 1833(t)(9)(A) of the Act that must be included in the budget neutrality adjustment under section 1833(t)(9)(B) of the Act.
Moreover, section 1833(t)(9)(C) of the Act specifies that if the Secretary determines under methodologies described in paragraph (2)(F) of section 1833(t) of the Act that the volume of services paid for under this subsection increased beyond amounts established through those methodologies, the Secretary may appropriately adjust the update to the conversion factor otherwise applicable in a subsequent year. We continue to interpret this provision to mean that the Secretary will have implemented a volume control method under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act in a non-budget neutral manner in the year in which the method is implemented. Further, as we stated in the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (83 FR 37138 through 37143), we believe that implementing a volume control method in a budget neutral manner would not appropriately reduce the overall unnecessary volume of covered OPD services and instead would simply shift the volume within the OPPS system in the aggregate.
In addition, the D.C. Circuit in AHA v. Azar held not only that budget neutrality is not required under a volume control method, but that making that method budget neutral would be contrary to the purpose and intent of the Medicare statute. For example, the appellate court emphasized that subparagraph (2)(F) of the Act “says nothing about budget-neutrality,” and specifically rejected the plaintiffs' claim that volume-control methods must be budget neutral. 964 F.3d at 1241. After all, it would be “anomalous” for the statute to require a rate cut made for purposes of volume control to be “implemented budget-neutrally” because, if we were required “to redistribute the costs traceable to the provision of unnecessary services throughout the OPPS,” the result would be “no net savings to Medicare,” “largely negating the point of reducing reimbursement in the first place.” Id. at 1241-42. This common-sense interpretation is thus supported by the text and structure of the OPPS statute, as both we (see 83 FR 37142 through 37143) and the D.C. Circuit have explained.
Comment: Several commenters raised concerns regarding the timeframe and data CMS used to evaluate changes in the volume of imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs. Commenters questioned CMS's use of CY 2016 as a baseline, noting that 2016 was the first year hospitals were required to report the informational “PO” modifier for services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs and stating that first-year reporting may have been incomplete or inconsistent. Commenters recommended that CMS test its findings using alternative baseline years, such as CY 2017 or CY 2018.
Some commenters also recommended that CMS place greater weight on more recent utilization trends. Commenters stated that the period analyzed by CMS spans implementation of section 603 of the BBA of 2015 and the mid-build exception and therefore captures growth associated with the acquisition, construction, and development of off-campus PBDs. Commenters stated that more recent data show relatively stable utilization in excepted off-campus PBDs and stated that CMS should focus on utilization following implementation of section 603 when determining whether there is currently an unnecessary increase in volume. Other commenters stated that CMS should consider a sufficiently long historical period because relying only on recent utilization could include prior shifts from freestanding physician offices to OPDs into the baseline and obscure the effects of consolidation and site-of-service payment differentials.
Several commenters also questioned CMS's use of the 70 HCPCS codes that accounted for more than 95 percent of imaging without contrast volume in excepted off-campus PBDs in CY 2025 to evaluate historical utilization. Commenters stated that these codes represented a smaller proportion of imaging without contrast volume in earlier years and that changes in HCPCS coding during the analysis period make comparisons using a fixed set of current codes potentially misleading. Commenters noted that analyses accounting for predecessor and successor codes and including the full set of imaging without contrast services produced substantially less growth than CMS's analysis. Commenters also stated that a significant portion of the growth identified by CMS was attributable to codes that did not exist or had no reported volume in the baseline year and recommended that CMS account for coding changes when evaluating historical utilization.
Several commenters also requested that CMS make available additional information regarding the data and methodology used to conduct its utilization analysis. Commenters stated that providing the underlying claims analysis, including information regarding the HCPCS codes, claims fields, settings of care, and methodology used to calculate changes in utilization, would allow interested parties to reproduce CMS's analysis and more fully evaluate the basis for the proposed policy.
Response: We thank the commenters for their input. Based on these comments, we conducted additional analyses to determine whether using alternative baseline periods or the full set of imaging without contrast services would change our conclusion that these services have experienced unnecessary increases in volume.
We first considered commenters' concerns regarding the use of CY 2016 as the baseline year. Using CY 2017 as the baseline, total utilization increased by approximately 5 percent through CY 2025, while utilization per FFS beneficiary increased by approximately 26 percent. Similarly, using CY 2018 as the baseline, total utilization increased by approximately 6 percent through CY 2025, while utilization per FFS beneficiary increased by approximately 26 percent. Even when examining the more recent period from CY 2021 through CY 2025, total utilization increased by approximately 9 percent and utilization per FFS beneficiary increased by approximately 20 percent. We therefore do not believe that our conclusion depends on the selection of CY 2016 as the baseline year.
We also considered commenters' concerns regarding the 70 HCPCS codes examined in the proposed rule. We acknowledge that these codes represented a smaller proportion of imaging without contrast services in the earlier years of our analysis than in more recent years. Specifically, these 70 HCPCS codes represented approximately 75 percent of imaging without contrast volume in excepted off-campus PBDs in CYs 2016 and 2017, compared with approximately 94 percent in CY 2018 and more than 95 percent in CY 2025. We therefore also examined historical utilization using the full set of HCPCS codes identified as ( printed page 70596) imaging without contrast services based on CY 2025 claims data, rather than limiting our analysis to the 70 high-volume HCPCS codes discussed in the proposed rule.
Our analysis of historical utilization for this full set of imaging without contrast HCPCS codes continues to demonstrate growth in utilization in excepted off-campus PBDs. Total volume increased from approximately 2.79 million claims in CY 2016 to approximately 3.03 million claims in CY 2025, an increase of approximately 9 percent. Moreover, after accounting for changes in Medicare FFS enrollment, utilization per FFS beneficiary increased by approximately 31 percent over this period. We therefore do not believe that our conclusion depends on limiting our analysis to the 70 HCPCS codes discussed in the proposed rule.
We also do not believe that it would be appropriate to examine only data from more recent years. In our CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule analysis, we started our claims review in CY 2016 to examine what volume looked like during and following the period of consolidation and growth of excepted PBDs and in subsequent years. Rather than a reason to exclude these data, we believe fully understanding how the growth of excepted off-campus PBDs affected the volume of imaging without contrast services is important in examining unnecessary increases in the volume of outpatient services.
Looking only at data from more recent years removes the context for the changes that occurred in the OPPS over the longer historical period. Even if utilization for a particular service has leveled off in recent years, that does not mean that earlier unnecessary increases in volume are no longer reflected in current utilization. If utilization increased unnecessarily in earlier years and subsequently remained at that higher level, examining only the more recent period would include that earlier increase into the baseline and could obscure the extent of the historical growth. Accordingly, we believe it is appropriate to consider utilization over a longer period when evaluating whether there have been unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services.
We also acknowledge commenters' requests for additional information regarding the data and methodology underlying our analysis. In the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, we described the data, time period, settings of care, and HCPCS codes used in our analysis and presented the utilization trends on which our proposal was based. We believe the information provided in the proposed rule was sufficient to allow interested parties to obtain the raw data and conduct analyses intended to replicate or test our analysis. Several commenters submitted their own analyses of utilization trends using Medicare claims data and the parameters described in the proposed rule, including analyses using alternative sets of HCPCS codes, baseline years, and settings of care. These analyses allowed commenters to identify specific methodological concerns and alternative interpretations of the data, which we have considered and addressed in this final rule with comment period.
Based on our review of the proposed-rule data and these additional analyses, we continue to believe that imaging without contrast services have experienced unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services and that it is appropriate to apply our volume control method to these services.
Comment: Several commenters stated that CMS's analysis does not support applying the volume control method to all HCPCS codes assigned to the four imaging without contrast APCs. Commenters noted that the proposed policy would apply to more than 300 HCPCS codes, while CMS's proposed rule utilization analysis focused on 70 high-volume codes. Commenters stated that the remaining codes encompass a broad range of imaging modalities and clinical circumstances and stated that CMS should identify unnecessary increases in volume at the individual HCPCS code level before applying the volume control method to a service.
Commenters further stated that some HCPCS codes subject to the proposed policy had little or no utilization in excepted off-campus PBDs during the period examined by CMS. Commenters stated that CMS cannot control an unnecessary increase in volume for a service for which there has been no utilization or no demonstrated increase in utilization. Commenters similarly identified services with little or no utilization in freestanding physician offices and stated that these services do not support CMS's premise that the affected services are being shifted from freestanding physician offices to OPDs because of payment incentives. Commenters therefore recommended that CMS limit the policy to individual services for which the agency has demonstrated unnecessary increases in OPD volume and meaningful utilization in lower-cost settings.
Response: We thank the commenters for their input. We disagree that we must demonstrate an unnecessary increase in volume independently for every individual HCPCS code assigned to the imaging without contrast APCs before applying our volume control method at the APC level. As we explained in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period in response to similar comments regarding drug administration services (90 FR 53815), we have evaluated unnecessary utilization at the APC level and intentionally chosen to apply the volume control method at the APC level rather than at the individual service level.
We continue to believe this approach is consistent with the structure of the OPPS established under section 1833(t) of the Act. Section 1833(t)(2)(A) of the Act requires the Secretary to develop a classification system for covered OPD services, and section 1833(t)(2)(B) of the Act provides for the establishment of groups of covered OPD services within that classification system so that the services within each group are comparable clinically and with respect to the use of resources. Consistent with these provisions, we group services under the OPPS into APCs and generally establish payment at the APC level. We therefore believe it is appropriate to evaluate unnecessary increases in volume and apply our volume control method to groups of clinically and resource-similar services at the APC level rather than requiring each individual HCPCS code within an APC to independently demonstrate the same utilization pattern.
In the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, we examined the 70 most frequently billed HCPCS codes for imaging without contrast services, which accounted for more than 95 percent of imaging without contrast volume furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs in CY 2025. As discussed previously, in response to comments regarding our use of these 70 HCPCS codes, we conducted an additional analysis of historical utilization using the full set of imaging without contrast HCPCS codes identified based on CY 2025 claims data. That additional analysis does not change our conclusion that imaging without contrast services have experienced unnecessary increases in volume.
We acknowledge that some individual HCPCS codes assigned to these APCs have little or no utilization in excepted off-campus PBDs or freestanding physician offices. However, as we explained in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53815), the fact that some less frequently used codes within an APC ( printed page 70597) are rarely utilized in either setting does not detract from the larger finding of unnecessary increases in volume for the services in the APCs as a whole. A code with no utilization in an excepted off-campus PBD also contributes no volume to the utilization trends on which our APC-level finding is based.
Consistent with our approach to the drug administration APC family, we believe applying the methodology to the imaging without contrast APCs is a practical and appropriate way to control unnecessary increases in the volume of this family of services. Accordingly, the fact that some less frequently used codes within these APCs are rarely utilized in either the OPD or freestanding physician office setting does not detract from our APC-level finding or our conclusion that application of the volume control method to the imaging without contrast APCs is appropriate.
Comment: Several commenters stated that the utilization trends for individual imaging without contrast services do not consistently support CMS's conclusion that payment differences are causing services to shift from physician offices to excepted off-campus PBDs. Commenters identified services for which utilization increased in both settings, remained stable in physician offices, or increased more rapidly in freestanding physician offices than in excepted off-campus PBDs. Commenters stated that these varying trends undermine the conclusion that a common payment incentive is responsible for increased utilization across imaging without contrast services.
Commenters also stated that observed increases in excepted off-campus PBD utilization may reflect factors other than shifts from freestanding physician offices attributable to payment incentives. Commenters cited shifts from inpatient to outpatient care, changes in clinical practice and screening recommendations, advances in imaging technology, changes in disease prevalence and beneficiary demographics, physician referral patterns, hospital investments in imaging capacity, and closures or acquisitions of independent imaging facilities as potential explanations for changes in utilization.
Several commenters also questioned CMS's reliance on increases in utilization per Medicare FFS beneficiary. Commenters stated that increased enrollment in Medicare Advantage may have changed the composition of the remaining FFS population, potentially leaving a population that is older or more clinically complex and requires more imaging services. Commenters stated that accounting for changes in the composition of the FFS population would reduce the measured increase in per-beneficiary utilization and recommended that CMS account for beneficiary case mix when evaluating utilization trends. Commenters also requested that CMS disclose whether its per-beneficiary analysis adjusts for changes in the composition of the Medicare FFS population, including changes associated with increasing enrollment in Medicare Advantage.
Response: We thank the commenters for their input. We acknowledge that utilization patterns vary across individual imaging without contrast services and that not every service demonstrates the same pattern of utilization across settings. However, we do not believe that an increase in utilization in the freestanding physician office setting, including an increase that occurs at the same time as growth in excepted off-campus PBDs, demonstrates that there is no unnecessary utilization in the excepted PBD setting. As we explained in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53814), taking individual utilization trends out of their full historical context does not provide an accurate gauge of the actual growth of services in excepted PBDs.
We also reviewed the specific utilization trends identified by commenters. Our review continues to show substantial increases in the volume of several high-volume imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs. For example, between CY 2016 and CY 2025, utilization in excepted off-campus PBDs increased by approximately 72 percent for HCPCS code 71250, 56 percent for HCPCS code 77080, 52 percent for HCPCS code 76641, 48 percent for HCPCS code 76536, and 41 percent for HCPCS code 70551. These increases occurred notwithstanding differing utilization trends for these services in freestanding physician offices. We therefore do not believe that differing utilization patterns for individual services demonstrate that payment differences are not a substantial cause of unnecessary increases in volume across the imaging without contrast APCs.
We also do not believe that the existence of other factors that may contribute to increased utilization, such as changes in clinical practice, screening recommendations, technology, beneficiary characteristics, referral patterns, or the availability of imaging capacity, demonstrates that the payment differential between the OPPS and PFS does not constitute a substantial cause of unnecessary increases in OPD volume. Our determination does not depend on a finding that payment differences are the sole cause of increased utilization. Rather, as we have explained in prior rulemaking, we consider shifts in the site of service unnecessary if the beneficiary can safely receive the same service in a lower-cost setting but instead receives care in a higher-cost setting due to the payment incentives created by the difference in payment amounts.
We specifically considered commenters' assertion that increases in utilization in excepted off-campus PBDs may reflect shifts from the inpatient to outpatient setting. We agree that shifts from inpatient to outpatient care may partially explain changes in utilization for particular services. However, this does not explain why services that can appropriately migrate from the inpatient setting are furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs rather than in freestanding physician offices or other lower-cost ambulatory settings. A decline in inpatient utilization accompanied by an increase in outpatient utilization demonstrates that the site of care has changed, but it does not establish what the distribution of that outpatient volume would have been absent the payment differential between the OPPS and PFS.
Once a service can safely be furnished outside of the inpatient setting, the payment differential between outpatient settings remains relevant. To the extent the same service can safely be furnished in a freestanding physician office or other lower-cost setting, the higher payment available in an excepted off-campus PBD creates a significant incentive for some portion of that volume to remain in or shift to the higher-paid OPD setting. Commenters did not demonstrate how much of the observed increase in excepted off-campus PBD utilization would have occurred absent that payment differential. Accordingly, evidence of an inpatient-to-outpatient shift does not demonstrate that the resulting increase in excepted off-campus PBD volume is necessary or that payment incentives do not contribute to the setting in which those services are ultimately furnished.
We also considered commenters' concerns regarding changes in the composition of the Medicare FFS population. We clarify that our per-beneficiary utilization analysis accounts for changes in the number of Medicare FFS beneficiaries by dividing utilization by Medicare Part B FFS enrollment for ( printed page 70598) the applicable year. The analysis does not adjust for changes in the demographic characteristics, health status, or clinical risk of the FFS beneficiary population over time. We do not believe that such an adjustment is necessary or appropriate for purposes of this analysis. The purpose of examining utilization per FFS beneficiary is to determine whether changes in aggregate utilization can be explained by changes in the size of the FFS population, rather than to estimate the amount of imaging that would be clinically necessary for a particular beneficiary population. Developing a case-mix adjustment for this purpose would require determining which beneficiary characteristics should be expected to affect utilization of the broad range of imaging services included in these APCs and the extent to which those characteristics should affect expected utilization. We do not believe commenters provided a sufficiently supported methodology for making such an adjustment. Moreover, even if such an adjustment could estimate the portion of increased imaging utilization attributable to changes in beneficiary characteristics, it would not establish the setting in which those medically necessary services needed to be furnished.
Moreover, even if changes in the composition of the FFS population explain some portion of the increase in imaging services per beneficiary, that would not demonstrate that the resulting increase in services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs is necessary. Beneficiaries with greater clinical needs may appropriately require more imaging services, but that does not mean those services must be furnished in the higher-paid OPD setting. As discussed previously, our concern is not whether the underlying imaging service is medically necessary. Rather, we consider increases in covered OPD services unnecessary when a beneficiary can safely receive the same medically necessary service in a lower-cost setting but instead receives it in the higher-paid OPD setting due to payment incentives. Our policy does not prevent a physician from determining that an OPD is the appropriate setting for a particular beneficiary based on the beneficiary's clinical needs.
Based on our review of the proposed-rule data, our additional analyses, and the information provided by commenters, we continue to believe that the payment differential between the OPPS and PFS is a significant driver of unnecessary increases in the volume of imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs. The fact that individual services may exhibit different utilization patterns, or that factors other than payment may also affect utilization, does not change our conclusion.
Comment: Several commenters stated that utilization trends in non-excepted off-campus PBDs undermine CMS's conclusion that the payment differential between the OPPS and PFS contributes to unnecessary increases in the volume of imaging without contrast services. Commenters noted that non-excepted off-campus PBDs already receive the PFS-equivalent payment rate and stated that utilization of imaging without contrast services in these departments has nevertheless increased substantially, in some cases more rapidly than in excepted off-campus PBDs. Commenters stated that this growth suggests that eliminating the payment differential may reduce Medicare expenditures without affecting where services are furnished.
Commenters also stated that CMS had not established an appropriate counterfactual for determining what utilization would have been in the absence of the OPPS payment differential. Commenters stated that growth in non-excepted off-campus PBD utilization may reflect factors such as growth in the number of these departments, hospital consolidation and referral patterns, beneficiary case mix, geography, and changes in the availability of independent imaging facilities.
Conversely, other commenters cited an analysis of Maryland, where hospitals operate under a global budget model, showing that the share of imaging without contrast services furnished in OPDs declined relative to the rest of the country. Commenters stated that this comparison provides evidence that payment incentives may influence the setting in which imaging services are furnished.
Response: We thank the commenters for their input. We disagree that growth in imaging without contrast services furnished in non-excepted off-campus PBDs demonstrates that the OPPS/PFS payment differential does not contribute to unnecessary increases in volume. Under section 603 of the BBA of 2015, new off-campus PBDs generally enter the Medicare program as non-excepted departments. Accordingly, growth in aggregate utilization in non-excepted off-campus PBDs reflects, at least in part, growth in the number of departments subject to that payment methodology and does not provide a direct comparison of how excepted and non-excepted PBDs respond to different payment rates.
We also cannot observe what utilization in non-excepted off-campus PBDs would have been had those departments instead received the higher OPPS payment. The fact that utilization increased under the PFS-equivalent payment methodology therefore does not establish that utilization would not have been greater in the absence of that methodology. More fundamentally, our concern is not that imaging utilization should never increase under PFS-equivalent payment. Rather, our concern is whether the higher payment available under the OPPS creates an additional incentive for services that can safely be furnished in a lower-cost setting to instead be furnished in the higher-paid OPD setting.
We also note that non-excepted off-campus PBDs continue to furnish substantial volumes of imaging without contrast services while receiving the PFS-equivalent payment rate. We believe the continued furnishing of these services at significant volume demonstrates that imaging without contrast services can be furnished in an off-campus hospital setting under the PFS-equivalent payment methodology.
We also considered the analysis submitted by commenters comparing utilization in Maryland, where hospitals operate under a global budget model, with the rest of the country. The analysis found that from CY 2017 through CY 2024, the regression-adjusted share of imaging without contrast services furnished in OPDs declined from approximately 32 percent to 24 percent in Maryland, while remaining approximately 50 percent outside Maryland.[163]
We recognize that Maryland's payment system differs from those applicable in other States and that this comparison does not establish what utilization in excepted off-campus PBDs would have been absent the OPPS/PFS payment differential. Nevertheless, because Maryland's global budget model creates different incentives regarding the volume of hospital outpatient services, we believe the differing utilization patterns provide additional evidence consistent with our conclusion that payment incentives can affect site of service.
For these reasons, we continue to believe that growth in non-excepted off-campus PBD utilization does not undermine our conclusion that the OPPS/PFS payment differential is a substantial cause of unnecessary increases in the volume of imaging ( printed page 70599) without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs.
Comment: A few commenters stated that CMS cannot determine that there have been unnecessary increases in the volume of imaging without contrast services without first identifying a necessary level or rate of growth. Commenters stated that CMS has not established what level of utilization would be considered necessary and therefore has no basis for determining what portion of the observed growth is unnecessary. Some commenters recommended that CMS establish a benchmark for expected utilization and monitor volume against that benchmark before applying a payment reduction.
Some commenters also stated that CMS appears to conflate unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services with medically unnecessary imaging. Commenters stated that the fact that an imaging service could potentially be furnished in a lower-cost setting does not establish that the underlying service was medically unnecessary or clinically inappropriate.
Commenters also recommended that CMS consider other methods for addressing unnecessary or inappropriate imaging utilization, including medical-necessity requirements, claims review, prior authorization or other utilization management policies, clinical practice guidelines, and appropriate use criteria. Some commenters specifically recommended that CMS reconsider or modernize the Medicare Appropriate Use Criteria program for advanced diagnostic imaging as an alternative to the proposed payment policy.
Response: We disagree that section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act requires us to establish a specific level or rate of necessary volume growth before determining that there have been unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services. As we explained in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53815), because site-of-service payment differentials affect utilization throughout the OPPS, it would be extremely difficult to determine, at the HCPCS or APC level, the precise amount of volume that would have occurred absent that influence. We do not believe that establishing a retrospective benchmark would materially improve our ability to identify unnecessary increases in volume and, as discussed in prior rulemaking, such an approach could raise concerns similar to those associated with prior benchmark-based volume control methodologies.
We also clarify that our use of the term “unnecessary” does not mean that the underlying imaging service was medically unnecessary for the beneficiary. Our concern under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act is with unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services. As we have explained in prior rulemaking, we consider a shift in site of service unnecessary when a beneficiary can safely receive the same medically necessary service in a lower-cost setting but instead receives it in the higher-paid OPD setting because of the payment incentive created by the difference in payment amounts. Accordingly, determining whether an individual imaging service satisfies Medicare medical-necessity requirements would not resolve the site-of-service issue addressed by this policy.
We appreciate commenters' recommendations regarding other approaches to addressing unnecessary utilization, including medical-necessity review, prior authorization, utilization management, clinical practice guidelines, and appropriate use criteria. As discussed in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53825), we previously solicited public comment on other methods that may be warranted to control unnecessary increases in the volume of outpatient services besides changes to payment rates, including prior authorization and other utilization management policies. We continue to appreciate interested parties' input regarding these alternative approaches and may consider these recommendations in future rulemaking.
For purposes of the policy finalized in this rule, however, we continue to believe that applying the PFS-equivalent payment rate to imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs is an appropriate method to address the site-of-service payment differential that is a substantial cause of unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services. We will continue to monitor the effects of this policy on utilization, as we have done for our clinic visit and drug administration volume control policies.
Comment: Commenters reiterated concerns raised in response to prior rulemaking that OPDs are more likely to serve Medicare patients who are sicker, more clinically complex, and more likely to be disabled or living in poorer, rural communities than patients treated in independent physician offices. In support of these concerns, commenters again cited studies prepared for the American Hospital Association that were also cited in comments on the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC proposed rule and discussed in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53819 through 53820).
Commenters again cited a study finding that, compared to beneficiaries treated in independent physician offices, beneficiaries receiving care in OPDs were more likely to be:
Under age 65 and disabled,
Reside in a rural county,
Be dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid,
Have serious chronic conditions, and
Have recently used hospital care, including emergency department and inpatient hospital services.
Commenters also again cited a related study comparing beneficiaries with cancer treated in OPDs to beneficiaries with cancer treated in freestanding physician offices, which similarly found that beneficiaries receiving cancer care in OPDs were more likely to be disabled, reside in rural areas, be dually eligible, have multiple serious chronic conditions, and have recently used emergency department or inpatient hospital services. We discussed these same studies and commenters' concerns regarding differences in the patient populations served by OPDs and physician offices in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53819 through 53820).
Commenters also provided additional analyses specific to the imaging without contrast services included in the CY 2027 proposal. One commenter stated that, based on 2025 Medicare claims data, beneficiaries receiving imaging without contrast services in OPDs were 51 percent more likely than beneficiaries receiving the same services in independent physician offices to be dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid, 64 percent more likely to be disabled, and 58 percent more likely to have end-stage renal disease. The commenter also stated that OPD beneficiaries receiving these services had greater clinical complexity, including being 50 percent more likely to have five or more complications or comorbidities and 92 percent more likely to have five or more major complications or comorbidities.
Commenters further stated that imaging without contrast services furnished in OPDs may be part of broader, coordinated episodes of care, including pre-operative evaluation, treatment planning, serial imaging for patients receiving complex therapies or cancer treatment, and multispecialty care. Commenters stated that OPDs may provide additional staff, specialized equipment, emergency response capabilities, and immediate access to laboratory, advanced imaging, surgical, ( printed page 70600) and other services that may be important for medically complex beneficiaries. Commenters also noted that physicians may refer higher-risk patients to OPDs because those settings can more readily manage complications or escalation of care.
Commenters noted that these differences demonstrate that OPDs and physician offices are not interchangeable for all beneficiaries and that higher-acuity patients may require additional time, staffing, coordination, and hospital-level resources. Commenters therefore stated that reducing payment for imaging without contrast services in OPDs could adversely affect access to care for medically complex beneficiaries.
Response: We appreciate commenters reiterating their concerns regarding differences in the patient populations served by OPDs and freestanding physician offices and providing additional information specific to imaging without contrast services. As we explained in response to similar comments in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53820), we appreciate that OPDs serve unique patient populations and provide services to medically complex beneficiaries. However, the data provided by commenters do not demonstrate how these factors necessitate a higher payment for all imaging without contrast services provided in OPDs. While commenters indicate that these patients are more frequently treated in OPDs and, in some cases, may require additional coordination or support, they do not show that OPDs alone are clinically capable of furnishing imaging without contrast services to medically complex patients or that freestanding physician offices and other lower-cost ambulatory settings would be unequipped to safely furnish these same services when clinically appropriate.
As we stated in the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53820), we continue to believe shifts in the sites of service described in the preceding paragraphs are inherently unnecessary if the beneficiary can safely receive the same services in a lower-cost setting but instead receives care in a higher-cost setting due to the payment incentives created by the difference in payment amounts. Our policy does not prevent a physician from determining that an OPD is the appropriate setting for a particular beneficiary based on the beneficiary's clinical needs.
Further, the OPPS contains mechanisms to increase payment to providers for complex care. Hospitals can receive outlier payments to help hospitals mitigate financial risks associated with complex and costly procedures that exceed the normal payment amount. We also use complexity adjustments to provide increased payment for certain comprehensive services.
Comment: Some commenters stated that the proposed policy does not appropriately account for the role of physicians in determining whether an imaging service is medically necessary and the appropriate site of service. Commenters stated that physicians, rather than hospitals or outpatient departments, generally order imaging services and that hospitals therefore have limited ability to control the volume of imaging services furnished in their outpatient departments. Commenters stated that reducing payment to the hospital may penalize the facility for utilization that is largely driven by physician clinical judgment.
Commenters further stated that physicians may determine that an OPD is the appropriate site of service for particular beneficiaries based on clinical complexity, comorbidities, availability of specialized equipment or personnel, or the potential need for other hospital resources. Commenters expressed concern that the proposed policy could interfere with or create incentives inconsistent with physicians' clinical judgment regarding the most appropriate setting for their patients.
Response: We thank the commenters for their input. We agree that physicians should determine whether an imaging service is medically necessary and should consider the medical needs of the beneficiary when determining the appropriate setting in which that service should be furnished. We believe that payment should have no influence on what setting of care a physician decides is most appropriate for their patient. Our policy does not limit a physician's ability to order a medically necessary imaging service or prevent a beneficiary from receiving that service in an OPD when that setting is clinically appropriate.
We also disagree that the role of physicians in ordering imaging services makes application of the volume control method to excepted off-campus PBDs inappropriate. Our concern is not with the physician's decision regarding whether a beneficiary requires a particular imaging service. Rather, our concern is with the financial incentives that may affect the setting in which that service is ultimately furnished. The fact that a physician determines that an imaging service is medically necessary does not establish that the service must be furnished in an excepted off-campus PBD or that the higher OPPS payment rate is necessary for that service.
We also do not believe that application of the volume control method depends on an individual hospital having direct control over a physician's decision to order a particular imaging service. The method is intended to address the broader payment structure that creates a systemic financial incentive for services that can safely be furnished in lower-cost ambulatory settings to be furnished in the higher-paid OPD setting and that we believe is a significant driver of unnecessary increases in covered OPD services over time. By aligning payment for the affected services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs with the PFS-equivalent payment methodology applicable to non-excepted off-campus PBDs, we are addressing the underlying payment differential that contributes to these site-of-service incentives rather than seeking to influence individual physicians' clinical ordering decisions.
As discussed previously, imaging without contrast services are routinely furnished in freestanding physician offices and non-excepted off-campus PBDs. Where a beneficiary can safely receive the same medically necessary service in a lower-cost setting but instead receives the service in a higher-paid OPD setting because of payment incentives, we consider the resulting increase in covered OPD services unnecessary for purposes of section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act. Applying the PFS-equivalent payment rate removes the payment differential while leaving physicians free to determine, based on the beneficiary's clinical needs, whether the hospital outpatient setting is appropriate.
Comment: Several commenters noted that CMS failed to adequately consider other explanations for increases in the volume of imaging without contrast services furnished in hospital outpatient departments. Commenters disagreed that higher OPPS payments are necessarily responsible for hospital acquisitions of physician practices and independent imaging facilities or resulting increases in OPD utilization. Commenters stated that correlation between payment differentials, consolidation, and increased OPD utilization does not establish that the payment differential caused the observed increase.
Similar to comments received in response to the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, commenters stated that physician practices may seek acquisition by or affiliation with hospitals because of financial and operational pressures unrelated to OPPS ( printed page 70601) payment rates. Commenters cited increasing practice expenses, regulatory and administrative burden, workforce shortages, physician burnout, payer mix, and declines in Medicare physician payment as factors contributing to physicians leaving independent practice. Commenters also stated that entities other than hospitals, including commercial insurers and private equity firms, have acquired physician practices and stated that broader consolidation trends cannot be attributed solely to Medicare site-of-service payment differences.
Commenters also identified other factors that may affect imaging utilization and site-of-service patterns, including changes in clinical practice and technology, beneficiary needs, physician referral patterns, hospital investment in imaging capacity, and changes in the availability of independent imaging facilities. Commenters recommended that CMS account for these factors before concluding that payment differences contribute to unnecessary increases in OPD volume.
Response: We thank the commenters for their input. As discussed earlier in this section, we recognize that multiple factors may affect changes in imaging utilization and the settings in which imaging services are furnished. However, the existence of other factors that may contribute to consolidation or changes in utilization does not mean that the substantial difference between OPPS and PFS payment rates does not also create an incentive to furnish services in the higher-paid setting.
As we explained in response to similar comments in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53819), hospitals did, in large quantities, acquire physician practices and convert them into PBDs, and a financial incentive to make these conversions existed. While physician practices may also be acquired by private equity firms, commercial insurers, or other entities, only acquisition by a hospital can result in services that were previously paid under the PFS being paid at the higher OPPS rate as a result of conversion to a provider-based department. We therefore do not believe that evidence of other causes of physician-practice consolidation eliminates the Medicare payment incentive created by the difference between OPPS and PFS payment rates.
We also acknowledge commenters' concerns regarding financial and operational pressures faced by freestanding physician practices that may encourage association with hospitals and a shift to OPD settings. However, as we stated in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53819), the OPPS was intended to pay for services provided in the hospital outpatient setting; it has no mandate to subsidize care or the cost of providing that care as a result of broader economic forces or the perceived inadequacy of other forms of payment. To the extent that commenters may believe payment under the PFS is inadequate, as discussed elsewhere in this section, such concerns do not provide a basis for maintaining a higher OPPS payment for services that can safely be furnished in lower-cost settings.
We similarly recognize that changes in clinical practice, technology, beneficiary needs, referral patterns, and the availability of imaging capacity may affect utilization of particular imaging services. However, our determination does not depend on a finding that the OPPS/PFS payment differential is the sole cause of changes in imaging utilization or consolidation. As discussed previously, our additional analyses continue to demonstrate increases in imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs, including increases in utilization per FFS beneficiary, and we have considered commenters' specific concerns regarding the timeframe of our analysis, coding changes, individual service trends, changes in the FFS population, inpatient-to-outpatient migration, utilization in non-excepted PBDs, and available counterfactual evidence.
After considering these alternative explanations, we continue to believe that the substantial payment differential between the OPPS and PFS creates a significant financial incentive to furnish imaging without contrast services in the higher-paid OPD setting and is a significant factor contributing to unnecessary increases in the volume of these services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs. Even if multiple factors affect where imaging services are furnished, we continue to believe that payment should have no influence on what setting of care is selected when a beneficiary can safely receive the same service in a lower-cost setting. Our policy removes the payment incentive that we believe is a substantial cause of unnecessary increases in covered OPD services while preserving the ability of physicians and beneficiaries to use the hospital outpatient setting when clinically appropriate.
Comment: Some commenters raised concerns regarding the direct comparison between OPPS and PFS payment rates for imaging without contrast services. Commenters stated that the OPPS and PFS reflect fundamentally different approaches to valuing and paying for services and stated that there is no basis for substituting payment rates developed under one payment system for rates under the other. Similar to comments received in response to the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, commenters stated that hospital outpatient departments incur costs and maintain capabilities that are not reflected in physician office payment rates, including regulatory and accreditation requirements, staffing and equipment, emergency and standby capacity, and other hospital infrastructure. Commenters stated that these differences make direct comparisons between OPPS and PFS payment rates inappropriate.
Commenters also stated that imaging services furnished in OPDs may require resources that differ from those reflected in PFS payment rates. Commenters cited differences in equipment acquisition and maintenance costs, staffing, quality and safety requirements, and the resources necessary to serve medically complex patients. Commenters stated that OPDs may maintain imaging capacity and specialized staff that allow them to furnish services to higher-acuity patients and respond to complications or other clinical needs. Commenters stated that these additional costs are not adequately reflected in PFS payment rates and that reducing OPPS payment based on PFS rates could adversely affect hospitals' ability to maintain imaging capacity and beneficiary access to care.
Other commenters questioned whether PFS payment rates themselves provide an appropriate benchmark for determining payment under the OPPS. Commenters stated that physician practices have experienced increasing practice expenses and reductions in inflation-adjusted Medicare payment and expressed concern that aligning hospital payment with PFS rates could extend payment inadequacies in the PFS to the hospital outpatient setting. Commenters also cited negative Medicare hospital margins and stated that further reductions in OPPS payment would exacerbate hospitals' existing financial pressures and could impair their ability to support emergency, standby, and other hospital capabilities. Some commenters stated that site-neutral payment should account for the actual resources required to furnish services across ambulatory settings rather than simply ( printed page 70602) reduce payment to the amount paid in the lowest-cost setting.
Response: We appreciate the commenters' concerns regarding comparisons between OPPS and PFS payment rates. As we stated in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53817), to the extent that similar services can be safely provided in more than one setting, we do not believe it is prudent for the Medicare program to pay more for these services in one setting than another. We believe that differences in payment for the same or similar services can create a payment incentive to provide those services in the higher-cost setting. Because these services can be safely provided in a lower-cost setting, we believe that growth in services paid under the OPPS that results from this payment incentive is unnecessary. Further, we believe that setting OPPS payment at a PFS-equivalent rate is an effective method to control the unnecessary increase in the volume of these services because the payment differential that is driving the site-of-service decision would be removed.
As discussed in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (91 FR 41912), we also compared OPPS and PFS payment rates using PFS payment rates for the most frequently billed imaging without contrast HCPCS codes furnished by excepted off-campus PBDs and volume-weighted those rates to create a PFS proxy average APC payment rate for imaging without contrast services. Using this approach, we found that, on average, OPPS payment rates for imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs were approximately 2.5 times higher than PFS payment rates, while payment rates for these services furnished in non-excepted off-campus PBDs were closely aligned with PFS payment rates. At the APC level, PFS payments ranged from approximately 31 percent to 54 percent of OPPS payments. We believe these findings demonstrate a substantial payment differential between the OPPS and PFS for the imaging without contrast services subject to this policy.
We observed a similar pattern for beneficiary cost sharing. Average beneficiary cost sharing for imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs was more than twice the amount for these services when furnished in freestanding physician offices, while beneficiary cost sharing for services furnished in non-excepted off-campus PBDs was closely aligned with beneficiary cost sharing in freestanding physician offices. These differences further support our concern that the payment differential not only creates an incentive to furnish services in the higher-paid setting but also results in higher costs for Medicare beneficiaries.
We appreciate that some hospital outpatient departments may incur costs that physician offices do not. We note that applying the PFS-equivalent payment methodology to these services does not eliminate payment to the hospital for furnishing the service. The hospital continues to receive payment for the facility component of the service under the applicable PFS-equivalent methodology, while the physician or other practitioner may receive separate payment under the PFS for the professional services furnished. Thus, the payment methodology continues to recognize a facility payment for services furnished in the off-campus PBD, although at a lower amount than would otherwise be paid under the OPPS. However, the issue we are addressing here is whether the difference between OPPS payment rates and PFS payment rates for imaging without contrast services distorts the market and incentivizes providers to shift volume to the higher-paying setting unnecessarily. The aspects of the OPD setting identified by commenters, including staffing and equipment, licensing and accreditation requirements, emergency and standby capacity, and the resources associated with caring for medically complex patients, do not change the fact that a specific imaging without contrast service provided in an off-campus provider-based department of a hospital is clinically similar to the provision of that same imaging service when provided in a freestanding physician office. We believe that imaging without contrast services included in this policy can generally be safely performed in the freestanding physician office setting and note that freestanding physician offices also incur costs to adhere to regulatory and safety standards and ensure that they are appropriately equipped to provide these services. While some hospital outpatient departments may have additional costs that freestanding physician offices do not, hospitals may also have efficiencies that freestanding physician offices do not, such as greater purchasing power, that may offset some of the additional costs identified by commenters. This is consistent with our response to similar comments regarding drug administration services in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53819).
We also acknowledge commenters' concerns regarding the adequacy of payment rates under the PFS. As we stated in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53817), the overall amount of Medicare payments to physicians and other entities made under the PFS is determined by the PFS statute, and the rates for individual services are determined based on the resources involved in furnishing these services relative to other services paid under the PFS. To the extent commenters believe that the PFS rate for a particular service is misvalued relative to other PFS services, commenters may nominate the service for review as a potentially misvalued service under the PFS.
We similarly do not believe that commenters' concerns regarding overall Medicare hospital margins demonstrate that the higher OPPS payment rate must be maintained for the imaging without contrast services subject to this policy. As discussed in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53819), the OPPS was intended to pay for services provided in the hospital outpatient setting; it has no mandate to subsidize care or the cost of providing that care as a result of broader economic forces or the perceived inadequacy of other forms of payment. Our volume control method addresses the payment incentive associated with the particular services subject to the policy rather than the overall financial condition of an individual hospital or the adequacy of Medicare payment across all hospital services.
We therefore continue to believe that applying the PFS-equivalent payment methodology to imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs is appropriate. Doing so directly addresses the payment differential that we believe is a significant driver of unnecessary increases in OPD volume while preserving physicians' ability to determine the clinically appropriate setting for each beneficiary.
Comment: Some commenters raised concerns related to the use of the 40-percent PFS relativity adjuster for the proposed volume control method. Commenters stated that the relativity adjuster does not necessarily produce the payment amount that would otherwise apply under the PFS for individual imaging services. Commenters presented analyses comparing 40 percent of the applicable OPPS payment amount with the PFS technical component payment and stated that, for some imaging services, application of the 40-percent relativity adjuster would result in payment below the applicable PFS technical component amount, while for other services it would result in payment above the PFS technical component amount. Commenters stated that these ( printed page 70603) differences demonstrate that the 40-percent factor does not consistently approximate PFS payment for imaging without contrast services.
Commenters also raised concerns regarding application of the relativity adjuster to imaging services paid through the multiple imaging composite APCs. Commenters stated that the composite APC methodology already reflects payment for multiple imaging services furnished during the same encounter and stated that applying the 40-percent relativity adjuster to the composite APC payment could result in an additional or duplicative payment reduction. Commenters also stated that comparisons between OPPS and PFS payment amounts should account for differences in packaging and other payment policies between the two systems.
Some commenters further stated that certain imaging services under the PFS are subject to the imaging payment cap established by the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 (DRA) and codified at section 1848(b)(4) of the Act. Commenters stated that the DRA imaging payment cap may contribute to differences between the applicable PFS technical component payment and the payment produced by applying the 40-percent PFS relativity adjuster and recommended that CMS account for these differences when establishing payment for imaging without contrast services under the volume control method.
Several commenters recommended that CMS modify the methodology so that payment would be no less than the applicable PFS technical component amount. Commenters suggested, for example, that CMS pay the greater of 40 percent of the OPPS payment amount or the applicable PFS technical component payment. Commenters stated that such a floor would ensure that hospitals are not paid less for an imaging service than would be paid for the technical component of the same service under the PFS.
Response: We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding the relationship between the 40-percent PFS relativity adjuster and the payment amounts that would otherwise apply under the PFS for particular imaging services. We note, however, that the PFS relativity adjuster itself was established through separate rulemaking and was not proposed for modification in this rulemaking. In the CY 2018 PFS final rule (82 FR 52976), we finalized a PFS relativity adjuster of 40 percent for purposes of establishing payment under the PFS for non-excepted items and services furnished by non-excepted off-campus PBDs. In doing so, we explained that the adjuster was intended to approximate the overall relativity between OPPS and PFS payment rather than reproduce the applicable PFS payment amount for each individual HCPCS code.
As we explained in the CY 2018 PFS final rule (82 FR 53023), the comparison between OPPS and PFS payment varies considerably across services, reflecting, among other things, differences in packaging, bundling, multiple procedure payment reductions, and the mix of services furnished in off-campus PBDs. We therefore recognized that an across-the-board relativity adjuster would necessarily be imprecise and that the actual difference between OPPS and PFS payment for an individual service may be higher or lower than the amount produced by application of the adjuster. We also recognized that PFS payment for some individual services may be lower or higher than the payment amount calculated using the PFS relativity adjuster.
When finalizing the 40-percent factor for CY 2018, we considered an updated analysis showing that the utilization-weighted applicable PFS payment amount for the most frequently billed services in off-campus PBDs was approximately 35 percent of the corresponding OPPS payment amount. Because we were unable at that time to fully account for differences in packaging between the OPPS and PFS, we finalized a 40-percent relativity adjuster as an upward adjustment to that 35-percent estimate. Thus, the 40-percent factor was not intended to establish exact code-specific PFS payment amounts.
For the CY 2027 imaging policy, our analysis similarly demonstrates variation in the relationship between OPPS and PFS payment across the affected services. As discussed in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (91 FR 41912), at the APC level, PFS payments for imaging without contrast services ranged from approximately 31 percent to 54 percent of OPPS payments. We believe that this range is consistent with the service-level variation that we anticipated when establishing an overall relativity adjuster. Accordingly, the fact that application of the 40-percent factor may result in payment above the applicable PFS technical component amount for some services and below it for others does not, by itself, demonstrate that use of the existing PFS relativity adjuster is inappropriate for purposes of the volume control method finalized in this rule.
We also disagree that application of the PFS relativity adjuster to imaging services paid through the multiple imaging composite APCs results in an inappropriate duplicative payment reduction. As discussed in the CY 2018 PFS final rule (82 FR 53024), when establishing payment for non-excepted items and services furnished by non-excepted off-campus PBDs, we included applicable OPPS packaging and payment policies, including comprehensive APCs, conditionally and unconditionally packaged items and services, and applicable multiple procedure payment reductions. We explained that retaining these OPPS payment policies was necessary to maintain the integrity of the PFS relativity adjuster because the adjuster is intended, in part, to account for methodological differences between the OPPS and PFS. Accordingly, where imaging services are paid through an applicable multiple imaging composite APC, the composite APC payment amount represents the OPPS payment amount to which the relativity adjuster applies. The methodology was not designed to reconstruct, on a service-by-service basis, the amount that would be paid under the PFS for each individual service comprising the composite.
We also considered commenters' concerns regarding the DRA imaging payment cap under section 1848(b)(4) of the Act. We recognize that the applicable PFS payment for certain imaging services may be affected by statutory payment limitations and that this may contribute to differences between the applicable PFS technical component payment and the payment produced by applying the 40-percent PFS relativity adjuster. However, this does not alter the purpose or design of the PFS relativity adjuster. As discussed previously, the relativity adjuster was intended to approximate the overall relationship between OPPS and PFS payment and may produce payment amounts that are higher or lower, on a code-by-code basis, than the payment that would otherwise apply under the PFS.
Several commenters recommended that, at a minimum, CMS establish the applicable PFS technical component payment as a floor, such that payment would equal the greater of 40 percent of the OPPS payment amount or the applicable PFS technical component amount. We appreciate commenters' recommendation. However, the PFS relativity adjuster itself was not proposed for modification in this rulemaking. Rather, the proposed volume control method relied on the existing site-specific PFS payment methodology applicable to non-excepted off-campus PBDs, including ( printed page 70604) the existing 40-percent PFS relativity adjuster.
Accordingly, we are not establishing a PFS technical component floor or otherwise modifying the PFS relativity adjuster in this final rule. However, we appreciate commenters' input regarding the relationship between the relativity-adjusted payment amount and the applicable PFS technical component payment. We believe commenters have raised important considerations regarding the continued use and design of the PFS relativity adjuster, including the variation between relativity-adjusted payment amounts and applicable PFS payment amounts for individual services. We intend to continue evaluating whether refinements to the PFS relativity adjuster, or the development of alternative relativity adjusters, may be appropriate and may consider such changes in future rulemaking.
Comment: Several commenters expressed concern that applying the volume control method to imaging without contrast services could adversely affect beneficiary access to preventive and screening services. Commenters identified several screening services assigned to the imaging without contrast APCs, including low-dose CT for lung cancer screening, CT colonography, abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) screening, and DXA bone density testing. Commenters stated that reductions in payment for these services could affect provider capacity and availability and create barriers to beneficiary participation in recommended screening. Some commenters recommended that CMS exempt imaging services that receive an A or B recommendation from the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) or are recommended by medical specialty societies, while other commenters recommended that CMS monitor payment adequacy and beneficiary access to preventive imaging following implementation of the policy.
