Several commenters raised particular concerns regarding bone mass measurement services. Commenters stated that DXA is an important preventive service used to identify beneficiaries at risk for osteoporosis and fracture and noted that the USPSTF recommends osteoporosis screening for certain populations. Commenters noted that DXA is already underutilized and cited analyses indicating that utilization of DXA among Medicare beneficiaries has declined over the longer term. Commenters stated that reductions in Medicare payment for office-based DXA have contributed to reductions in the number of physician offices furnishing the service and stated that the increase in hospital-based DXA utilization may reflect migration of services from physician offices rather than unnecessary increases in the overall volume of DXA testing. Commenters further stated that reduced access to screening could result in beneficiaries remaining undiagnosed and untreated until after experiencing a fracture, potentially resulting in greater downstream Medicare expenditures.
Commenters also cited prior CMS rulemaking concerning payment for DXA services. Commenters noted that in the CY 2017 OPPS rulemaking CMS proposed to assign CPT code 77080 to a lower-paying APC but did not finalize that proposal after commenters raised concerns regarding beneficiary access to bone density testing. Commenters stated that although the payment policy proposed for CY 2027 differs from the policy considered in that prior rulemaking, similar concerns regarding the effects of reduced payment on access to preventive bone density screening remain relevant.
Commenters raised similar concerns regarding other preventive imaging services. For example, commenters stated that AAA screening is a preventive service for which increased utilization may be clinically appropriate and cautioned against treating increases in the volume of such screening as unnecessary solely because the service is furnished in an off-campus PBD. Commenters generally stated that CMS should distinguish medically appropriate increases in recommended screening from increases attributable to site-of-service payment incentives.
Response: We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding the application of the volume control method to preventive services, including bone mass measurement, abdominal aortic aneurysm screening, and lung cancer screening services. We recognize the important role that preventive services play in identifying disease at an earlier stage and improving health outcomes for Medicare beneficiaries. However, we do not believe that the preventive nature of a service, by itself, warrants exclusion from the volume control method. The policy finalized in this rule does not change Medicare coverage of these preventive services, applicable eligibility or frequency requirements, or the clinical criteria for determining when these services are appropriate.
We also do not interpret increases in the utilization of preventive services in excepted off-campus PBDs to mean that clinically appropriate screening or preventive care is itself unnecessary. Rather, consistent with the volume control method finalized in this rule, our concern is with an unnecessary increase in the volume of covered OPD services when a clinically appropriate service that can safely be furnished in a lower-cost setting is instead furnished in the higher-paid OPD setting because of the payment incentive created by the difference in payment amounts.
The preventive and screening nature of these services also does not, in itself, indicate that they require the hospital outpatient setting. Preventive services are generally planned ambulatory services and are frequently ordered or furnished as part of routine physician and primary care. Encouraging beneficiaries to obtain appropriate preventive care does not require Medicare to maintain a higher payment when that care is furnished in an excepted off-campus PBD. We are concerned that substantial differences in Medicare payment across settings may create incentives for preventive services that can safely and appropriately be furnished in freestanding physician offices or other lower-cost ambulatory settings to migrate to the higher-paid OPD setting.
We considered commenters' concerns regarding historical trends in the availability and utilization of DXA services. We recognize that commenters cited evidence of declines in DXA utilization and in the number of freestanding physician offices furnishing DXA over longer historical periods. However, the information submitted by commenters does not demonstrate that maintaining the higher OPPS payment rate for DXA services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs is necessary to preserve beneficiary access to these services. DXA remains a frequently furnished outpatient service. For example, CPT code 77080 had more than 1.2 million single-frequency claims used in the CY 2027 OPPS rate-setting process, and the number of such claims has exceeded 1.1 million in each of the past five OPPS rate-setting years.
Moreover, our utilization analysis demonstrates a substantial shift in the site of service for CPT code 77080. Between CY 2016 and CY 2025, utilization of CPT code 77080 in excepted off-campus PBDs increased by more than 55 percent, while utilization in freestanding physician offices remained relatively stable. We acknowledge commenters' view that some of this change may reflect historical reductions in physician-office capacity and recognize that multiple factors may contribute to changes in site of service. However, the existence of other factors does not demonstrate that the OPPS/PFS payment differential has ( printed page 70605) no effect on where DXA services are furnished. As discussed previously, acquisition of a physician practice or imaging facility by a hospital uniquely permits services that otherwise would be paid under the PFS to receive the higher OPPS payment when furnished in an excepted off-campus PBD. We therefore do not believe these historical trends support maintaining a higher OPPS payment simply because DXA is a preventive service.
We also considered commenters' discussion of the CY 2017 OPPS rulemaking regarding the APC assignment for CPT code 77080. In the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, we proposed to assign CPT code 77080 to APC 5521, which would have reduced the OPPS payment for the service from $100.69 in CY 2016 to $63.33 in CY 2017. In response to public comments, we reconsidered the proposed APC assignment. In the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule (81 FR 79629), we assigned CPT code 77080 to APC 5522 based on our analysis of its geometric mean cost and its resource comparability to other services within the imaging APCs. Specifically, we noted that CPT code 77080 had a geometric mean cost of $91.08 and that its assignment to APC 5521 increased the probability of a violation of the 2 times rule when compared with other significant procedures assigned to that APC. We therefore assigned CPT code 77080 to APC 5522, with a final CY 2017 payment rate of $112.69.
That determination addressed a different payment question from the policy finalized in this rule. APC assignments establish the relative payment for services within the OPPS based on the applicable OPPS classification and ratesetting methodology, including the clinical characteristics and relative resource costs of services grouped within an APC. The determination of the appropriate APC assignment for a service is not based on whether the resulting OPPS payment approximates the payment that would otherwise be made for the service under the PFS. Here, we are not reconsidering the appropriate APC assignment for CPT code 77080. Rather, under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act, we are applying a method to control unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services by addressing the payment differential between excepted off-campus PBDs and lower-cost settings in which these services can safely be furnished.
Application of the volume control method also does not preclude us from reevaluating the APC assignment for CPT code 77080 in future rulemaking. We review APC groups and relative payment weights annually and may revise APC assignments based on changes in medical practice, technology, new cost data, and other relevant information and factors. Accordingly, if future OPPS claims data or other relevant information support a different APC assignment for CPT code 77080, we may consider such a change through future OPPS rulemaking.
For these reasons, we do not believe that preventive services, including DXA and other imaging without contrast services that qualify as Medicare preventive services, should be excluded from the volume control method finalized in this rule.
Comment: Several commenters expressed concern that applying the volume control method to imaging without contrast services could adversely affect beneficiary access to care. Commenters stated that payment reductions could cause hospitals to reduce imaging capacity, discontinue certain services, close off-campus imaging locations, or limit investments in imaging equipment and staffing. Commenters stated that these effects could be particularly significant in rural, low-income, medically underserved, and other communities where freestanding physician offices or freestanding imaging facilities may not have sufficient capacity or may not offer comparable services. Commenters also stated that reduced hospital outpatient imaging capacity could result in longer wait times or travel distances, delayed diagnosis, greater fragmentation of care, and increased reliance on emergency departments or other higher-cost settings.
Some commenters further stated that off-campus PBDs may improve access by locating imaging services closer to where beneficiaries live while maintaining integration with the hospital and other physicians involved in the beneficiary's care. Commenters noted that freestanding physician offices and independent imaging facilities may lack the capital, equipment, workforce, or operational capacity to absorb imaging services currently furnished in hospital outpatient departments. Commenters therefore recommended that CMS reconsider the proposal, adopt additional access protections, or closely monitor the effects of the policy on service availability, wait times, travel distances, and beneficiary access.
Response: We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding beneficiary access to imaging services. We agree that maintaining access to clinically appropriate imaging is important, particularly in communities where alternative sources of care may be limited. However, we do not believe that the information provided by commenters demonstrates that applying the PFS-equivalent payment rate to imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs will generally result in the loss of access to these services.
As discussed previously, imaging without contrast services are routinely furnished in physician offices, freestanding facilities, and non-excepted off-campus PBDs. Our experience with non-excepted off-campus PBDs is particularly relevant because these departments already receive the PFS-equivalent payment rate for applicable services. We also believe that non-excepted off-campus PBDs are relevant to commenters' concerns that some beneficiaries may benefit from receiving imaging in a hospital-affiliated setting with access to hospital clinical resources. The choice of setting is not limited to an excepted off-campus PBD receiving the full OPPS payment rate or a freestanding physician office. Non-excepted off-campus PBDs are also hospital departments and furnish imaging without contrast services while receiving the PFS-equivalent payment rate.
As discussed in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (91 FR 41911), there are approximately four times as many providers billing the “PN” modifier for non-excepted off-campus PBDs as providers billing the “PO” modifier for excepted off-campus PBDs. Nevertheless, excepted off-campus PBDs continue to account for the substantial majority of combined off-campus PBD volume for many of the highest-volume imaging without contrast services. In CY 2025, excepted off-campus PBDs accounted for approximately 81 percent of combined PBD volume for HCPCS code 77080, 79 percent for HCPCS code 71046, 79 percent for HCPCS code 93306, and 83 percent for HCPCS code 71250. We believe these patterns are relevant because they demonstrate that, despite a substantially broader base of non-excepted off-campus PBDs furnishing services under the PFS-equivalent payment methodology, utilization of these high-volume services remains disproportionately concentrated in the smaller group of excepted off-campus PBDs receiving the higher OPPS payment.
We recognize that section 603 of the BBA of 2015 established different payment treatment for excepted and non-excepted off-campus PBDs, and the policy finalized in this rule does not alter that statutory framework. Rather, ( printed page 70606) as discussed previously, we are exercising our separate authority under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act to develop a method to control unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services. For purposes of addressing commenters' access concerns, we believe the continued furnishing of imaging without contrast services in non-excepted off-campus PBDs is relevant evidence that these services can be furnished in a hospital-affiliated off-campus setting under the PFS-equivalent payment methodology. Thus, maintaining access to hospital affiliation and hospital clinical resources does not, by itself, demonstrate that the higher OPPS payment applicable to an excepted off-campus PBD is necessary for these services.
We also note that, consistent with our approach in prior rulemaking, we have taken specific access concerns into account in determining the scope of this policy. As discussed later in this section, we are finalizing an exemption for rural SCHs because of their historical treatment under the OPPS, documented additional resource costs, and importance in maintaining access to care in rural communities. In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53822), we similarly recognized that rural SCHs are often the only source of care in their communities and that rural beneficiaries may have fewer alternative sites of care.
We acknowledge that particular communities may differ in the availability of alternative imaging providers and that individual hospitals may make operational decisions in response to changes in Medicare payment. However, commenters did not demonstrate that freestanding physician offices, freestanding imaging facilities, and non-excepted off-campus PBDs generally lack the capacity to furnish imaging without contrast services or that maintaining the higher OPPS payment rate for all affected services is necessary to preserve beneficiary access. Moreover, our policy does not prevent a beneficiary from receiving imaging in an OPD when that setting is clinically appropriate and does not restrict a physician's ability to determine the appropriate setting of care based on the beneficiary's medical needs.
We will continue to monitor the effects of this change in Medicare payment policy, including changes in the volume and availability of imaging without contrast services and beneficiary access to care. If future data indicate that the policy is creating significant access concerns, we may consider whether additional refinements are appropriate in future rulemaking.
Comment: Several commenters recommended that, if CMS finalizes the volume control method for imaging without contrast services, CMS phase-in the payment reduction, delay implementation, or otherwise provide a transition period. Commenters stated that immediately applying the full PFS-equivalent payment rate could result in a significant reduction in payment for affected services and could give hospitals insufficient time to adjust staffing, equipment, contracts, referral arrangements, and other operational considerations. Some commenters recommended that CMS initially apply a less significant payment reduction and transition to the PFS-equivalent rate over multiple years.
Other commenters recommended that CMS establish hardship protections or other mechanisms to address providers that may experience significant financial or access impacts as a result of the policy. Commenters stated that transition or hardship protections could reduce the risk of service reductions or disruptions in beneficiary access while allowing CMS to evaluate the effects of the policy before fully implementing the payment reduction.
Response: We appreciate commenters' recommendations regarding a phase-in, delayed implementation, or other transition or hardship protections. We do not believe that a phase-in or delay is necessary for the volume control method finalized in this rule. The policy applies to a defined set of imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs, and these same services are routinely furnished in freestanding physician offices and other lower-cost ambulatory settings.
We also believe our experience with non-excepted off-campus PBDs supports implementation of the PFS-equivalent payment rate without a phase-in. Non-excepted off-campus PBDs already receive the PFS-equivalent payment rate for applicable services and continue to furnish imaging without contrast services at substantial volume. We believe this experience demonstrates that imaging without contrast services can continue to be furnished in an off-campus hospital setting under the PFS-equivalent payment methodology.
As discussed later in this section, we are finalizing an exemption for rural SCHs based on their historical treatment under the OPPS, documented additional resource costs, and importance in maintaining access to care in rural communities.
Moreover, a phase-in would continue, during the transition period, the payment differential that we have determined contributes to unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services. The purpose of the volume control method is to remove that payment incentive by applying the PFS-equivalent payment rate to the affected services. We therefore believe that implementing the PFS-equivalent payment rate beginning in CY 2027 is appropriate.
We will continue to monitor the effects of this change in Medicare payment policy, including the volume and availability of imaging without contrast services and beneficiary access to care, and may consider whether additional refinements are appropriate in future rulemaking.
Comment: Some commenters questioned whether the proposed reduction in payment would actually control unnecessary increases in volume. Commenters stated that reducing the payment amount for individual services could create an incentive for hospitals to increase the number of services furnished in off-campus PBDs to offset the reduction in revenue. Commenters stated that CMS therefore had not demonstrated that reducing payment for imaging without contrast services would result in a reduction in volume rather than simply lower Medicare payment for the same volume or potentially lead to additional utilization.
Commenters pointed to CMS's experience with the sustainable growth rate methodology and other prior discussions of volume control as evidence that reducing unit payment does not necessarily result in lower utilization. Commenters therefore stated that the proposed methodology is not reasonably designed to control unnecessary increases in volume as required under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act.
Response: We thank the commenters for their input. We disagree that the possibility that a provider could respond to a reduction in payment by increasing volume means that our volume control method is not reasonably designed to control unnecessary increases in volume. As we explained in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period in response to similar comments (90 FR 53811), our volume control method is specifically designed to address unnecessary increases in OPD volume that result from site-of-service payment differentials. By applying a PFS-equivalent payment rate, the method removes the payment differential that creates an incentive to furnish a service in the higher-paid OPD setting when the ( printed page 70607) same service can safely be furnished in a lower-cost setting.
We recognize that changes in payment may affect provider behavior in different ways. However, the relevant incentive addressed by this policy is the additional Medicare payment available when an imaging without contrast service is furnished in an excepted off-campus PBD rather than in a physician office or non-excepted off-campus PBD. Once payment for the service furnished in the excepted off-campus PBD is aligned with the PFS-equivalent payment applicable in the lower-paid setting, the financial incentive to furnish the service in the excepted off-campus PBD solely because of the higher OPPS payment is removed. We therefore continue to believe that applying the PFS-equivalent payment rate is an appropriate method to control the unnecessary increase in volume attributable to that payment differential.
We also do not believe that commenters' references to the sustainable growth rate (SGR) methodology lead to a different conclusion. The SGR established an aggregate spending target under the PFS and adjusted physician payment updates based on whether aggregate expenditures exceeded that target. Our volume control method does not establish an aggregate expenditure target or reduce payment in response to providers exceeding a predetermined volume benchmark. Rather, it prospectively addresses a specific payment differential that we have determined is a substantial cause of unnecessary increases in covered OPD services by eliminating that differential for the affected services.
We will continue to monitor utilization following implementation of this policy, as we have done for our clinic visit and drug administration volume control policies. We continue to believe that prospectively applying the PFS-equivalent payment rate to imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs is an appropriate method under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act to control unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services.
Comment: Several commenters requested additional information and implementation guidance regarding how the volume control method for imaging without contrast services would be operationalized. Commenters requested that CMS clearly identify the HCPCS codes subject to the policy and explain how changes in HCPCS coding or APC assignments would affect application of the volume control method in future years.
Commenters also requested clarification regarding the treatment of imaging services paid through the multiple imaging composite APCs and encounters involving multiple imaging services. Commenters requested CMS to clarify how the PFS-equivalent payment methodology would apply when imaging without contrast services are furnished together with other imaging services, including services that may not otherwise be subject to the volume control method, and how the policy would interact with existing OPPS packaging and composite payment policies.
Some commenters also requested sufficient implementation guidance and lead time for hospitals to update billing, claims-processing, financial, and other operational systems before the policy takes effect.
Response: We appreciate commenters' requests for additional implementation guidance. As finalized in this rule, the volume control method applies to imaging without contrast services assigned to APCs 5521 through 5524, as well as imaging without contrast services paid through the applicable multiple imaging composite APCs (APCs 8004, 8005, and 8007), when furnished by an off-campus PBD excepted from section 1833(t)(21) of the Act and billed with the “PO” modifier. We identify the applicable HCPCS codes and their APC assignments through the applicable OPPS Addenda, consistent with our usual process for publishing annual OPPS payment information.
We also clarify that this policy does not change the existing OPPS packaging or composite APC policies. Where an imaging without contrast service is otherwise paid through a composite APC under the OPPS, the existing requirements for determining whether the composite payment applies will continue to apply. When the applicable imaging without contrast composite APC is paid for a service furnished by an excepted off-campus PBD, the payment for that composite APC will be subject to the volume control method finalized in this rule. Similarly, existing OPPS packaging rules will continue to determine whether other items and services furnished during the encounter are separately payable or packaged.
The volume control method does not change hospitals' existing requirements for reporting the “PO” modifier for services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs. Rather, the modifier will continue to identify services furnished by these departments for purposes of applying the appropriate payment methodology. Services furnished in other settings or not otherwise within the scope of the volume control method will continue to be paid under the applicable Medicare payment methodology.
We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding implementation and the need for hospitals to update their billing and operational systems. The policy will be implemented through the annual OPPS payment system and associated claims-processing instructions, consistent with our established processes for implementing annual OPPS payment changes. We believe these existing mechanisms provide an appropriate framework for communicating the HCPCS and APC information necessary to implement the policy.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to use our authority under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Act to apply an amount equal to the site-specific PFS payment rate for non-excepted items and services furnished by a non-excepted off-campus PBD (the PFS payment rate) for HCPCS codes assigned to the imaging without contrast APCs or paid through the imaging without contrast composite APCs, when provided at an off-campus PBD excepted from section 1833(t)(21) of the Act (departments that bill the modifier “PO” on claim lines) without modification. In addition, we are finalizing our proposal to implement this policy in a non-budget neutral manner without modification. We will monitor the impacts of this policy to ensure that beneficiaries continue to have access to quality care.
9. Exemption for Rural Sole Community Hospitals
As stated previously, we proposed to expand our method to control unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services by paying a PFS-equivalent payment rate for imaging without contrast services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs. We believe that this policy is an appropriate method for controlling unnecessary volume of imaging without contrast services in excepted off-campus PBDs because beneficiaries can generally safely receive these same services in a lower-cost setting but instead may receive care in a higher-cost setting due to payment incentives. In these cases, we maintain that, similar to the clinic visit volume control policy established in the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (83 FR 59004 through 59015) and the drug administration volume control policy established in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53806 through 53821), to the extent ( printed page 70608) similar services can be safely provided in more than one setting, we do not believe it is appropriate for the Medicare program to pay more for these services in one setting than another. We continue to believe the difference in payment for these services is a significant factor in the shift in services from the freestanding physician's office setting to the hospital OPD.
In the CY 2023 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (87 FR 72047 through 72051) and the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53821 through 53824), we finalized exemptions to our clinic visit and drug administration volume control policies for PBDs of rural SCHs. Under these exemptions, we pay the full OPPS payment rate, rather than the PFS-equivalent rate, when the clinic visit or drug administration service is furnished in excepted PBDs of rural SCHs. In those rules, we explained that rural SCHs have historically received special payment treatment to account for their higher costs and the disproportionately harmful impact that payment reductions could have on them. Because we proposed a volume control payment policy for imaging without contrast services, we have additionally considered whether a similar policy for rural SCHs or other provider types would be appropriate.
a. Special Payment Treatment for Rural SCHs
Across the various Medicare payment systems, CMS has established several special payment provisions for rural providers to ensure access to high quality care for beneficiaries in rural areas. CMS administers several statutory hospital payment designations in which rural or isolated hospitals that meet specified eligibility criteria receive higher reimbursement for hospital services than they otherwise would receive under Medicare's standard payment methodologies. A rural hospital may qualify as a Critical Access Hospital (CAH),[164] Sole Community Hospital (SCH),[165] Rural Emergency Hospital (REH),[166] or Medicare Dependent Hospital [167] —each of which has different eligibility criteria and payment methodologies. With the exception of CAHs, rural hospitals may also qualify as Low Volume Hospitals [168] and Rural Referral Centers (RRCs),[169] which qualify these hospitals for additional payments or exemptions. Not all rural or isolated hospitals receive special payment treatment under the OPPS. For instance, CAHs are not paid under the OPPS and are reimbursed at 101 percent of reasonable costs for outpatient services.
Rural SCHs are a hospital type that has received special payment treatment under the OPPS to account for their higher costs and the disproportionately harmful impact that payment reductions could have on them. In the CY 2006 OPPS final rule with comment period (70 FR 68556 through 68561), we finalized a payment increase for rural SCHs of 7.1 percent for all services and procedures paid under the OPPS, excluding separately payable drugs and biologicals, items paid at charges reduced to costs, and devices paid under the pass-through payment policy. This policy was adopted under section 1833(t)(13)(B) of the Act, which required the Secretary, by January 1, 2006, to provide for an appropriate adjustment under subparagraph (t)(2)(E) to reflect the higher costs of hospitals in rural areas if the Secretary determined, pursuant to a study required by section 1833(t)(13)(A) of the Act, that the costs to rural hospitals by APC exceeded those costs for hospitals in urban areas. Our analysis revealed that rural SCHs had significantly higher costs per unit than urban hospitals. We have continued to adjust payments for rural SCHs by 7.1 percent each year since 2006. As discussed in section II.E. of this final rule with comment period, for CY 2027 we proposed to continue the current policy of utilizing a 7.1 percent payment adjustment for rural SCHs.
As noted previously, in the CY 2023 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (87 FR 72051), we finalized an exemption for clinic visits to our policy to pay the PFS-equivalent rate for the clinic visit service at excepted off-campus PBDs to control unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services. Commenters were generally supportive of this proposal and noted that rural SCHs are typically the chief, if not sole, source of community outpatient care for rural residents and stated that this exemption would be vital to ensuring continued access to the care they need. Some commenters stated that the exemption should be extended to other types of hospitals, including urban SCHs. In that rule, we explained that our analysis did not find that urban SCHs had the additional resource costs for covered OPD services that rural SCHs have and only finalized applying the clinic visit policy exemption to rural SCHs (87 FR 72049).
Similarly, in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53824), we finalized an exemption for rural SCHs to our policy to pay the PFS-equivalent rate for drug administration services at excepted off-campus PBDs to control unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services. Commenters were again generally supportive of the proposal and emphasized that rural SCHs have higher costs and are important for access in rural areas. Some commenters suggested extending the exemption to other types of hospitals such as urban SCHs, Medicare Dependent Hospitals (MDHs), urban and rural safety-net hospitals, REHs, FQHCs, and all rural hospitals. However, because our historical analysis did not demonstrate that these facilities had the additional resource costs that rural SCHs do, we did not finalize any exemptions beyond our exception for rural SCHs (90 FR 53823).
b. Exemption to Volume Control Payment Policy for Imaging Without Contrast Services Furnished in Off-Campus Provider-Based Departments of Rural SCHs
Earlier in this section, where we proposed the volume control method policy for imaging without contrast services, we stated that to the extent there are lower-cost sites of service available, beneficiaries and the physicians treating them should be able to choose the appropriate care setting and not be encouraged to receive or provide care in settings for which payment rates are higher solely for financial reasons. However, as we have previously noted, many rural providers, and rural SCHs in particular, are often the only source of care in their communities,[170] which means beneficiaries and providers are not choosing between a higher paying off-campus PBD of a hospital and a lower paying freestanding physicians' office setting. The closure of inpatient departments of hospitals and the shortage of primary care providers in rural areas likely further drives utilization to off-campus PBDs in areas where rural SCHs are located.
As with clinic visits and drug administration services, we do not believe that rural SCH site-of-service decisions for imaging without contrast services are being driven by differences in payment rates. As we have previously observed, rural areas often experience lower availability of health care professionals and hospitals than urban ( printed page 70609) areas.[171] Hospital closures in rural communities are associated with lower access to health care and worse health outcomes.[172] Access to outpatient services, particularly in rural areas, is vital to keeping beneficiaries from being admitted as an inpatient because beneficiaries in rural settings face unique challenges that impact their health. In the CY 2023 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we explained that we believe that exempting rural SCHs from the clinic visit policy would help to maintain access to care in rural areas by ensuring rural providers are paid for clinic visit services provided at off-campus PBDs at rates comparable to those paid at on-campus departments (87 FR 72049). We extended this exemption to drug administration in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period on the same basis (90 FR 53822), and we proposed to extend it to our proposed imaging without contrast policy for similar reasons. Specifically, we proposed to exempt rural SCHs from payment of the site-specific PFS-equivalent payment for imaging without contrast services, as described by APCs 5521 through 5524, 8004, 8005, and 8007, when furnished at an off-campus PBD exempted from section 1833(t)(21) of the Act (departments that bill the modifier “PO” on claim lines). Under the proposed policy, a rural SCH would continue to bill services in APCs 5521 through 5524, 8004, 8005, and 8007 with the “PO” modifier for CY 2027 and the payment rate for such services would continue to be the full OPPS payment without the PFS relativity adjuster.
This exemption would result in higher payments to excepted off-campus PBDs of rural SCHs compared to if rural SCHs were subject to the proposed volume control method. By exempting rural SCHs, the Medicare payments for these services would remain at the OPPS level. We note, however, that these figures do not represent increases in costs to Medicare or the beneficiaries above the current policy, as our proposed exemption would maintain current payment rates at excepted off-campus PBDs of rural SCHs of 107.1 percent of the OPPS payment rate for these services. These figures are solely for the purpose of comparing potential savings from this policy.
We invited comments on all aspects of the proposed exemption for rural SCHs from the method to control unnecessary volume of imaging without contrast services. Specifically, we requested comments on whether such an exemption was appropriate for rural SCHs; what the impact on SCHs would be, should we finalize the method without an exemption for rural SCHs; and whether we should consider any other hospital types for an exemption to any of the three policies to control unnecessary volume of outpatient services at off-campus PBDs. Additionally, we requested comments on whether the current exemptions for rural SCHs from the method to control unnecessary volume of clinic visit and drug administration services remained appropriate.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: The majority of commenters supported our proposal to exempt rural Sole Community Hospitals (rural SCHs) from payment of the site-specific Medicare PFS-equivalent payment for any HCPCS codes assigned to the imaging without contrast APCs or paid through the imaging without contrast composite APCs, when furnished at an off-campus PBD excepted from section 1833(t)(21) of the Act (departments that bill the modifier “PO” on claim lines). Several commenters opposed the volume control method generally but stated that should CMS finalize the policy, CMS should also finalize the proposed exemption for rural SCHs. Commenters stated that rural SCHs have higher costs, operate with limited financial and workforce resources, and are important for maintaining access to care in rural areas where alternative sources of imaging services may be limited. Commenters also stated that applying the volume control method to rural SCHs could result in reduced service availability or require beneficiaries to travel greater distances for care. One commenter opposed a broad exemption for all rural SCHs and recommended that CMS instead target the exemption to independent rural hospitals or hospitals that demonstrate greater financial vulnerability. The commenter stated that some rural SCHs are affiliated with large health systems and may be better positioned to absorb payment reductions than independent hospitals.
Response: We thank the commenters for their support of the proposed exemption for rural SCHs. As discussed in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (91 FR 41918), and consistent with our historical analysis that indicated rural SCHs have higher costs, we agree that their financial health is vital to ensure continued access to care in rural areas. We acknowledge the nuanced perspective that many commenters took in supporting the proposed exemption while disagreeing with the volume control methodology overall.
We appreciate the commenter's recommendation that any exemption be targeted to independent rural hospitals or hospitals demonstrating greater financial vulnerability. However, as we stated in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53823), we believe the rural SCH designation generally indicates that a hospital has additional costs and is vital for access in rural areas. We do not believe that the exemption should be limited to independent hospitals, as rural SCHs that are part of larger health systems may also face similarly heightened costs. We continue to believe that these considerations support exempting rural SCHs from the volume control method. We intend to continue to monitor costs at rural SCHs and to ensure that this exemption continues to be warranted for our volume control policies.
Comment: Several commenters supported the proposed rural SCH exemption but recommended that CMS extend the exemption to additional types of hospitals and providers. Commenters recommended exemptions for, among others, all rural hospitals, Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs), Rural Emergency Hospitals (REHs), Medicare Dependent Hospitals (MDHs), Rural Referral Centers, low-volume hospitals, safety-net hospitals, hospitals serving Health Professional Shortage Areas or Medically Underserved Areas, Qualifying Disadvantaged Hospitals, children's hospitals, and other geographically isolated or essential providers. Commenters generally stated that hospitals other than rural SCHs may face similar financial, workforce, and geographic challenges and may likewise be important for maintaining beneficiary access to imaging services in communities where alternative sites of care are limited.
Some commenters also recommended exempting hospitals that have reclassified as rural. Other commenters recommended exempting children's hospitals, noting their generally limited Medicare utilization and expressing concern regarding the potential effects of the policy on pediatric access.
Response: We appreciate commenters' recommendations regarding additional types of hospitals and providers for which they believe further exemptions would be warranted. We note that CAHs ( printed page 70610) and REHs are not subject to the volume control method finalized in this rule, and therefore an exemption for these hospital types is not necessary.
We also appreciate commenters' discussion of rural reclassifications and clarify that the exemption for rural SCHs includes SCHs that have reclassified as rural, consistent with our rural SCH exemptions from the clinic visit and drug administration volume control methods.
We appreciate commenters' recommendation to exempt children's hospitals based on their generally limited Medicare utilization and concerns regarding pediatric access. We recognize the unique role that children's hospitals play in furnishing specialized pediatric care and appreciate commenters' interest in ensuring that Medicare payment policies do not adversely affect access to these services. We also recognize that children's hospitals generally have limited Medicare utilization, which may limit the overall impact of this policy on these hospitals. Based on the information available to us, we do not believe that a separate exemption for children's hospitals is necessary at this time. As discussed previously, the policy does not prevent a physician from determining that the hospital outpatient setting is clinically appropriate for a particular beneficiary. We will continue to consider the effects of our volume control policies on different types of hospitals and beneficiary access to care and may consider whether additional exemptions are appropriate in future rulemaking.
With respect to the other hospital types suggested by commenters, as we discussed in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule and in prior rulemaking (90 FR 53823), our historical analysis has found that rural SCHs have higher costs, which we believe is appropriate to consider when developing a payment policy such as this. Rural SCHs have historically received special treatment under the OPPS due to these higher costs. As we stated in the CY 2023 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (87 FR 72047 through 72051), we believe exempting rural SCHs, which have demonstrated additional resource costs, is appropriate to ensure these hospitals can remain open to serve the beneficiaries who rely on them for their care.
We proposed a narrow exemption largely based upon the historical treatment and documented additional resource costs of rural SCHs under the OPPS. We continue to believe in the underlying principles of the volume control method, and that same rationale continues to justify application of the volume control method for imaging without contrast services to other hospitals subject to this policy. Where differences in payment lead to unnecessary increases in the volume of covered outpatient department services, we remain concerned that shifts in the site of care increase beneficiary cost-sharing liability because Medicare payment rates for the same or similar services are generally higher in hospital outpatient departments than in physician offices.
We share commenters' concerns about maintaining access to care in rural and medically vulnerable communities, including concerns regarding pediatric access. However, we do not believe that commenters provided sufficient reasoning or data to demonstrate that the other hospital types subject to this policy have the additional resource costs that our historical analysis has demonstrated for rural SCHs and therefore should also be exempted from this OPPS payment policy. We will continue to study access and costs to determine whether further exemptions to the volume control policy are appropriate in future rulemaking.
Comment: Some commenters recommended that CMS use criteria other than hospital type in determining whether a provider should qualify for an exemption. Commenters suggested considering factors such as geographic isolation, the availability of alternative imaging providers, beneficiary travel times, financial vulnerability, local workforce shortages, and the role of a hospital in maintaining access to essential services. Some commenters recommended that CMS monitor the effects of the policy on beneficiary access, including changes in imaging availability, wait times, travel distances, and service volumes, particularly in rural and underserved communities.
Response: We appreciate commenters' thoughtful suggestions regarding alternative criteria for determining whether an exemption may be appropriate. As discussed previously, for purposes of this policy we believe that the rural SCH designation provides an appropriate basis for the exemption because of the historical treatment and documented additional resource costs of rural SCHs under the OPPS. We are not adopting additional exemption criteria at this time. We will, however, consider commenters' suggestions as we continue to evaluate the effects of our volume control policies and whether additional exemptions may be appropriate in future rulemaking.
We also appreciate commenters' concerns regarding beneficiary access. Consistent with our approach to the clinic visit and drug administration volume control policies, we will continue to monitor the effects of this change in Medicare payment policy, including the volume of these types of OPD services and beneficiary access to care, including for beneficiaries with disabilities, and may revisit the policy in future rulemaking.
Comment: Some commenters recommended that CMS exempt certain imaging services or clinical circumstances from the volume control method based on the type of service furnished or the needs of the patient. Several commenters recommended exempting preventive and screening imaging services from the volume control method based on concerns regarding beneficiary access to recommended screening and early detection services. As discussed previously in this section, commenters specifically identified certain preventive and screening services included in the imaging without contrast APCs and recommended that CMS exclude these services from the policy.
Other commenters recommended exemptions for certain oncology-related imaging services. One commenter requested that CMS exempt diagnostic and procedural imaging directly associated with planned or same-day interventional oncology procedures, including pre- and post-procedural imaging used for treatment planning, procedural guidance, or assessment following a procedure. Other commenters recommended exemptions or other protections for imaging furnished to high-acuity oncology patients or imaging that is integrated with specialty oncology care, stating that these services may require hospital-level clinical infrastructure, specialized staff, immediate access to other hospital resources, or coordination with other services furnished as part of the patient's treatment.
Some commenters also raised concerns that applying the volume control method to imaging without contrast services, while imaging services furnished with contrast or an enhancing agent would not be subject to the policy, could create a payment incentive affecting the use of contrast or enhancing agents. Commenters specifically noted that ultrasound enhancing agents may be clinically appropriate for certain echocardiography services but stated that the decision to use an enhancing agent should be based on the clinical needs of the patient rather than differences in payment. Commenters expressed concern that increased use of ( printed page 70611) enhancing agents in response to payment differences could also increase costs associated with the agent, intravenous access, nursing, and other related resources.
Some commenters more generally recommended exempting imaging furnished as part of a medically complex diagnostic workup, imaging integrated with same-day procedures requiring hospital-level resources, or services that rely on hospital infrastructure or specialty resources. Commenters stated that these circumstances may involve medically-complex beneficiaries or additional resources that are not available in freestanding imaging facilities or physician offices.
Response: We appreciate the commenters' thoughtful suggestions regarding exemptions for particular imaging services or clinical circumstances. As we stated in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period in response to similar recommendations regarding drug administration services (90 FR 53824), we are concerned that exempting a small subset of services from the volume control methodology could inadvertently incentivize an increase in the provision of those services in the higher cost setting of care. Furthermore, we do not believe that commenters have provided a clear clinical justification for exempting certain imaging without contrast services while leaving other imaging without contrast services non-exempted. We believe it would be most transparent to propose any service-specific exceptions through notice-and-comment rulemaking.
We address commenters' recommendations regarding preventive and screening imaging services in detail previously in this section. As discussed there, we recognize the important role that preventive services play in identifying disease at an earlier stage and improving health outcomes for Medicare beneficiaries, but we do not believe that the preventive nature of a service, by itself, warrants exclusion from the volume control method.
We also appreciate commenters' concerns regarding the potential for differences in payment to affect the use of contrast or enhancing agents. We agree that the decision to use a contrast or enhancing agent should be based on the clinical needs of the beneficiary and not on differences in Medicare payment. The volume control method finalized in this rule does not change the clinical criteria for determining when the use of a contrast or enhancing agent is appropriate. As discussed previously, our policy is intended to remove a payment incentive that we believe contributes to unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services, not to influence clinical decisions regarding how an imaging service should be furnished. We will monitor utilization following implementation of this policy and may consider changes in utilization patterns, including the use of contrast or enhancing agents, as part of our evaluation of the effects of the volume control method.
With respect to commenters' recommendations regarding imaging furnished to high-acuity or medically complex patients, imaging furnished in connection with planned or same-day procedures, or imaging furnished as part of integrated oncology care or other complex episodes of care, we appreciate that OPDs serve unique patient populations and provide services to medically complex beneficiaries. However, we do not believe that these circumstances demonstrate the need for higher payment for all imaging without contrast services furnished to these beneficiaries or in connection with these episodes of care. The fact that an imaging service is furnished on the same day as, or in connection with, another hospital service also does not necessarily establish that the imaging service itself requires the hospital outpatient setting or should be excluded from the volume control method. Our policy does not prevent a physician from determining that an OPD is the appropriate setting for a particular beneficiary based on the beneficiary's clinical needs.
We also are not certain how we would reliably identify the particular patients, services, or clinical circumstances suggested by commenters for purposes of administering an exemption. We appreciate commenters' input and may consider these suggestions in future rulemaking.
Comment: Several commenters discussed the impact of the proposed method to control volume for imaging without contrast services on PPS-exempt cancer hospitals. Commenters noted that payments to PPS-exempt cancer hospitals are subject to the cancer hospital payment adjustment based on a payment-to-cost ratio and stated that reducing OPPS payment for imaging without contrast services could indirectly affect payments to these hospitals through the payment-to-cost ratio methodology.
Response: We appreciate commenters' discussion of the impact of this policy on PPS-exempt cancer hospitals. We note that any reduction in the initial OPPS payment to a PPS-exempt cancer hospital as a result of this policy would lower the hospital's payment-to-cost ratio and would result in a corresponding increase in the cancer hospital payment adjustment at cost report settlement. We therefore do not believe that the application of the volume control method to imaging without contrast services warrants a separate exemption for PPS-exempt cancer hospitals.
We also recognize that this policy may affect the target payment-to-cost ratio used in determining the cancer hospital payment adjustment because the target payment-to-cost ratio is based on the payment-to-cost ratios of hospitals paid under the OPPS other than PPS-exempt cancer hospitals. We believe the effect of this policy on the target payment-to-cost ratio, through its effect on non-cancer hospitals' payment-to-cost ratios, would be relatively small. Moreover, because we believe the reduced payment for imaging without contrast services furnished by non-cancer hospitals subject to this policy is appropriate, we likewise believe that any resulting effect on the target payment-to-cost ratio is appropriate.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to exempt rural Sole Community Hospitals (rural SCHs) from payment of the site-specific Medicare PFS-equivalent payment for any HCPCS codes assigned to the imaging without contrast APCs or paid through the imaging without contrast composite APCs, when furnished at an off-campus PBD excepted from section 1833(t)(21) of the Act (departments that bill the modifier “PO” on claim lines). We believe that exempting rural SCHs from the volume control policy for imaging without contrast services will help to maintain access to care in rural areas by ensuring rural providers are paid for imaging without contrast services provided at off-campus PBDs at the same rate paid when the service is furnished in on-campus departments. Finalizing this policy also aligns with the special payment treatment rural SCHs receive under the OPPS. We will continue to monitor the effects of this change in Medicare payment policy.
B. OPPS Payments for SaMS Diagnostic Services
1. Payment for Software as a Medical Service (SaMS)
In recent years, there have been rapid developments in the use of software-based technologies with novel functionalities to support clinical decision-making in the outpatient and physician office settings. New clinical software, which includes clinical ( printed page 70612) decision support software, clinical risk modeling, and computer aided detection (CAD), is becoming increasingly available to providers. These technologies often perform data analysis of diagnostic images from patients, relying on complex algorithms or statistical predictive modeling to aid in the diagnosis or treatment planning of a patient's condition. In previous rulemaking, we have referred to these algorithm-driven services that assist practitioners in making clinical assessments or diagnoses as Software as a Service (SaaS). Unlike prescription digital therapeutics (PDTs), for example PDTs that provide cognitive behavioral therapy to treat substance disorders or chronic insomnia, SaaS technologies as we refer to them do not currently treat illnesses or patient injuries. SaaS is also separate from remote patient monitoring (RPM) and remote therapeutic monitoring (RTM), which are digital healthcare tools for tracking patient data outside traditional office settings (90 FR 49394). For CY 2027, we proposed-a change in terminology. We noted that we now understand that in other industries, the existing SaaS terminology is used for general cloud-based computing service models outside of a health care context, which may cause confusion as we are using it to describe specific services that provide a medical function for purposes of OPPS/ASC Medicare payment policy. To dispel any ambiguity and clarify that distinction, we proposed to change our terminology from SaaS to Software as a Medical Service (SaMS) to refer to software-based technologies that support clinical decision making through algorithmic analysis, including those that provide clinical or diagnostic functionality. We welcomed public comments on the proposed change in terminology.
CMS has been evaluating how to develop a comprehensive and consistent approach to SaMS payment for several years with the novel and evolving nature of these technologies. We have sought public input through two comment solicitations (87 FR 72035 through 87 FR 72036, 89 FR 94129 through 89 FR 94131) and expressed our objective to seek a payment strategy that aligns with our agency's mission to increase quality, improve health, reduce costs, and strengthen the healthcare system. However, questions remain regarding how best to structure payment for these services. One challenge is that current Medicare Part B payment systems for SaMS, including in the OPPS, are primarily designed to pay for services that rely on material resources, rather than technologies whose value is driven by proprietary algorithms and scalable, non-material costs. This creates difficulties in establishing appropriate valuation methodologies, as the current cost-based system often offers only limited transparency into underlying costs and may not effectively constrain pricing. Another challenge is determining how to account for the various ways in which these technologies are acquired and billed by hospital OPDs, particularly in cases with subscription- or license-based arrangements, as well as per-use or “per-click” fees, which raises concerns regarding program integrity.
As coding for SaMS continues to rapidly increase and technologies evolve, establishing a consistent and timely payment methodology for these services is a priority. New SaMS technologies are continuing to be introduced to the market, each often accompanied by unique CPT codes reflecting their proprietary algorithms or specific characteristics. Interested parties are frequently seeking Medicare payment and coding for SaMS technologies through the new technology APC process or requesting clinical APC assignments. As a result, CMS is continuously assessing and evaluating payment for SaMS through different pathways. As we consider this policy, we want to ensure that we are moving toward a more standardized approach that reduces payment rate variation across similar technologies.
Given the growing need for a comprehensive and tailored payment methodology, as we work to gather additional data to better understand and more fully address the inherent payment challenges in this area, we proposed an interim payment policy for SaMS for CY 2027 while we examine a range of approaches to payment for these kinds of technologies. Specifically, we proposed to assign SaMS technologies to new technology APCs for CY 2027. We propose d to designate 36 HCPCS codes as SaMS services and reassign the proposed designated SaMS services that are currently paid separately (assigned to status indicator “S”) under clinical APCs, to new technology APCs that closely align with their current CY 2026 payment rates. We proposed to assign the separately paid SaMS technologies to new technology APCs because we believed that the existing clinical APC structure did not adequately accommodate SaMS. We believed that the new technology APCs were more appropriate to accommodate SaMS on a temporary basis, as there have historically been placements under the OPPS that allow us to provide consistent payment for new procedures that are not yet reflected in our claims data or for which we lack sufficient clinical information and cost data until we can identify an appropriate clinical APC. In certain circumstances, we have also assigned some services to new technology APCs through rulemaking, even when they have not met the specific regulatory criteria (66 FR 59897 through 59903) or have not applied for new technology APC assignment through the subregulatory process. For example, we have assigned certain services to new technology APCs in special cases where an appropriate clinical APC to which to assign the service does not exist. In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we maintained the new technology APC assignment for HCPCS codes G2082 and G2083 because we did not believe there was an appropriate clinical APC to which to assign the service (90 FR 53551). This proposed approach of assigning SaMS services to the same APC series would allow CMS to take the first step towards standardization and applying a consistent payment methodology across these services as we consider more comprehensive long-term approaches, including those that may better align payment with clinical outcomes.
We also believed it was important to distinguish SaMS technologies from other services that are assigned to new technology APCs because not all new services assigned to new technology APCs are SaMS technologies. Therefore, we proposed to create a new status indicator under OPPS specifically for SaMS technologies. For CY 2027, we proposed to create status indicator “O1” (Software as a Medical Service, Paid under OPPS; separate APC payment) and assign all services that we proposed to designate as SaMS to status indicator “O1.” Functionally, we proposed for status indicator “O1” to have the same payment specifications as status indicator “S,” to allow for separate payment. We requested public comment on this proposal. We also requested public comment regarding whether a new status indicator with the same specification as status indicator “T” (Procedure or service subject to multiple procedure discounting) would provide more appropriate payment for these services while addressing any potential program integrity concerns.
For CY 2027, we proposed to designate the HCPCS codes listed in Table 83 as SaMS technologies. Of these, we proposed to assign 21 HCPCS codes to new technology APCs from clinical APCs, maintaining approximate ( printed page 70613) payment rate continuity with CY 2026 payment, and status indicator “O1”. Table 84 provides the list of HCPCS codes and proposed new technology APC and status indicator assignments for CY 2027. For SaMS that are already assigned to new technology APCs for CY 2026, we proposed to continue to assign these services to new technology APCs for CY 2027 while proposing to update the status indicator assignment to “O1” to designate these technologies as SaMS. We refer readers to section III.C. of the proposed rule-(91 FR 41803 through 91 FR 41807) for a discussion on our proposals for SaMS technologies that are currently assigned to new technology APCs for CY 2026.
We note that there are a small number of technologies we consider to be SaMS that are currently paid under the OPPS and assigned to an OPPS status indicator of “Q1” (STV-Packaged Codes; Paid under OPPS), indicating that the service is conditionally packaged. Services assigned to an OPPS status indicator of “Q1” will receive packaged payment when furnished with a significant procedure but will be separately paid when the service appears on the claim without a significant procedure. Because services assigned to new technology APCs are exempt from C-APC packaging policies, we did not believe it would be appropriate to propose to assign SaMS HCPCS codes that are currently conditionally packaged for CY 2026 to new technology APCs with status indicator “S” (Procedure or Service, Not Discounted When Multiple) to indicate separate payment. As an alternative, we considered unconditionally packaging SaMS services that are currently assigned to status indicator “Q1” by proposing to assign the services a status indicator of “N” (Items and Services Packaged into APC Rates). However, we stated that we believe proposing to unconditionally package payment for CY 2027 for SaMS technologies that are currently conditionally packaged under the OPPS may have resulted in interruptions to patient access. Given that we intended for this policy to be a first step towards more comprehensive payment policy changes and sought to minimize disruption, we believed it was more appropriate to propose to maintain the clinical APC and status indicator assignments for these codes. Therefore, for CY 2027, we proposed to maintain the clinical APC and status indicator assignments for SaMS that are currently conditionally packaged under the OPPS.
Similarly, there are other HCPCS codes that describe SaMS assigned to status indicator “E1” (Items, codes, and services not covered by any Medicare outpatient benefit category; statutorily excluded; not reasonable and necessary), status indicator “N” (Items or services packaged into APC rates), or status indicator “M” (Items and services not billable to the FI or MAC). Since these are not separately paid services under the OPPS for CY 2026, for CY 2027, we proposed to maintain the OPPS status indicators to which they are currently assigned.
We provided a table with the various SaMS HCPCS codes that were impacted by our proposals. Table 83 provides the proposed CY 2027 APC and status indicator assignments for codes we proposed to designate as SaMS services and that are currently assigned to clinical APCs or are not separately paid under the OPPS for CY 2026. We referred readers to section III.C. of the proposed rule for a discussion on the proposed CY 2027 payment rates for SaMS codes that are currently assigned to new technology APCs for CY 2026. In addition, we referred readers to Addendum B of the proposed rule for proposed CY 2027 OPPS payment rates and status indicators for HCPCS codes that we proposed to designate as SaMS. We requested comment on our proposals, including the list of HCPCS codes we proposed to designate as SaMS and that we proposed to reassign to new technology APCs for CY 2027, including whether there were any additional HCPCS codes we should consider.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Several commenters supported the proposed terminology change from SaaS to SaMS. One commenter explained that the proposed terminology would clarify the distinction between clinical algorithms and generic cloud tooling. A commenter requested that we clarify whether the transition to SaMS is intended solely as a naming convention or whether it reflects broader distinctions regarding the scope, classification, valuation or payment treatment of these technologies.
Response: We thank the commenters for their support. The terminology change from SaaS to SaMS seeks to clarify, as one commenter explained, the distinction between clinical algorithms used to furnish these services and generic cloud tooling.
Based on the comments received, for CY 2027, we are finalizing our proposal to change the terminology for these algorithm-based software services that are paid under Medicare from “SaaS” to “SaMS.”
Comment: Many commenters requested clarification regarding the types of services that would be considered SaMS for purposes of this policy. For example, commenters asked whether remote care delivery or non-device clinical decision support (CDS) would be considered SaMS for purposes of separate payment. Similarly, we received comments regarding how CMS will distinguish separately paid software that supports clinical decision making from software that provides broader operational, administrative, or business functions. One commenter specifically requested that we expand our scope of services that we designate as SaMS to include those that perform analyses on structured clinical data conforming to recognized interoperability standards such that super intelligence-enabled comprehensive clinical trial eligibility analysis would be payable under the OPPS.[173]
Response: We thank the commenters for their interest in better understanding the scope of our policy. Regarding whether we would consider remote care delivery services as SaMS for purposes of this policy, we refer the commenter to our proposal where we specified that SaMS is separate from RPM and RTM, which are digital health tools for remotely tracking patient data. Furthermore, software that includes broader operational, administrative, or business functions, including clinical trial eligibility analysis, would not be considered SaMS under current policy. These kinds of software services can provide operational efficiencies but would not have a Medicare benefit category to allow for separate payment under OPPS.
We also appreciate commenters' input regarding whether CMS would consider non-device CDS as SaMS. The 36 services that we proposed to designate as SaMS, and that we previously referred to as SaaS, are regulated by the FDA as devices and therefore would not be considered non-device CDS. We note that although SaMS described in this section of this final rule with comment period (section X.B.1.), are required to have FDA marketing authorization to receive Medicare payment, “SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests,” which are described in the following section of this final rule with comment period (section X.B.2.), currently do not require FDA marketing authorization in order to receive payment. As the CY ( printed page 70614) 2027 SaMS policy is an interim policy that seeks to maintain payment for CY 2027, we are declining to expand the scope of our policy to include non-device CDS at this time, although we note that there are existing non-device CDS services assigned to clinical APCs for CY 2026. We will consider expanding and further clarifying the scope of the SaMS policy for future rulemaking.
Comment: We received several comments requesting information on CMS's process for identifying the 36 proposed HCPCS codes to be designated as SaMS. Commenters requested that we adopt, in the future, specific criteria that CMS will use to determine whether a service is payable as a SaMS under OPPS. For example, a commenter requested that we include the definitions and criteria from the recently updated Appendix S, effective June 2026, available via the AMA's website to identify SaMS codes. Other commenters requested that we identify SaMS codes based on functionality rather than input modality. We also received comments requesting that CMS align its clinical or diagnostic functionality criteria with the definitions that are used by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for their review of indications for use and device descriptions in their guidance documents and clearance processes.
Response: We appreciate the comments. To identify the 36 proposed SaMS CPT codes, we examined all CPT codes currently paid under the OPPS to determine which codes aligned with the SaMS terminology provided in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, specifically “software-based technologies that support clinical decision making through algorithmic analysis, including those that provide clinical or diagnostic functionality” as a framework. We excluded RTM, RPM, non-device CDS, and services that we did not believe would fall under a Medicare benefit category, including those that are administrative in function. For instance, software that serves as the infrastructure that the provider uses to furnish another separately paid service.
Given the interim nature of the proposed policy, we will take the criteria concerns raised by the commenters, including establishing specific criteria for SaMS service for purposes of payment under the OPPS, into consideration for future rulemaking. We welcome public engagement from interested parties on these issues, including whether there are services that should be designated as SaMS in the future.

Some of the requests included services that we did not identify as SaMS for the proposed rule and interested parties requested that they be added to the SaMS list. Several commenters requested that we refrain from reassigning these services from clinical APCs until the new payment framework and policy has been defined to avoid unnecessary disruption for hospital outpatient departments. Response: We appreciate the input and feedback from commenters. Once again, we emphasize that this is an interim first step to a broader payment policy for SaMS. We intended to preserve current payment rates for these services as much as possible for CY 2027 while assigning these services to new technology APCs. Many commenters claimed resources costs for these services are higher than the proposed payment rates and that they are concerned about beneficiary access to these clinical meaningful services. We are committed to developing a comprehensive and consistent approach for these technologies and our objective remains to have this new payment strategy align with CMS's mission to increase quality, improve health, reduce costs, and strengthen the healthcare system. We proposed to maintain current payment rates as much as possible for these services that we designated as SaMS as we moved them to new technology APCs and we continue to believe that that is the right approach. We thank the commenters again for their input and we will consider this feedback as part of our deliberations regarding our long-term payment methodology for SaMS.
Comment: Commenters were very supportive of the proposed new “O1” status indicator for SaMS. Commenters opposed mirroring the payment specifications of the new “O1” status indicator using “T,” which would apply multiple procedure discounting to SaMS. Several commenters explained that the rationale behind multiple-procedure discounting does not apply to SaMS because, unlike other non-software based services which share physical resources, and therefore, subsequent procedures are less expensive, SaMS do not rely on shared resources. Commenters noted that algorithmic services do not rely on these shared resources: when two distinct algorithms are run on a single claim, each represents an independent service with its own development, validation, and computational costs, not a marginal add-on to a shared setup. Commenters further explained that separate payment is appropriate because SaMS tests are distinct diagnostic services that are separately ordered, performed after specimen collection or after or concurrently with an imaging scan, and reported to inform subsequent treatment planning. Commenters also believed it would not be appropriate to address program integrity concerns through the status indicator specifications and thought they would be better addressed through the claims-level tracking that the “O1” status indicator itself enables, together with medical-necessity review.
Response: We agree with commenters, at this time, that these services are currently furnished as separate, independent services and that payment should reflect that for our interim maintenance policy. Therefore, we are creating the proposed new status indicator “O1” and use the same payment specifications as status indicator “S” to allow for separate payment without multiple procedure discounting.

Therefore, SaMS designation and assignment to status indicator “O1” and a new technology APC does not imply coverage.

As such, we are finalizing the status indicators of the HCPCS codes we proposed to assign to Q1 or N as proposed. We refer readers to Table 84 for the clinical APC assignments and status indicators for the relevant HCPCS codes.
