G. Proposed Calculation of the ASC Payment Rates and the ASC Conversion Factor
In the August 2, 2007 ASC final rule (72 FR 42493), we established our policy to base ASC relative payment weights and payment rates under the revised ASC payment system on APC groups and the OPPS relative payment weights. Consistent with that policy, and the requirement at section 1833(i)(2)(D)(ii) of the Act that the revised payment system be implemented so that it would be budget neutral, the initial ASC conversion factor (CY 2008) was calculated so that estimated total Medicare payments under the revised ASC payment system in the first year would be budget neutral to estimated total Medicare payments under the prior (CY 2007) ASC payment system (the ASC conversion factor is multiplied by the relative payment weights calculated for many ASC services in order to establish payment rates). That is, application of the ASC conversion factor was designed to result in aggregate Medicare expenditures under the revised ASC payment system in CY 2008 being equal to aggregate Medicare expenditures that would have occurred in CY 2008 in the absence of the revised system, taking into consideration the cap on ASC payments in CY 2007, as required under section 1833(i)(2)(E) of the Act (72 FR 42522). We adopted a policy to make the system budget neutral in subsequent calendar years (72 FR 42532 through 42533; § 416.171(e)).
In the CY 2008 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (72 FR 66857 through 66858), we set out a step-by-step illustration of the final budget neutrality adjustment calculation based on the methodology finalized in the August 2, 2007 ASC final rule (72 FR 42521 through 42531) and as applied to updated data available for the CY 2008 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period. The application of that methodology to the data available for the CY 2008 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period resulted in a budget neutrality adjustment of 0.65.
For CY 2008, we adopted the OPPS relative payment weights as the ASC relative payment weights for most services and, consistent with the final policy, we calculated the CY 2008 ASC payment rates by multiplying the ASC relative payment weights by the final CY 2008 ASC conversion factor of $41.401. For covered office-based surgical procedures, covered ancillary radiology services (excluding covered ancillary radiology services involving certain nuclear medicine procedures or involving the use of contrast agents, as discussed in section XIII.D.2. of the CY 2023 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (87 FR 44715 through 44716)), and certain diagnostic tests within the medicine range that are covered ancillary services, the established policy is to set the payment rate at the lower of the PFS unadjusted nonfacility PE RVU-based amount or the amount calculated using the ASC standard ratesetting methodology. Further, as discussed in the CY 2008 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (72 FR 66841 through 66843), we also adopted alternative ratesetting methodologies for specific types of services (for example, device-intensive procedures).
As discussed in the August 2, 2007 ASC final rule (72 FR 42517 through 42518) and as codified at § 416.172(c) of the regulations, the revised ASC payment system accounts for geographic wage variation when calculating individual ASC payments by applying the pre-floor and pre-reclassified IPPS hospital wage indexes to the labor-related share, which is 50 percent of the ASC payment amount based on a GAO report of ASC costs using 2004 survey data. Beginning in CY 2008, CMS accounted for geographic wage variation in labor costs when calculating individual ASC payments by applying the pre-floor and pre-reclassified hospital wage index values that CMS calculates for payment under the IPPS, using updated Core Based Statistical Areas (CBSAs) issued by OMB in June 2003.
The reclassification provision in section 1886(d)(10) of the Act is specific to acute care hospitals. We believe that using the most recently available pre-floor and pre-reclassified IPPS hospital wage indexes result in the most appropriate adjustment to the labor portion of ASC costs. We continue to believe that the pre-floor, pre-reclassified hospital wage indexes, which are updated yearly and are used by several other Medicare payment systems, appropriately account for geographic variation in labor costs for ( printed page 70675) ASCs (89 FR 23424). -Therefore, the wage index for an ASC is the pre-floor and pre-reclassified hospital wage index for the fiscal year under the IPPS of the CBSA that maps to the CBSA where the ASC is located.
On July 21, 2023, OMB issued OMB Bulletin No. 23-01, which provided the delineations of all Metropolitan Statistical Areas, Metropolitan Divisions, Micropolitan Statistical Areas, Combined Statistical Areas, and New England City and Town Areas in the U.S. and Puerto Rico based on the standards published on July 16, 2021, in the Federal Register (86 FR 37770) and 2020 Census Bureau data. (A copy of this bulletin may be obtained at https://www.whitehouse.gov/​wp-content/​uploads/​2023/​07/​OMB-Bulletin-23-01.pdf.) As discussed in the FY 2025 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule with comment period (89 FR 69253 through 69266), we finalized our proposal to use the new CBSAs delineations issued by OMB in OMB Bulletin No. 23-01 for the IPPS hospital wage index beginning in CY 2025. Therefore, because the ASC wage indexes for the calendar year are the pre-floor and pre-reclassified IPPS hospital wage indexes for the fiscal year, in the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (89 FR 94362 through 94363) we finalized our proposal to include the new OMB delineations into CY 2025 ASC wage indexes. We believe that using the revised delineations based on OMB Bulletin No. 23-01 will increase the integrity of the ASC wage index system by creating a more accurate representation of current geographic variations in wage levels. In addition to adopting the revised delineations based on OMB Bulletin No. 23-01, we also finalized our proposal to limit year-to-year ASC wage index value changes to no more than a 5-percent decrease, similar to the policy of other Medicare payment systems under Parts A and B. This 5-percent cap, implemented in a budget neutral manner through the wage index scalar, mitigates any large negative impacts of adopting the new delineations and prevents large year-to-year declines in wage index values as a means to reduce volatility in Medicare payments.
The proposed CY 2027 ASC wage indexes reflect the OMB labor market area delineations (including the revisions to the OMB labor market delineations discussed previously, as set forth in OMB Bulletin No. 23-01). We note that, in certain instances, there might be urban or rural areas for which there is no IPPS hospital that has wage index data that could be used to set the wage index for that area. When all of the areas contiguous to the CBSA of interest are rural and there is no IPPS hospital that has wage index data that could be used to set the wage index for that area, our policy has been to determine the ASC wage index by calculating the average of all wage indexes for urban areas in the State (75 FR 72058 through 72059). For CY 2026, we applied this methodology to ASCs located in CBSA 35 (Rural North Dakota) (90 FR 53911). For CY 2027, we proposed to continue to apply a proxy wage index based on this methodology to ASCs located in CBSA 35 (Rural North Dakota). In other situations, where there are no IPPS hospitals located in a relevant labor market area, we apply our current policy of calculating an urban or rural area's wage index by calculating the average of the wage indexes for CBSAs (or metropolitan divisions where applicable) that are contiguous to the area with no wage index. For CY 2027, we proposed that we continue to apply a proxy wage index based on this methodology to ASCs located in CBSA 25980 (Hinesville, GA). Further, the proposed CY 2027 ASC wage index includes our policy finalized in the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period that limits wage index changes to decrease by no more than 5 percent from the final CY 2026 ASC wage index value. As we discussed in the April 2025 Update to the Ambulatory Surgical Center Payment System (Change Request 14017), to limit wage index changes by no more than 5 percent from the final CY 2026 ASC wage index, some counties may require a transition CBSA before being fully reflected in the OMB labor market delineations as set forth in OMB Bulletin No. 23-01.
We received one public comment on our proposal. The following is a summary of the comment we received and our response.
Comment: A commenter supported policies to mitigate the effects of inadequate wage indices on rural ASCs and requested greater alignment between the ASC and OPPS wage-index methodologies. The commenter stated that, unlike hospitals, ASCs cannot obtain geographic reclassification to another labor market area and do not receive the frontier-state wage-index floor of 1.0. As an example, the commenter noted that the projected CY 2027 rural wage index applicable to ASCs in South Dakota is 0.7979, while hospitals in the State receive a wage index of at least 1.0 under the frontier-state floor. The commenter requested that CMS extend hospital geographic-reclassification and frontier-state wage-index-floor policies to ASCs.
Response: We appreciate the concerns the commenter has raised. The reclassification provision in section 1883(d)(10) of the Act is specific to acute care hospitals. The reclassification provision does not apply to an area but reflects the circumstances of the reclassified hospital and its own reported wages. Therefore, complete alignment between ASC and OPPS wage index methodologies is not currently possible. While we believe that using the most recently available pre-floor and pre-reclassified IPPS hospital wage indexes results in the most appropriate adjustment to the labor portion of ASC costs, we will continue to monitor wage index differences between the OPPS and ASC payment systems and may take the commenter's recommendation into consideration in future rulemaking.
After consideration of public comments we received, we are finalizing our proposal to use the most recently available pre-floor and pre-reclassified IPPS hospital wage indexes to the labor-related share to create the final CY 2027 ASC wage indexes and to limit wage index decreases by no more than 5 percent from the final CY 2026 ASC wage index for a particular CBSA. The final CY 2027 ASC wage indexes reflect the OMB labor market area delineations (including the revisions to the OMB labor market delineations discussed previously, as set forth in OMB Bulletin No. 23-01) unless the county is otherwise in a transition CBSA. Additionally, based on the absence of IPPS hospitals, we are also finalizing our proposal to apply a proxy wage index based to ASCs located in CBSA 25980 (Hinesville, GA) and in CBSA 35 (Rural North Dakota).
2. Calculation of the ASC Payment Rates
a. Updating the ASC Relative Payment Weights for CY 2027 and Future Years
We update the ASC relative payment weights each year using the national OPPS relative payment weights (and PFS nonfacility PE RVU-based amounts, as applicable) for that same calendar year and uniformly scale the ASC relative payment weights for each update year to make them budget neutral (72 FR 42533). The OPPS relative payment weights are scaled to maintain budget neutrality for the OPPS. We then scale the OPPS relative payment weights again to establish the ASC relative payment weights. To accomplish this, we hold estimated total ASC payment levels constant between calendar years for purposes of maintaining budget neutrality in the ASC payment system. That is, we apply the weight scalar to ensure that ( printed page 70676) projected expenditures from the updated ASC payment weights in the ASC payment system are equal to what would be the current expenditures based on the scaled ASC payment weights. In this way, we ensure budget neutrality and that the only changes to total payments to ASCs result from increases or decreases in the ASC payment update factor.
As discussed in section II.A.1.a. of this final rule with comment period, we are using the CY 2025 claims data to be consistent with the OPPS claims data for this final rule with comment period. Consistent with our established policy, we proposed to scale the CY 2027 relative payment weights for ASCs according to the following method. Holding ASC utilization, the ASC conversion factor, and the mix of services constant from CY 2025, we proposed to compare the estimated total payment using the CY 2026 ASC relative payment weights with the estimated total payment using the CY 2027 ASC relative payment weights to take into account the changes in the OPPS relative payment weights between CY 2026 and CY 2027.
In consideration of our policy to provide a higher ASC payment rate with ASC complexity adjustment codes for certain primary procedures when performed with add-on packaged services, we included estimated total spending and estimated utilization for these codes in our budget neutrality calculation for CYs 2023 and 2024. For this final rule with comment period, our proposed ASC complexity adjustment codes for CY 2027 did not impact the ASC weight scalar.
Additionally, as discussed in section XIII.E. of the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (89 FR 94342 through 94361), section 4135(a) and (b) of the CAA, 2023, titled “Access to Non-Opioid Treatments for Pain Relief”, amended sections 1833(t)(16) and 1833(i) of the Act, respectively, to provide for temporary separate payments for non-opioid treatments for pain relief. As discussed in further detail in section XIII.E. of the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, for qualifying non-opioid products, we finalized applying an 18 percent payment limitation on the volume-weighted payment average of the top 5 services associated with the use of the qualifying non-opioid product. In CY 2024, four of these qualifying nonopioid products were separately payable without the 18 percent payment limitation—HCPCS Codes C9089 (Bupivacaine implant, 1 mg), J0666 (Inj, bupivacaine liposome), J1096 (Dexametha opth insert 0.1 mg), and J1097 (Phenylep ketorolac opth soln). Therefore, to maintain budget neutrality, we estimated the total anticipated reduction in ASC spending for these qualifying non-opioid products for CY 2025 as a result of the 18 percent payment limitation required by section 4135 of the CAA, 2023. Based on the updated 18 percent payment limitations and CY 2025 utilization, we estimate that the proposed CY 2027 payment limitations will not impact the ASC weight scalar.
We proposed to use the ratio of estimated CY 2026 to estimated CY 2027 total payments (the weight scalar) to scale the proposed ASC relative payment weights for CY 2027. The proposed CY 2027 ASC weight scalar was 0.809. Consistent with historical practice, we proposed to scale, using this method (with an ASC weight scalar rounded to the nearest thousandth), the ASC relative payment weights of covered surgical procedures, covered ancillary radiology services, and certain diagnostic tests within the medicine range of CPT codes, which are covered ancillary services for which the ASC payment rates are based on OPPS relative payment weights.
We proposed that we would not scale ASC payment for separately payable covered ancillary services that have a predetermined national payment amount (that is, their national ASC payment amounts are not based on OPPS relative payment weights), such as drugs and biologicals that are separately paid or services that are contractor-priced or paid at reasonable cost in ASCs. Any service with a predetermined national payment amount, would be included in the ASC budget neutrality comparison, but scaling of the ASC relative payment weights would not apply to those services or the portion of those services. The ASC payment weights for those services without predetermined national payment amounts would be scaled to eliminate any difference in the total payment between the current year and the update year.
Historically, the device portions of device-intensive procedures were not scaled so that payment for device portions would remain constant between the OPPS and ASC payment systems. However, due to increased utilization of orthopedic procedures in the ASC setting, ASC expenditures on device portions of device-intensive procedures represent a substantially larger share of total ASC expenditures than in prior years. We estimate that spending attributable to device portions increased from approximately 5.4 percent of total ASC expenditures in CY 2016 to roughly 32.4 percent of total ASC expenditures in 2026. As device expenditures account for an increasingly significant share of total ASC spending, large year-to-year increases in the estimated device portions of surgical procedures require correspondingly larger reductions to the non-device portions of surgical procedures and certain ancillary services to maintain budget neutrality.
The change in the proposed ASC weight scalar for CY 2027 illustrates this effect. Specifically, the ASC weight scalar would decrease from 0.872 in CY 2026 to a proposed 0.809 in CY 2027. This reduction is largely attributable to the substantial increase in expenditures for device portions of device-intensive procedures under the ASC payment system. In turn, this increase in device portions results from the proposed budget-neutral increase in OPPS payment rates for surgical procedures that would offset the drug payment reductions associated with our proposed payment policy for 340B acquired drugs as a result of the OPPS Drug Acquisition Cost Survey.
As the ASC payment system uses the OPPS conversion factor to determine payment for the device portions of device-intensive procedures, this alters the payment relativity between services under the OPPS because the entire portion of ASC payment rates for non-device-intensive procedures is based on the lower ASC conversion factor. Because of the proposed large increase in the device portions for device-intensive procedures in CY 2027 as a result of the proposed 340B drug payment policy, we solicited comment on whether the device portions of device-intensive procedures calculated using the OPPS conversion factor should continue to be excluded from the ASC weight scaler, or alternatively, whether these device portions should be subject to scaling through the ASC weight scaler. We estimated that treating device expenditures for device-intensive procedures as scalable prospective expenditures would increase the proposed ASC weight scaler from 0.809 to 0.865 in CY 2027 and would reduce the device portions of device intensive procedures by approximately 14 percent.
For any given year's ratesetting, we typically use the most recent full calendar year of claims data to model budget neutrality adjustments. We proposed to use the CY 2025 claims data to model our budget neutrality adjustment for CY 2027.
We received public comments on our proposal. The following is a summary of ( printed page 70677) the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Commenters opposed the proposed CY 2027 ASC weight scalar of 0.809, stating that the secondary scaling adjustment unnecessarily reduces ASC payments, widens the disparity with HOPD payments, and discourages migration to lower-cost ASCs. Many commenters urged CMS to eliminate the ASC weight scalar because continued annual application is not statutorily required, or alternatively to establish a single budget-neutrality calculation using combined OPPS and ASC utilization and service mix. Some commenters supported CMS's alternative of including device portions of device-intensive procedures in scalable expenditures, which would increase the scalar to approximately 0.865 and mitigate reductions for non-device-intensive services, although some recommended phasing in or partially applying this approach. Other commenters opposed scaling device portions because device acquisition costs are fixed and warned that the resulting approximately 14-percent reduction could impair access to device-intensive procedures. These commenters recommended maintaining the device-payment exclusion and instead removing the 340B-related OPPS conversion-factor increase from the ASC ratesetting and scalar calculations so that a hospital drug-payment policy does not distort ASC payment rates.
Response: We appreciate the public comments we received on our proposed ASC weight scalar for CY 2027 and our comment solicitation on whether the device portions of device-intensive procedures calculated using the OPPS conversion factor should continue to be excluded from the ASC weight scalar, or alternatively, whether these device portions should be included in the expenditures subject to scaling through the ASC weight scalar. We agree with commenters that our budget neutrality adjustment places the budget neutrality burden on non-device portions of surgical procedures subject to the ASC weight scalar; however, we remain concerned with both the potential payment reduction and payment asymmetry between the OPPS and ASC payment systems from applying the ASC weight scalar to the device portions of device-intensive procedures. We believe that applying the ASC weight scalar to device portions of device-intensive procedures would significantly reduce the ASC payment rate for such procedures and could potentially reduce future access to device-intensive procedures in the ASC setting which are predominantly performed in the hospital outpatient setting. For these reasons, we are not revising our methodology to include device portions as subject to scaling through the ASC weight scalar. We also considered the commenters' recommendation to use an OPPS conversion factor that excludes the 340B-related OPPS budget neutrality adjustment. Unfortunately, this approach would introduce the same payment asymmetry between the OPPS and ASC payment systems for device portions of device-intensive procedures as applying the ASC weight scalar to device portions as well as continuing the budget neutrality burden placed on non-device portions. For these reasons, we did not believe adopting an alternative OPPS conversion factor was appropriate. Therefore, for CY 2027, we are finalizing our proposal to continue our longstanding policy of using the ratio of total payments based on the CY 2026 relative payment weights to total payments based on the CY 2027 relative payment weights to scale the ASC relative payment weights, while continuing to exclude the device portions of device-intensive procedures from expenditures subject to scaling. We will continue to explore alternative methodologies that maintain budget neutrality under the ASC payment system—which preserves the Part B trust fund and reduces beneficiary cost-sharing—while advancing payment policies that expand access to site-neutral options for beneficiaries.
Comment: Commenters opposed proposed CY 2027 ASC payment reductions for ophthalmic, interventional pain, and dialysis vascular-access procedures. Commenters stated that the reductions would occur despite the overall ASC payment update and, in some cases, while corresponding HOPD payments would increase. They stated that the reduced payments do not adequately reflect the costs of the staff, supplies, devices, imaging, equipment, and other resources required to furnish these services, particularly in independent and rural ASCs. Commenters expressed concern that continued reductions could limit access, encourage consolidation, delay time-sensitive care, or shift services to more costly HOPDs or other less desirable treatment alternatives.
With respect to ophthalmic services, commenters opposed reductions for cataract, glaucoma, retinal, and other procedures, including vitreoretinal procedures described by CPT codes 67036, 67041 through 67043, 67108, 67110, 67113, 67210, 67227, and 67228. Commenters requested that CMS verify that the claims data capture all associated device, supply, and equipment costs; consider HOP Panel review and site-of-service substitution; publish relevant claims-volume and trimming information; and provide procedure-specific explanations for any reductions that are finalized. Commenters also requested that CMS reverse or reassess reductions for interventional pain procedures described by CPT codes 62321, 62323, 64479, 64483, 64490, 64493, 64633, and 64635 and evaluate the cumulative effects of successive payment reductions on beneficiary access. Finally, commenters opposed the effect of the reduced ASC weight scalar on dialysis vascular-access services, particularly non-device-intensive procedures such as CPT code 36902 and supported including device expenditures in the weight-scalar calculation. Commenters generally requested that CMS adopt payment methodologies that more accurately recognize ASC resource costs, stabilize or increase payment for these services, and preserve access to care in lower-cost non-hospital settings.
Response: We appreciate the comments regarding our proposed CY 2027 ASC payment rates for the procedures identified by the commenters and understand the concerns raised regarding the potential effects of payment reductions on beneficiary access. ASCs currently do not submit cost reports, so the absence of these data limits our ability to independently assess whether our proposed rates adequately reflect the costs of the staff, supplies, devices, imaging, equipment, and other resources. Additionally, the HOP Panel advises on OPPS matters and the ASC budget neutrality calculation is outside the scope of its charter. We did not revise claims trimming or the underlying ratesetting methodology involved—the payment rate reductions for these procedures are driven by the ASC budget neutrality adjustment providing a corresponding decrease in total nondevice portion expenditures in response to the increase in OPPS device portion expenditures adopted under the ASC payment system.
For the reasons previously described with respect to our budget neutrality methodology, we are finalizing our longstanding budget neutrality calculation because of concerns about underpayment of the significant device costs associated with device-intensive procedures and the importance of preserving beneficiary access to device-intensive procedures in the ASC setting. We intend to continue monitoring beneficiary access to non-device- ( printed page 70678) intensive procedures in the ASC setting and may consider future payment policies to address this issue.
After consideration of the public comments we received, we are finalizing our proposal to use scaled OPPS relative weights to establish ASC relative payment weights and to use the ratio of CY 2026 to CY 2027 total payments (the weight scalar) to ASC relative payment weights for CY 2027. We are also finalizing our proposal to continue using the OPPS conversion factor, which we are finalizing as $99.970 for CY 2027 in this final rule with comment period, to continue maintaining device portions between the OPPS and ASC payment systems for device-intensive surgical procedures. While we understand the concerns raised by interested parties regarding the payment reductions for non device-intensive procedures for CY 2027, we currently are not adopting an alternative methodology and are maintaining our longstanding calculation of budget neutrality under the ASC payment system and holding device portions constant between the OPPS and ASC payment systems for device-intensive procedures. We will continue to explore alternative methodologies to address concerns with the payment rates for non-device intensive procedures under the ASC payment system while providing budget neutrality under the ASC payment system for future rulemaking. The final CY 2027 ASC weight scalar is 0.814. Consistent with historical practice, we are finalizing our proposal to scale the ASC relative payment weights of covered surgical procedures, covered ancillary radiology services, and certain diagnostic tests within the medicine range of CPT codes, which are covered ancillary services for which the ASC payment rates are based on OPPS relative payment weights.
b. Updating the ASC Conversion Factor
Under the OPPS, we typically apply a budget neutrality adjustment for provider-level changes, most notably a change in the wage index values for the upcoming year, to the conversion factor. Consistent with our final ASC payment policy, for the CY 2017 ASC payment system and subsequent years, in the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (81 FR 79751 through 79753), we finalized our policy to calculate and apply a budget neutrality adjustment to the ASC conversion factor for supplier-level changes in wage index values for the upcoming year, just as the OPPS wage index budget neutrality adjustment is calculated and applied to the OPPS conversion factor.
For CY 2027, we calculated the proposed adjustment for the ASC payment system by using the most recent CY 2025 claims data available and estimating the difference in total payment that would be created by introducing the proposed CY 2027 ASC wage indexes. Specifically, holding CY 2025 ASC utilization, service-mix, and the proposed CY 2027 national payment rates after application of the weight scalar constant, we calculated the total adjusted payment using the CY 2026 ASC wage indexes and the total adjusted payment using the proposed CY 2027 ASC wage indexes which included the 5-percent cap on wage index decreases for an ASC. We used the 50 percent labor-related share for both total adjusted payment calculations. We then compared the total adjusted payment calculated with the CY 2026 ASC wage indexes to the total adjusted payment calculated with the proposed CY 2027 ASC wage indexes and applied the resulting ratio of 1.0016 (the proposed CY 2027 ASC wage index budget neutrality adjustment) to the CY 2026 ASC conversion factor to calculate the proposed CY 2027 ASC conversion factor.
Section 1833(i)(2)(D)(v) of the Act requires that the ASC conversion factor be reduced by a productivity adjustment in each calendar year. Section 1886(b)(3)(B)(xi)(II) of the Act defines the productivity adjustment to be equal to the 10-year moving average of changes in annual economy-wide private nonfarm business multifactor productivity (MFP). We finalized the methodology for calculating the productivity adjustment in the CY 2011 PFS final rule with comment period (75 FR 73394 through 73396) and revised it in the CY 2012 PFS final rule with comment period (76 FR 73300 through 73301) and the CY 2016 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (80 FR 70500 through 70501). The proposed productivity adjustment for CY 2027 was projected to be 0.8 percentage point, as published in the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS proposed rule (91 FR 19496) based on IGI's 2025 fourth quarter forecast.
Section 1833(i)(2)(C)(i) of the Act requires that, if the Secretary has not updated amounts established under the revised ASC payment system in a calendar year, the payment amounts shall be increased by the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for all urban consumers (CPI-U), U.S. city average, as estimated by the Secretary for the 12-month period ending with the midpoint of the year involved. The statute does not mandate the adoption of any particular update mechanism, but it requires the payment amounts to be increased by the CPI-U in the absence of any update. Because the Secretary updates the ASC payment amounts annually, we adopted a policy, which we codified at § 416.171(a)(2)(ii)), to update the ASC conversion factor using the CPI-U for CY 2010 and subsequent calendar years.
In the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (83 FR 59075 through 59080), we finalized a policy to apply the hospital market basket update (which is the inpatient hospital market basket percentage increase reduced by the productivity adjustment) to ASC payment system rates for an interim period of 5 years (CY 2019 through CY 2023), during which we would assess whether there was a migration of the performance of procedures from the hospital setting to the ASC setting as a result of the use of a hospital market basket update, as well as whether there were any unintended consequences, such as less than expected migration of the performance of procedures from the hospital setting to the ASC setting. At that time, the most recently available full year of claims data to assess the expected migration applying the productivity-adjusted hospital market basket update during the interim period was within the period from CY 2019 through CY 2022. However, the impact of the COVID-19 PHE on health care utilization, CY 2020 in particular, was tremendously profound, particularly for elective surgeries, because many beneficiaries avoided healthcare settings, when possible, to avoid possible infection from the SARS-CoV-2 virus. As a result, it was nearly impossible to disentangle the effects from the COVID-19 PHE in our analysis of whether the higher update factor for the ASC payment system caused increased migration to the ASC setting. To analyze whether procedures migrated from the hospital setting to the ASC setting, we needed to use claims data from a period during which the COVID-19 PHE had less of an impact on health care utilization. Therefore, for CY 2024, we finalized our proposal to extend the 5-year interim period an additional 2 years through CY 2024 and CY 2025 which we subsequently extended through CY 2026 in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53914 through 53915). We believed hospital outpatient and ASC utilization data from CYs 2023 through 2025 would enable us to more accurately analyze whether the application of the hospital market basket update to the ASC payment ( printed page 70679) system had an effect on the migration of services from the hospital setting to the ASC setting. We revised our regulations at § 416.171(a)(2)(iii), (iv), (vi), (vii), and (viii) which establish the annual update to the ASC conversion factor, to reflect these extensions.
For the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, we proposed to extend our utilization of the hospital market basket update factor in the ASC payment system for one additional year, through CY 2027, as we continue to review and evaluate hospital outpatient and ASC utilization data, as well as the migration of surgical procedures between settings. In conjunction with our proposal, we proposed revising our regulations at § 416.171(a)(2)(iii), (iv), (vi), (vii), and (viii), which establish the annual update to the ASC conversion factor, the 2.0 percentage point reduction for ASCs that fail to meet the standards for reporting ASC quality measures, and the productivity adjustment, to reflect this one-year extension.
We received public comments on this proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Most commenters supported CMS's proposal to extend use of the productivity-adjusted hospital market basket, rather than the CPI-U, as the ASC payment update factor through CY 2027. Commenters stated that the hospital market basket better reflects ASC cost growth because ASCs purchase similar supplies, equipment, devices, and implants as HOPDs and compete for the same clinical workforce. They also stated that aligning the ASC and OPPS update factors supports migration to lower-cost ASCs, reduces payment disparities, and generates Medicare and beneficiary savings, and many commenters urged CMS to make the hospital market basket update policy permanent rather than extending it for one year. Other commenters opposed the extension, stating that hospitals and ASCs have different cost structures and patient populations and that the hospital market basket does not accurately measure ASC input costs. These commenters recommended that CMS collect minimally burdensome ASC cost data and develop an ASC-specific market basket, while some supporters stated that any new index should apply consistently to both ASCs and HOPDs to preserve alignment between the payment systems.
Response: We appreciate the feedback from commenters. We did not propose to collect ASC-specific cost data in our CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule. ASCs currently do not submit cost reports, so we are unable to discern if there is a meaningful difference in the cost structures between the hospital and ASC setting and if such differences would necessitate a different update factor. We agree with commenters that providing the same annual update mechanism under the OPPS and ASC payment systems can support the migration of services to the lower-cost ASC setting. We are finalizing our proposal to apply the productivity-adjusted hospital market basket update to the ASC payment system for CY 2027.
2. CY 2027 Final ASC Conversion Factor
For CY 2027, we finalized our proposal to utilize the final inpatient hospital market basket percentage increase of 3.2 percent reduced by the productivity adjustment of 0.9 percentage point, resulting in a final hospital market basket update of 2.3 percent for ASCs meeting the quality reporting requirements. Therefore, we are finalizing our proposal to apply a 2.3 percent hospital market basket update factor to the CY 2026 ASC conversion factor for ASCs meeting the quality reporting requirements to determine the CY 2027 ASC payment amounts. The ASCQR Program affected payment rates beginning in CY 2014 and, under this program, there is a 2.0 percentage point reduction to the hospital market basket update factor for ASCs that fail to meet the ASCQR Program requirements. We refer readers to section XIV.E. of the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (83 FR 59138 through 59139) and section XIV.E. of this final rule with comment period for a detailed discussion of our policies regarding payment reduction for ASCs that fail to meet ASCQR Program requirements.
For CY 2027, we are adjusting the CY 2026 ASC conversion factor ($56.322) by a wage index budget neutrality factor of 1.0018 in addition to the productivity-adjusted hospital market basket update of 2.3 percent, discussed previously, which results in a final CY 2027 ASC conversion factor of $57.721 for ASCs meeting quality reporting requirements. For ASCs not meeting quality reporting requirements, we are adjusting the CY 2026 ASC conversion factor ($56.322) by the wage index budget neutrality factor of 1.0018 in addition to the reduced productivity-adjusted hospital market basket update of 0.3 percent, discussed previously, which results in a final CY 2027 ASC conversion factor of $56.592 for ASCs not meeting the quality reporting requirements.
3. Display of the Final CY 2027 ASC Payment Rates
Addenda AA and BB to this final rule with comment period (which are available on the CMS website) display the final ASC payment rates for CY 2027 for covered surgical procedures and covered ancillary services, respectively. The final payment rates included in Addenda AA and BB to this final rule with comment period reflect the full ASC payment update and not the reduced payment update used to calculate payment rates for ASCs not meeting the quality reporting requirements under the ASCQR Program.
These Addenda contain several types of information related to the final CY 2027 payment rates. Specifically, in Addendum AA, a “Y” in the column titled “To be Subject to Multiple Procedure Discounting” indicates that the surgical procedure would be subject to the multiple procedure payment reduction policy. As discussed in the CY 2008 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (72 FR 66829 through 66830), most covered surgical procedures are subject to a 50 percent reduction in the ASC payment for the lower-paying procedure when more than one procedure is performed in a single operative session.
Comment: Numerous commenters opposed CMS' proposed change from “No” to “Yes” for multiple-procedure discounting of device-intensive procedures, including CPT codes 54401, 54405, 54410, 54416, 63650, 63655, 63663, 63664, 63685, 64553, 64555, 64561, 64575, and 64590, and requested continuation of the current exemption.

Therefore, for CY 2027, we are not finalizing the proposed change in the multiple-procedure discounting designation for CPT codes 54401, 54405, 54410, 54416, 63650, 63655, 63663, 63664, 63685, 64553, 64555, 64561, 64575, and 64590. These procedures will continue to be identified with an “N” in the “Subject to Multiple Procedure Discounting” column of ASC Addendum AA. The final relative payment weights for all covered surgical procedures and covered ancillary services where the ASC payment rates are based on OPPS relative payment weights were scaled for budget ( printed page 70680) neutrality. Therefore, scaling was not applied to the device portion of the device-intensive-procedures; services that are paid at the PFS nonfacility PE RVU-based amount; separately payable covered ancillary services that have a predetermined national payment amount, such as drugs and biologicals and brachytherapy sources that are separately paid under the OPPS; or services that are contractor-priced or paid at reasonable cost in ASCs. XIV. Measure Removal for the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting and Ambulatory Surgical Center Quality Reporting Programs
We refer readers to sections XV. and XVII. of this final rule with comment period for program-specific background information, including statutory authority and program measure sets, regarding the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting and Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) Quality Reporting Programs, respectively.
B. Removal of the Appropriate Follow-Up Interval for Normal Colonoscopy in Average Risk Patients Measure in the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting and the ASC Quality Reporting Programs
We refer readers to the CY 2014 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period where we adopted the Appropriate Follow-Up Interval for Normal Colonoscopy in Average Risk Patients (the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval) measure into the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting and the ASC Quality Reporting Programs (78 FR 75101 through 75102 and 78 FR 75127 through 75128), and the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period where we modified the measure to align with updated clinical guidelines (88 FR 81972 through 81973 and 88 FR 82020 through 82021). The Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval measure assesses the percentage of patients aged 45 to 75 years receiving a screening colonoscopy without biopsy or polypectomy who had a recommended follow-up interval of at least 10 years for repeat colonoscopy documented in the colonoscopy report.[179]
When we adopted the Colonoscopy Follow-up Interval measure, we sought to address what was, at the time, the critical issue of colonoscopies potentially performed too frequently and potentially increasing patients' exposure to procedural harm.[180 181] The measure was designed to promote adherence to recommended screening intervals through documentation of follow-up recommendations in the colonoscopy report, thereby increasing provider and patient awareness of appropriate screening intervals. Importantly, this measure assesses whether the recommended 10-year interval for a follow-up colonoscopy is documented in the colonoscopy report, rather than whether appropriate clinical care is delivered. In other words, the measure does not assess whether the follow-up colonoscopy was performed according to this recommended interval.
We continue to believe that it is important to encourage high-quality colonoscopy care in hospital outpatient departments and ASCs. We note that the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program and ASC Quality Reporting Program measure sets both currently include another measure that is tied more closely to outcomes of continued interest and importance—the Facility 7-Day Risk-Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy measure (79 FR 66948 through 66955 and 79 FR 66970 through 66979, respectively), which assesses the incidence of hospital returns within 7 days of a colonoscopy, including emergency department visits, observation stays, and unplanned readmissions. The Facility 7-Day Risk-Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy measure is therefore a more patient-outcome focused measure of procedure-related adverse events across both programs in contrast to the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval measure, which assesses documentation of recommended follow-up intervals rather than patient outcomes.[182] For these reasons, in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (91 FR 41957), we proposed to remove the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval measure from the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting and the ASC Quality Reporting Programs, beginning with the CY 2027 reporting period/CY 2029 payment determination. For both programs, removal is appropriate under removal factor 6 (42 CFR 419.46(i)(3)(i)(F) and 416.320(c)(2)(vi)), the availability of a measure that is more strongly associated with a desired ( printed page 70681) patient outcome for the particular topic. The Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program and ASC Quality Reporting Program measure sets would continue to retain the Facility 7-Day Risk-Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy measure.
Additionally, we continue to prioritize appropriate colonoscopy care in our other quality reporting or value-based programs. For example, we have a Colorectal Cancer Screening measure within the gastroenterology Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) Value Pathway [183] and the Medicare Shared Savings Program,[184] which assesses the percentage of adults 45 to 75 years of age who had appropriate screening for colorectal cancer.
We invited and received public comments on this proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Many commenters supported removing the Appropriate Follow-Up Interval for Normal Colonoscopy in Average Risk Patients measure stating that this measure primarily assesses whether a recommended follow-up interval was documented rather than whether appropriate clinical care occurred or meaningful patient outcomes were achieved. Many commenters supported streamlining quality reporting by removing measures and reporting requirements that are duplicative, redundant, or no longer needed and focusing on more clinically meaningful, patient-centered measures that better reflect care quality, patient safety, and outcomes.
Many commenters supported removing the measure stating that chart abstraction, data collection, and reporting requirements create administrative burden, and that removal would allow facilities to focus on higher-priority quality improvement activities that more directly benefit patients. A few commenters supported removing the measure due to consistently high performance with limited meaningful differentiation thereby reducing its value as a quality measure. A few commenters noted that the measure may be topped out and supported focusing resources on measures with greater potential to drive meaningful improvements in patient outcomes and care quality.
Response: We thank commenters for their support. We agree that removing the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval measure will reduce reporting burden and allow hospitals and ASCs to focus resources on measurable clinical outcomes and direct patient care. We agree with commenters that the measure has consistently high performance in the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting and ASC Quality Reporting Programs.
Comment: A few commenters supported removing the measure from facility-based programs, stating that it was developed to assess clinician performance and is not appropriate for evaluating hospital or ASC performance.
Response: We appreciate commenters' support; however, we disagree that the measure is not appropriate for evaluating hospital outpatient department or ASC performance. As we stated when we adopted the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval Measure into the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting and ASC Quality Reporting Programs, while this measure was originally developed at the clinician-level, the measure steward later respecified the measure at the facility level and performed field testing for this measure in the Hospital Outpatient Department and ASC settings and CMS determined, based on that testing, that the measure was appropriate and feasible for those settings (78 FR 75099 through 75100 and 78 FR 75125).
We are removing the measure now because another measure is available that more directly assesses procedure-related adverse events, not because we believe this measure is not appropriate for the hospital outpatient department and ASC settings. The retained measure, Facility 7-Day Risk-Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy, assesses hospital returns within 7 days of a colonoscopy, including emergency department visits, observation stays, and unplanned readmissions.
Comment: A few commenters expressed concern that removing the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval measure could weaken efforts to prevent unnecessary or low-value colonoscopies which could increase procedural risks.
Response: We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding unnecessary or low-value colonoscopies, health care costs, patient safety, continuity of care, and colorectal cancer prevention and follow-up. When we adopted the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval measure, we sought to address issues related to colonoscopies potentially being performed too frequently which would increase patients' exposure to procedural harm.[185 186] The measure was designed to promote adherence to recommended screening intervals through documentation of follow-up recommendations. However, the measure assesses whether the recommended 10-year follow-up interval is documented in the colonoscopy report, rather than whether appropriate clinical care is delivered or whether the follow-up colonoscopy is performed according to the recommended interval. The Facility 7-Day Risk-Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy measure allows us to better assess procedure-related adverse events than the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval measure.
Comment: A few commenters expressed concern that removing this measure could undermine efforts to reduce health care costs.
Response: We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding health care costs. We agree that avoiding unnecessary colonoscopies can reduce health care costs. As we previously stated, however, the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval measure does not assess whether a follow-up colonoscopy is performed according to the recommended 10-year follow-up interval. Retaining the Facility 7-Day Risk-Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy measure prioritizes a measure more strongly associated with a desired patient outcome and assesses procedure-related adverse events, including hospital returns within 7 days of a colonoscopy,[187] that can increase health care costs.
Comment: A few commenters stated that this measure supports colorectal cancer prevention. A few commenters expressed concern about removing a measure that aligns with United States Preventive Services Task Force's recommendations and is included in the Core Quality Measures Collaborative (CQMC) Gastroenterology core measure set.
Response: The CQMC's Gastroenterology core measure set is ( printed page 70682) focused on ambulatory care measures at the clinician reporting level. We agree that the measure's inclusion in this measure set indicates that it has clinical value but note that the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting and ASC Quality Reporting Programs assess facility-level performance. In the CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule proposed rule, the Colonoscopy Follow-up Interval measure was proposed for removal from MIPS because it is topped-out, meaning the median performance rate is 95 percent or higher (91 FR 44160 through 44162 and 91 FR 44416). We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding alignment with United States Preventive Services Task Force recommendations, which recommends screening for colorectal cancer in adults aged 45 to 75 years.[188] We continue to prioritize appropriate colorectal cancer screening in other quality reporting or value-based programs, such as the Colorectal Cancer Screening measure in the gastroenterology MIPS Value Pathway [189] and the Medicare Shared Savings Program.[190]
Comment: A few commenters stated that removing the measure would eliminate a distinct and complementary aspect of quality measurement. These commenters stated that the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval and the Facility 7-Day Risk-Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy measure assess different aspects of care, so maintaining both provides a more comprehensive assessment of quality.
Response: We understand commenters' concerns that the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval measure and the Facility 7-Day Risk-Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy measures do not assess the same clinical areas. The Facility 7-Day Risk-Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy measure provides an outcome-focused assessment of procedure-related adverse events, including hospital returns within 7 days of a colonoscopy.[191] We seek to implement measures that are focused on patient outcomes to evaluate the results of clinical care. The Colorectal Cancer Screening measure, which assesses the percentage of adults 45 to 75 years of age who had appropriate screening for colorectal cancer,[192] is more complementary to the Facility 7-Day Risk-Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy measure than the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval measure, which assesses documentation of a recommended follow-up interval.11
As discussed above, the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval measure sought to address patients' exposure to procedural harm from unnecessarily frequent colonoscopies, while the Facility 7-Day Risk-Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy measure assesses procedure-related adverse events. Moreover, the Facility 7-Day Risk-Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy measure is more strongly associated with patient outcomes than the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval measure. Thus, removal of the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval measure is appropriate under removal factor 6 (42 CFR 419.46(i)(3)(i)(F) and 416.320(c)(2)(vi)), the availability of a measure that is more strongly associated with a patient outcome for the particular topic.
Comment: A few commenters recommended evaluating or monitoring whether removal of the measure results in unintended effects on clinical practice or adherence to screening recommendations. A commenter recommended improving the reliability of the Facility 7-Day Risk-Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy measure to ensure it provides useful information to facilities. A commenter recommended considering less burdensome approaches, including provider education, clinical decision support tools, or broader quality improvement initiatives, to support guideline-concordant screening practices without maintaining a standalone reporting measure.
Response: We thank commenters for their recommendations and will consider them as we evaluate the effects of removing the Colonoscopy Follow-Up Interval measure. As part of our measure maintenance process, we will conduct ongoing monitoring and evaluation analyses to evaluate measure performance of the Facility 7-Day Risk-Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy measure, and to identify any potential unintended consequences. Regarding burden, the Facility 7-Day Risk Standardized Hospital Visit Rate after Outpatient Colonoscopy measure is calculated from Medicare claims and administrative data making associated burden related to data collection minimal for hospitals and ASCs in contrast to the Colonoscopy Follow-up Interval measure which requires chart-abstraction. Regarding reliability of the measure, sufficient case numbers for reliability purposes were assessed during the measure development process and would be reassessed through the measure maintenance review process.

title: Deputy foreign minister pitches Europe on 'Made with Taiwan'

content:
外交部副部长向欧洲推介“台湾制造” - 聚焦台湾
外交部副部长向欧洲推介“台湾制造”
要激活文字转语音服务，请首先同意以下隐私政策。
周三，台湾外交部副部长吴弗朗索瓦（右二）出席第 25 届柏林安全会议。中央通讯社照片2026年11月4日
中新社柏林11月6日电 台湾外交部副部长吴志中周三敦促欧洲在“台湾制造”的方针下深化产业合作，称台湾的半导体和制造优势可以提高欧洲的竞争力，有利于双方的经济和安全利益。
吴在11月3日至4日举行的第25届柏林安全会议上提出了这一建议，会议重点讨论了欧洲的防御能力、俄罗斯的安全威胁和乌克兰战争。
在由退役德国少将莱因哈德·沃尔斯基主持的一场边会上，吴仪与其他高级官员一起讨论了中国对台湾的安全威胁、台湾的防御能力以及台湾与欧洲的合作。
吴说，台湾和欧洲在民主制度和经济发展方面有共同点，欧洲应将台湾视为亚洲重要的民主伙伴。
他建议超越“台湾制造”，迈向“台湾制造”，将欧洲的研究和设计优势与台湾的制造能力结合起来。
周三，台湾外交部副部长吴弗朗索瓦。中央通讯社照片2026年11月4日
连续11年出席该会议的吴向中央社表示，欧洲重新关注制造业和经济安全，为与台湾的合作提供了新的机遇。
他表示，这种伙伴关系具有长期潜力，并补充说，台湾没有地缘政治野心，也不会利用经济关系作为施压工具，这与他所说的中国将经济关系武器化的做法不同。
他表示，与台湾的更密切合作将支持民主伙伴，同时帮助欧洲加强其工业竞争力和安全。

Deputy foreign minister pitches Europe on 'Made with Taiwan'
To activate the text-to-speech service, please first agree to the privacy policy below.
Taiwan's Deputy Foreign Minister François Wu (second right) attends a talk at the 25th Berlin Security Conference on Wednesday. CNA photo Nov. 4, 2026
Berlin, Nov. 6 (CNA) Taiwan's Deputy Foreign Minister François Wu (吳志中) urged Europe on Wednesday to deepen industrial cooperation under a "Made with Taiwan" approach, saying Taiwan's semiconductor and manufacturing strengths could boost European competitiveness and benefit both sides' economic and security interests.
Wu made the proposal at the 25th Berlin Security Conference, held Nov. 3-4, which focused on Europe's defense capabilities, security threats from Russia and the war in Ukraine.
At a side event, chaired by retired German Major General Reinhard Wolski, Wu joined other senior officials to discuss China's security threat to Taiwan, the island's defense resilience and Taiwan-Europe cooperation.
Wu said Taiwan and Europe shared common ground in their democratic systems and economic development, and that Europe should view Taiwan as an important democratic partner in Asia.
He proposed moving beyond "Made in Taiwan" toward "Made with Taiwan," combining Europe's strengths in research and design with Taiwan's manufacturing capabilities.
Taiwan's Deputy Foreign Minister François Wu on Wednesday. CNA photo Nov. 4, 2026
Wu, who has attended the conference for 11 years, told CNA that Europe's renewed focus on manufacturing and economic security offered new opportunities for cooperation with Taiwan.
He said the partnership had long-term potential, adding that Taiwan had no geopolitical ambitions and would not use economic ties as a tool of pressure, unlike what he described as China's practice of weaponizing economic relations.
Closer cooperation with Taiwan, he said, would support a democratic partner while helping Europe strengthen its industrial competitiveness and security.

summary: 香港专案组捣毁与三合会有关的66人串通投标团伙中国劳工布告栏 星期六, 2026 年 11 月 7 日 · 香港 香港和中国劳工英文新闻 香港专案组捣毁与三合会有关的 66 人串通投标团伙 联合专案组逮捕了 66 人，其中包括建筑和咨询公司的董事，涉嫌操纵价值超过 1 亿港元的楼宇修缮招标。据称，该组织采用贿赂、恐吓和虚假投标等手段，并与黑社会有联系。为解决建筑修缮工程中的串通投标问题而成立的联合工作组已被粉碎
content:
香港专案组捣毁与三合会有关的66人串通投标团伙中国劳工公告栏
星期六, 7 十一月 2026 · 香港 香港及中国劳工新闻英文版
香港专案组捣毁涉及三合会的66人串通投标团伙
一个联合专案组逮捕了 66 人，其中包括建筑和咨询公司的董事，涉嫌操纵价值超过 1 亿港元的建筑修缮招标。据称，该组织采用贿赂、恐吓和虚假投标等手段，并与黑社会有联系。
官员们 11 月 6 日表示，为解决建筑修缮工程中的串通投标问题而成立的联合工作组捣毁了一个涉嫌串通投标的犯罪团伙，逮捕了 66 人。
此次“联丰”行动涉及香港警方、竞争事务委员会等机构，共拘捕54名男性和12名女性，年龄介乎29岁至79岁。被拘捕的人包括6间承包商公司的7名董事和6名员工、10家顾问公司的10名董事和2名员工、1间物业管理公司的1名董事和1名员工，以及1名业主立案法团成员。一些被捕者被指控与三合会有联系。
调查发现，该集团（当局称该集团与有组织犯罪有关）曾试图在政府推出建筑修缮工程资格预审清单之前匆忙签订合同。该集团被指控以材料价格波动和迫切需要维修为由，欺骗业主签署合同，然后将工作交给其控制的顾问和承包商。
该集团被指控通过贿赂业主立案法团成员、利用幌子公司提交“虚假”或“虚假”投标以制造竞争的假象以及恐吓或贿赂竞争对手来控制招标过程。据称，在赢得合同后，该集团隐瞒了工程的真实范围，后来增加了昂贵的额外费用，迫使业主支付更高的费用。据称，涉案合约总价值超过1亿港元，涵盖全港12个住宅及工厂大厦。
在行动中，专案组搜查了 78 个场所，包括承包商和顾问的办公室，并没收了文件和会计记录。在打击黑社会活动的同时，警方突击搜查了7个非法场所，包括5个非法赌博场所和2个妓院，并逮捕了另外38人（30男8女），罪名包括经营赌博场所和管理妓院。
大多数被捕者仍被拘留接受审问。专责小组表示，将联系相关顾问公司仍在处理重大维修合同的建筑物的业主立案法团，以警告他们有关风险。它还设立了24小时热线182000，并设立了公众举报涉嫌串通投标活动的奖励计划。
政府警告说，任何被发现串通投标罪的人都将受到起诉并面临法律的全部制裁。

Hong Kong task force smashes 66-person bid-rigging ring linked to triads | China Labour Bulletin Board
Saturday, 7 Nov 2026 · Hong Kong Hong Kong and China labour news in English
Hong Kong task force smashes 66-person bid-rigging ring linked to triads
A joint task force arrested 66 people, including directors of construction and consultancy firms, for allegedly rigging building-repair tenders worth over HK$100 million. The group is said to have used bribery, intimidation and phantom bids, and had triad links.
A joint task force set up to tackle bid-rigging in building-repair works has smashed a syndicate suspected of colluding to fix tenders, arresting 66 people, officials said on 6 November.
The “Lian Fung” operation, which involved the Hong Kong police, the Competition Commission and other agencies, resulted in the arrest of 54 men and 12 women aged between 29 and 79. Among those detained were seven directors and six staff of six contractor companies, 10 directors and two staff of 10 consultancy firms, a director and a staff member of a property-management company, and a member of an owners’ corporation. Some of those arrested are alleged to have triad connections.
Investigations found that the syndicate, which the authorities say is linked to organised crime, had tried to rush through contracts before the government introduced a pre-qualification list for building-repair works. The group is accused of tricking owners into signing contracts by citing volatile material prices and the urgent need for repairs, and then steering the work to consultants and contractors it controlled.
The syndicate is alleged to have controlled the tender process by bribing owners’ corporation members, using front companies to submit “phantom” or “dummy” bids to create a false impression of competition, and intimidating or bribing rival bidders. After winning contracts, the group is said to have concealed the true scope of works and later added expensive extras, forcing owners to pay much higher sums. The total value of the contracts involved is said to exceed HK$100 million, covering 12 residential and factory estates across Hong Kong.
In the operation, the task force searched 78 premises, including offices of contractors and consultants, and seized documents and accounting records. In a parallel crackdown on triad activities, officers raided seven illegal venues, including five illegal gambling dens and two brothels, arresting another 38 people (30 men and eight women) on charges including operating gambling premises and managing brothels.
Most of those arrested remain in custody for questioning. The task force said it will contact owners’ corporations of buildings where the consultancy firms involved are still handling major repair contracts to warn them of the risks. It has also set up a 24-hour hotline, 182000, and a reward scheme for the public to report suspected bid-rigging activities.
The government warned that anyone found guilty of bid-rigging will be prosecuted and face the full force of the law.

华盛顿（路透社）——根据路透社看到的一封信，众议院共和党高层议员呼吁英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋本月向国会通报一则新闻报道，该报道称他与一名向北京传递信息的中国女商人关系密切。
《纽约时报》上个月报道称，美国当局正在调查新加坡公司 Megaspeed 的前高管 Alice Huang，该公司从 Nvidia 购买人工智能芯片。美国当局对 Megaspeed 进行了审查，怀疑它帮助北京获得了被禁止运往中国的先进人工智能芯片。
在 11 月 4 日的一封信中，众议院外交事务委员会主席布莱恩·马斯特 (Brian Mast)、中国特别委员会主席约翰·穆勒纳尔 (John Moolenaar) 和情报委员会主席埃里克·克劳福德 (Eric Crawford) 要求黄仁勋在 11 月 18 日就《纽约时报》的报道和 Nvidia 的“针对外国对手间谍活动的安全协议”提供闭门简报。
他们写道，该报告提出了“关于（中国）获取美国敏感技术和信息的重大国家安全担忧”。他们补充说：“国会确定美国国家安全面临风险的程度至关重要。”
英伟达没有对这封信发表评论，但表示黄每年都会与“数千名客户高管”进行交谈，并强调亚洲的云客户收到的是普通商业信息，而不是敏感的英伟达商业机密或与美国国家安全有关的任何信息。
英伟达补充说：“我们经常收到美国政府有关受关注各方和实体的最新信息，并始终采取相应行动。”

Key Republicans seek briefing from Nvidia CEO over Chinese spy allegations - Nikkei Asia
Key Republicans seek briefing from Nvidia CEO over Chinese spy allegations
Congressmen ask Jensen Huang to explain AI chip giant's anti-espionage protocols
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks onstage at the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin on Oct. 19. © Reuters
November 6, 2026 23:31 JST
WASHINGTON (Reuters) -- Top Republican lawmakers in the House of Representatives are calling on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to brief Congress this month about a news report alleging he had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing, according to a letter seen by Reuters.
The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities were investigating Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia. U.S. authorities have scrutinized Megaspeed over suspicions it helped Beijing gain access to advanced AI chips that are barred from shipment to China.
In a letter dated Nov. 4, Brian Mast, who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee, John Moolenaar, who leads the China Select Committee, and Intelligence Committee Chair Eric Crawford asked Jensen Huang to provide a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 about the New York Times report and Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage."
The report raises "significant national security concerns regarding [China's] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," they wrote. "It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk," they added.
Nvidia did not comment on the letter but said Huang talks with "thousands of customer executives every year" and emphasized that cloud customers in Asia receive ordinary business information, not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets or anything tied to U.S. national security.
"We often receive updates from the U.S. government regarding parties and entities of concern and always act accordingly," Nvidia added.

2026-11-07 00:05 聯合報／ 記者蔣永佑、林孟潔、唐筱恬、張曼蘋／台北報導
立委高金素梅被控接受中共巨額資金，為大陸公務機構發展組織，並試圖培養「第五縱隊」，昨被高檢署依違反國安法、違背職務收賄罪起訴、求刑十四年。聯合報系資料照
立委高金素梅前辦公室主任張俊傑涉共諜偷渡出境，台灣高等檢察署調查，高金素梅與張俊傑合謀接受中共一億七千萬巨資，發展共諜組織，並接受捐贈經營原民部落選區，試圖作為「第五縱隊」使用，昨依違反國安法、違背職務收賄罪起訴高金、張俊傑、高金辦公室主任陳智葟、助理林怡君共四人，對高金與張各求刑十四、十五年，陳、林移審法院裁定續押。
起訴指出，張俊傑與高金素梅收受境外敵對勢力提供的資源及巨額資金，安排人員赴大陸接受統戰訓練，滲透原民部落地區，並依中共指示，在國會發聲影響議事進行，惡性極為重大，對二人求處重刑。
高金素梅等人二○○五至二○一六年間，將部落工作隊及國會團隊統合成「祖靈之邦團隊」，以「一套人馬，兩塊招牌」手法，由張俊傑、林怡君統領團隊的競選、問政及原鄉部落聯繫工作，林還當高金與張的代理人，穿梭兩岸接受中共官員指示進行傳達。
起訴指出，檯面上由張俊傑出面接受中共捐贈原鄉部落建設經費，充實高金素梅競選連任資源；檯面下，張再利用親友帳戶，將一億七千餘萬元資金匯入國內，替大陸公務機構發展組織。
高金素梅依中共官員及派遣之人指示，在立法院分別以召開組團赴聯合國反日記者會、對日本代表處質詢刪除預算，並針對「反軍購」、「課綱微調」及兩岸、外交等議題配合發聲，透過程序委員會委員身分，影響法案審議，對國家安全造成重大危害，有貪汙職務上收賄對價。
檢方指出，高金素梅為連任及牟取不法利益，與張俊傑共謀發展組織，企圖動搖民心，更利用立委監督問政職權，對軍購、兩岸、外交、國防等重要議題，內外勾結配合中共發聲，所犯情節重大，偵查期間推諉卸責，應予嚴懲。
高金素梅發六點聲明強調，她沒為中共發展組織，也沒收取任何陸資，檢方草率起訴，對她羅織入罪，將在審判中提出證據捍衛自身清白、絕不妥協。
聲明指出，她到聯合國抗議、反對軍購、課綱微調，是她一貫主張，並非中共授意，更沒有一毛錢流入口袋。起訴書所載部落工作隊，在另案已釐清，與她無關。
高金素梅強調，她無法想像連任七屆立委，竟然會遭指控，她收取陸資才能連任，若真的如起訴書所述，她早就涉犯國安法，有需要被監聽廿多年嗎？還在事隔十年後、選舉前，將她起訴。
高金素梅涉共諜案遭起訴...辦公室主任、助理自白認罪 出庭不發一語
立委高金素梅前辦公室主任張俊傑成功偷渡，檢警掌握情資，張此次開出一五○○萬天價，力拚潛逃出境，沒想到真讓張找到「滿瑞富六號」漁船，由陸籍船長陳華亭掌舵開船，張登船後藉由「漁網隱身」躲過安檢，為釐清有無裡應外合，台北地檢署聲押陳華亭、台籍人頭船長黃新嘉及四名印尼漁工，法院裁定六人均羈押禁見。
立委高金素梅前辦公室主任張俊傑涉共諜偷渡出境，台灣高等檢察署調查，高金素梅與張俊傑合謀接受中共一億七千萬巨資，發展共諜組織，並接受捐贈經營原民部落選區，試圖作為「第五縱隊」使用，昨依違反國安法、違背職務收賄罪起訴高金、張俊傑、高金辦公室主任陳智葟、助理林怡君共四人，對高金與張各求刑十四、十五年，陳、林移審法院裁定續押。
Bolt司機林宇濬今年一月二十五日凌晨，於台六十四快速道路，丟包酒醉的温姓政大高材生替代役，導致温男慘遭後方接連駛來的四車輾死，新北地院國民法官認定，林男不符自首資格，昨依違背法令契約遺棄致死罪重判林男十三年徒刑，比檢方求刑十一年還重。
人工智慧（ＡＩ）科技進步，高雄卅八歲林姓男子透過ＡＩ撰寫程式，非法駭入公家機關及私人企業網站後台，竊取廿三萬餘筆民眾個資，透過暗網販售。

Unpacking the rebuttal for the appeal to the Cape Town Municipal Planning Tribunal approval for the Equinix data centres near the airport raises more questions than answers.
Illustrative image: A data centre in Ashburn, Virginia, United States. Housing developments there will soon be walled in by data centres, exemplifying the tensions over their unfettered growth. (Photo: Charles A Fazio / Bloomberg via Getty Images) | Cape Town skyline. (Photo: Gallo Images / Foto24 / Michael Hammond) | (By Daniella Lee Ming Yesca)
Getting one thing straight about the data centres planned for opposite Cape Town International Airport is that the developer on record, which is handling all the wheeling and dealing and issued the formal response to the appeal, is a crowd called Planning Partners.
They’re acting on behalf of King Air Industria (KAI, which is co-developed by Atterbury) and Equinix. According to the 91-page response that could be obtained only via a Paia request, which Daily Maverick has now studied, Equinix’s involvement in the KAI project centres on a long-term commercial lease and infrastructure funding arrangement.
Crucially, Equinix’s legal counsel (Baker & McKenzie) advised the company not to proceed with multi-hundred-million-rand investments unless the City of Cape Town provided explicit statutory certainty that data centres are legally permitted under municipal zoning rules. This legal warning directly prompted the City to amend its Municipal Planning By-law to explicitly include “data centre” under the definition of a warehouse.
Now that we’re all on the same page, we can dive into the primary defence.
Planning Partners argues that the objectors misunderstand municipal planning law under Item 136 of the Development Management Scheme.
They state that, under this framework, large precincts are developed in stages. The developer contends that the current application merely subdivides, consolidates and rezones land to create a buildable site (Erf 180451 for Data Centre 2).
The argument is that granular operational details – such as building architecture, cooling mechanics, noise propagation, fuel storage and National Environmental Management Act (Nema) environmental triggers – belong strictly to the subsequent Site Development Plan and Building Plan stages.
But while co-developer Atterbury publicly described the application as an “inconsequential” 280m² boundary correction and claimed Equinix’s involvement was purely speculative, the appeal response submitted by Planning Partners explicitly confirms Equinix as the primary party driving the development.
“In August, Equinix’s South Africa MD said there was a ‘misnomer’ in the public perception of data centres’ consumption of critical resources,” Daniel Hartford, the South African lead for UK legal advocacy non-profit Foxglove, explained in response to Daily Maverick’s questions about the rebuttal.
Foxglove and the Legal Resources Centre (LRC) made the Paia request for the document after the City decided to handle the appeal hearing behind closed doors.
“Since then, his company’s response to Foxglove’s appeal has been revealed. It confirms – despite repeated denials to the press – that Equinix is indeed behind the planning application. It says this in black and white on the second page of Equinix’s appeal response. When the audience was the City, the site was Equinix’s data centre. When the audience was journalists and the public, it was 280 square metres of nothing in particular.”
In October 2024, the City approved the site for the first data centre (Erf 180444) under General Industry 1 (GI1) zoning. At the time, the Development Management Scheme contained no mention or definition of a “data centre”. As Daily Maverick reported previously, the City treated data centres as a primary permitted right under General Industry 1 by interpreting digital data as “goods stored in a warehouse”.
In 2025, Baker & McKenzie and senior counsel challenged this interpretation. They advised Equinix that categorising a data centre as a warehouse storing physical goods would not withstand legal scrutiny under standard statutory interpretation.
Equinix formally notified the City that due to the multi-hundred-million-rand investment required, it would not proceed with the development without explicit statutory legal certainty.
Data centre deal — Cape Town forced back to the drawing board
To resolve the legal concerns, the City initiated an amendment to the Municipal Planning By-law (read: Development Management Scheme). Passed by Council on 26 June 2026 and coming into full operation on 1 October 2026, the amendment inserted explicit definitions into municipal law:
Definition of ‘data centre’: “ ‘data centre’ means a building or dedicated space within a building or a group of buildings used to store computer systems and associated components, such as telecommunication and storage systems;”
Amended definition of ‘warehouse’: “ ‘Warehouse’ means a building used primarily for the storage of goods, except those that are offensive or dangerous, and includes property used for a data centre or a business of a retail or wholesale nature;”
Amended definition of ‘business premises’: Explicitly updated to include “data centre” alongside shops and offices.
By linking “data centre” directly into the definitions of “warehouse” and “business premises”, data centres automatically now became a primary permitted right across all General Industry (GI1) and Mixed Use (MU1) properties city-wide without requiring individual rezoning or consent use approvals.
Wait, but what is the City’s stance?
Good question. Upon reviewing the evidence and gleaning conversations with the main characters in Geordin Hill-Lewis’ administration, the City of Cape Town is operating under an investor-focused “open for business” agenda, seeking to establish the metro as Africa’s premier digital hub. To secure hyperscale tech investments, the City has demonstrated extreme responsiveness – amending municipal planning laws, facilitating land swaps, and accepting upfront infrastructure contributions.
From an administrative perspective, it seems to be a done deal. Why? Because the record shows that:
The City has already accepted R33.3-million in Shared Network Charges from Equinix.
The executive mayor signed off on the underlying land swap in May 2026.
The City proactively altered its Municipal Planning By-law specifically to remove legal hurdles raised by Equinix’s attorneys.
The City has shielded Equinix’s appeal submissions from public scrutiny and held appeal advisory hearings in private.
The City has already approved five data centres across the metro, with two more under assessment.
The wildest disclosure in the 91-page rebuttal, however, is how it deals with the environmental authorisation (EA) and water usage rights.
KAI received an environmental authorisation from the Western Cape Department of Environmental Affairs and Development Planning on 11 May 2018 for a generic mixed-use industrial park.
The project Environmental Assessment Practitioner (Chand Consultants) asserts that data centres fit inside this broad baseline envelope.
A new Nema Environmental Impact Assessment will only be triggered at the Site Development Plan stage if detailed designs exceed specific thresholds – such as backup diesel generator capacity exceeding 10MW under Listing Notice 2.
KAI holds a General Authorisation issued under Section 21(c) and 21(i) of the National Water Act on 15 March, 2018 for watercourse and wetland alterations. The Environmental Assessment Practitioner confirms that constructing the data centres remains within this General Authorisation scope and requires no new Water Use License Application.
The developer argues that detailed environmental, water, and energy assessments belong strictly to the future Site Development Plan stage under a “Package of Plans” framework. The Legal Resources Centre (LRC) counters that deferring these critical studies leaves communities unprotected while offering no legally binding commitments on green energy or water security.
“On cooling and renewables it contradicts itself: air-source cooling is ‘confirmed’ and ‘not yet finalised’; renewable PPAs are ‘confirmed’ and ‘will be decided upon at a later date’… Nothing binds the applicant,” was what the LRC had to say in response to Daily Maverick’s inquiry.
Following the conclusion of the appeal panel hearing, the appellants are awaiting the final ruling from the Appeal Authority (none other than City of Cape Town Executive Mayor Geordin Hill-Lewis).
The LRC says that it is now focusing on the appeals process. Once a decision has been made, they will consider their options and determine the most appropriate route to take the matter forward.
One option may involve a review challenge in the high court under Paja [Promotion of Administrative Justice Act]. However, their approach will depend on the decision of the mayor and other circumstances at that stage.
“South Africa needs a discussion about digital infrastructure: about why it is needed, who it is for, who will pay the cost and how it will affect us,” says Foxglove’s Hartford.
“It is disappointing that instead of being transparent about its plans... Equinix has chosen – through omission and contradiction – to deepen the very confusion it has complained about publicly. Capetonians deserve better.” DM
